#35750. Trump weighs Iran deal or military action as Netanyahu warns of attacks

US President Donald Trump said Sunday he was weighing whether to reach a deal with Iran or take further military action, while Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu warned Tehran against launching attacks to disrupt Israel's upcoming parliamentary elections.

"Do I make a deal with them or do I finish them off? That's the only question," Trump told Fox News in an interview aired Sunday.

Trump said the United States now controlled the Strait of Hormuz amid Washington's naval blockade of Iran.

"We now control the Hormuz Strait. We get everything, they get nothing," he said.

However, Trump ruled out an immediate attack on Iran when questioned by reporters before departing the White House for Michigan.

"The answer is no. There will not be a strike today," he said.

In Israel, Netanyahu said his government had intelligence indicating that Iran and its allied groups might launch attacks to interfere with Tuesday's vote.

"We have intelligence signs that our enemies, Iran and its proxies, could challenge us with attacks in order to disrupt the elections," Netanyahu said in a video released by his office Sunday.

Speaking at an Arrow anti-ballistic missile battery, Netanyahu said Israel's military was prepared for both defensive and offensive operations.

"Don't test us. You will suffer disproportionate blows," he warned. "We are much stronger than you think."

Earlier Sunday, Netanyahu shared an AI-generated image depicting a nuclear explosion over Tel Aviv, alongside a post by right-wing commentator Yuval Bloomberg warning that Iran acquiring nuclear weapons could pose an existential threat to Israel.

The post warned that electing a leader unable to confront Iran could expose Israelis to the danger of a "second Holocaust."

The statements from both leaders came as diplomatic efforts to reduce tensions continued.

Qatari mediators were in Tehran on Sunday as part of a US-coordinated effort to ease regional tensions, Reuters reported, citing an official briefed on the situation.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is making regime change in Iran an explicit goal ahead of Israel’s election, while political rivals advocate tough measures against Tehran and criticize his failure to eliminate the Iranian threat.

The debate puts competing promises of security before voters whom analysts describe as exhausted by years of conflict, raising questions about what would constitute victory and how far Israel would go to achieve it.

“We must complete the elimination of the Iranian regime — that is the primary objective,” Netanyahu said Tuesday at Tel Hai University in Kiryat Shmona, near the Lebanese border.

Netanyahu has long welcomed the prospect of the Islamic Republic’s collapse. Now, with Israelis voting on October 27, he is placing the removal of Iran’s leadership at the forefront of his message.

Netanyahu argued that weakening Iran militarily would not guarantee Israel’s security. As long as the Islamic Republic remains in power, he said, it will attempt to rebuild its nuclear capabilities and regional network.

“Finishing the job means bringing down the terrorist regime in Iran,” Netanyahu said, describing Tehran as the head of a “poisonous octopus” whose removal, he argued, would also bring down Hezbollah in Lebanon.

The declaration followed discussions with US President Donald Trump and an unannounced visit by US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. Washington, however, has not publicly committed to regime change, emphasizing instead the prevention of a nuclear-armed Iran.

Netanyahu’s declaration comes as he seeks another term following three years of war and repeated military confrontations with Iran and its regional allies.

Itai Reuveni, director of communications and outreach at NGO Monitor, said the prime minister was articulating what many Israelis had already understood to be the broader ambition behind military operations against Tehran.

“I think he just summarized all the things that everyone meant,” Reuveni told Iran International.

Making regime change the declared objective raises questions about whether weakening Iran’s military and nuclear capabilities would be sufficient for Netanyahu to claim victory.

Yaakov Katz, former editor-in-chief of The Jerusalem Post and author of four books on Israel’s military, said repeated strikes alone cannot permanently eliminate the Iranian threat.

“You can bomb them, you can destroy facilities, you can set back nuclear programs, but they will rebuild,” Katz told Iran International.

Netanyahu is presenting regime change as the route to lasting Israeli security, a message delivered in Kiryat Shmona, a historically Likud-supporting community repeatedly targeted by Hezbollah.

Vivian Bercovici, Canada’s former ambassador to Israel and founder and editor-in-chief of State of Tel Aviv, said the location allowed Netanyahu to appeal directly to voters who have experienced the consequences of Iran’s regional influence.

But she questioned whether the declaration would persuade Israelis beyond his existing supporters.

“I really think that people have tuned him out,” she said.

Those interviewed described opposition to the Islamic Republic as extending across much of Israel’s political spectrum, while drawing a distinction between agreement on the threat and enthusiasm for another military confrontation.

“It’s the one issue on which there’s no daylight in Israel,” Bercovici said.

Yet she described a public exhausted by years of fighting.

“I don’t think that Israel has any appetite for war,” she said. “We’ve had way too much war in the last three years.”

Reuveni described a similar tension. Many Israelis believe Iran’s immediate military threat has diminished following Israeli and American strikes, he said, complicating the case for further military action.

“People are tired from the war,” he said.

Katz said the election ultimately comes down to which leader Israelis trust to protect them, rather than any single declaration about Iran.

“What is important is the belief in which leader do Israelis think can keep them safe,” he said.

Does Netanyahu’s declaration set him apart?

Netanyahu’s explicit objective does not necessarily distinguish him from his political rivals, several of whom have advocated aggressive measures against Tehran and criticized his failure to eliminate the Iranian threat.

Former prime ministers Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid are contesting the election together under the joint list Together (Beyachad).

Lapid has advocated striking Iran’s energy infrastructure, including Kharg Island, while Bennett has long promoted confronting Tehran directly rather than focusing on its regional proxies.

Gadi Eisenkot, the former military chief who leads the centrist Yashar party, has questioned whether regime change is achievable through military action, emphasizing the permanent dismantling of Iran’s nuclear capabilities.

Avigdor Lieberman, leader of Yisrael Beiteinu, has also advocated overthrowing the Islamic Republic and criticized previous Israeli efforts as insufficient.

Eric Mandel, founder and director of the Middle East Political and Information Network, said the broad agreement on Iran means a change of government in Israel would not necessarily produce a fundamental shift in policy.

“I think most Israelis know that it doesn’t matter who’s going to get elected, they’re going to have the same policy in Iran,” Mandel told Iran International.

But agreement on the threat is different from agreement on how to eliminate it.

Mandel said achieving regime change would require American involvement, underscoring the gap between Netanyahu’s declared ambition and Washington’s publicly stated objectives.

“Israel is a regional power, America is a superpower,” he said. “Israel could be very helpful, but Israel can’t do it on its own.”

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said on Tuesday that toppling Iran’s regime was Israel’s “primary objective,” a day after discussing Iran with US War Secretary Pete Hegseth during an unannounced visit to Israel.

Netanyahu said he had also discussed bringing down Iran’s leadership with US President Donald Trump on Sunday, placing the issue at the center of his latest contacts with Washington.

“We must complete the elimination of the Iranian regime — that is the primary objective,” Netanyahu said at the opening of the academic year at the new Tel Hai University in Kiryat Shmona, near the Lebanese border.

“I have spoken about this with President Trump more than once, including the day before yesterday.”

His remarks did not indicate whether Trump had agreed to pursue that objective or committed to further military action.

Danny Citrinowicz, an Iran specialist and former head of the Iran branch in Israeli Defense Intelligence, told Iran International that while the two leaders might agree on military targets, their strategic objectives could diverge.

"Netanyahu seeks to topple the regime, and Trump seeks to reach a good agreement with the same regime that Netanyahu seeks to topple," he said.

Hegseth discussed Iran with Netanyahu on Monday, three Israeli officials told Reuters. Netanyahu’s spokesman, Doron Spielman, confirmed that they met at Uvda air force base in Israel’s southern Negev desert.

Spielman said the talks covered regional threats and US-Israeli cooperation in confronting them through offensive and defensive measures.

Hegseth also thanked Israel for hosting US forces, which Spielman said numbered in the thousands, and discussed Trump’s support for Netanyahu.

Speaking on Tuesday, Netanyahu linked his stated objective in Iran to Israel’s campaign against Hezbollah, saying the military had made major progress against the Lebanese group but pledging to “finish the job.”

“Finishing the job means bringing down the terrorist regime in Iran. It is the head of this poisonous octopus. You cut it off, and it will fall. We will also have peace with Lebanon,” he said.

Netanyahu argued that Iran’s leadership, even “battered, wounded and beaten,” would seek to pursue nuclear weapons and rebuild its regional network of allied armed groups.

“Therefore, the only way to prevent this is to bring down this regime, and then the elimination of Hezbollah will follow,” he said.

The Hegseth meeting came eight days before Israel’s October 27 election. Trump endorsed Netanyahu on Sunday, ahead of the country’s first parliamentary vote since the October 7, 2023, Hamas attack.

In his endorsement message, Trump praised Netanyahu’s role in confronting Iran and warned that Washington might have to act alone if another leader took office.

US and Israeli forces launched joint strikes against Iran in late February, setting off a wider regional war. The latest consultations come amid renewed tensions between Washington and Tehran over the Strait of Hormuz and intensifying attacks by Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis on Saudi Arabia.

Washington and Tehran may still reach a limited deal, but fundamental disagreements leave open the prospect of renewed escalation, analysts told Iran International, with the period after elections in Israel and the United States emerging as a potential turning point.

Diplomatic efforts are continuing, with Qatar and Pakistan pushing for an agreement and The New Arab reporting Monday, citing sources familiar with mediation efforts, that a breakthrough could be announced this week.

The analysts interviewed by Iran International were more cautious, however, seeing little evidence that either side has made the concessions required for a broader agreement and identifying the coming elections as a factor that could shape the timing of diplomacy or renewed military action.

Danny Citrinowicz, an Iran specialist and former head of the Iran branch in Israeli Defense Intelligence, said continuing diplomatic exchanges did not amount to evidence of an imminent breakthrough because neither side appeared ready to make the compromise required for one.

"In order to have a breakthrough, one side needs to show significant compromise. And I don't see that in the Iranian side," he told Iran International.

Washington wants substantial restrictions on Iran's uranium enrichment capabilities, while Tehran is prioritizing relief from the US blockade and sanctions, alongside the restoration of maritime traffic through the Strait of Hormuz.

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Sunday that Tehran's seven-day proposal remained on the table. Under the proposal, Iran would reopen the strait within seven days if Washington accepted Tehran's conditions, paving the way for renewed negotiations.

Alex Vatanka, director of the Iran Program at the Middle East Institute, saw greater scope for a limited arrangement than a comprehensive settlement, arguing that both Trump and Tehran have short-term incentives to reduce tensions without resolving their fundamental differences.

Trump, he argued, faces political pressure ahead of the November 3 midterm elections and could benefit from a diplomatic achievement. Tehran, meanwhile, needs economic relief as the blockade continues to undermine its finances.

"You might have a deal that could create ceasefire conditions for a short period of time, of weeks and months," Vatanka told Iran International.

But he said he had seen little indication that Tehran was willing to accept the kind of comprehensive agreement Trump could present as a major improvement over the 2015 nuclear deal.

Iran's leadership, Vatanka argued, believes it has paid a heavy price for its nuclear program while demonstrating its ability to disrupt the global economy through the Strait of Hormuz. Economic pressures could encourage a narrow agreement, but sweeping concessions risk exposing divisions within the Islamic Republic's leadership.

The diplomatic activity comes as US President Donald Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu have intensified warnings of renewed military action.

On Sunday, Trump threatened to "soon finish the job" against Iran unless Tehran changed course, while giving Netanyahu his endorsement ahead of Israel's October 27 election.

Netanyahu, who has explicitly identified the removal of the Islamic Republic as an Israeli objective, has said Israel is prepared to act independently of Washington if necessary.

On Monday, Netanyahu released a video of a telephone conversation with Trump following the US president's endorsement of his reelection campaign.

"Donald, we have a job to finish, you said it, and we'll finish it together. We'll finish it, and no one else will do it," Netanyahu told Trump.

Shayan Samii, a geopolitical and national security analyst, said Trump's combination of negotiations and military threats allowed him to preserve both outcomes: claiming a diplomatic victory if talks succeed or demonstrating resolve through military action if they fail.

"The United States wants to keep the diplomatic avenue still open and valid. Why? Because it helps for domestic political purposes," Samii told Iran International.

"It allows Trump to say, I'm giving diplomacy all the chances in the world, but at the same time I'm keeping the pressure on them."

He also interpreted Trump's endorsement of Netanyahu as an attempt to increase Washington's leverage over the Israeli leader should he remain in power.

Samii suggested Iran or its regional allies could provoke a confrontation ahead of Israel's election, potentially providing a pretext for renewed strikes. He presented this as a possible scenario, not evidence of a planned operation.

Russia could influence the diplomatic track

Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov's visit to Tehran on Monday added another dimension to the diplomatic maneuvering.

Vatanka said Russia possesses considerably greater leverage over Iran than mediators such as Pakistan, Qatar or Oman, partly because Tehran depends on Moscow for diplomatic support.

That influence could become significant if negotiations require difficult concessions, including a possible arrangement to transfer Iran's highly enriched uranium to Russia.

But Vatanka questioned whether Moscow's interests necessarily aligned with Tehran's.

Russia would mediate "primarily to use it to get what Putin wants from Trump on the Ukraine front," he said.

Vatanka suggested Moscow could seek concessions from Washington over Ukraine in exchange for helping facilitate an agreement with Iran.

Tehran, however, may resist being used as a bargaining chip, particularly if Russian pressure requires abandoning positions the Islamic Republic considers fundamental.

Why the post-election period could prove decisive

If diplomacy fails to produce a breakthrough, Citrinowicz sees renewed escalation as increasingly difficult to avoid — but the elections may affect when it happens.

"With no breakthroughs, escalation is inevitable, because the status quo is unstable," he said.

He cautioned, however, that inevitable did not necessarily mean imminent.

The upcoming elections could influence the timing of any military operation. Israelis vote on October 27, followed by the US midterms on November 3.

Citrinowicz identified the period after the November 3 US midterms but before the newly elected Congress takes office in January as a possible window for military action, particularly if Republicans lose control of one or both chambers.

Vatanka similarly identified the post-election period as a potential turning point, arguing that Washington and Israel could consider additional pressure against Tehran once immediate electoral calculations had passed.

He said options could include continued enforcement of the blockade, limited military strikes and other measures designed to weaken or divide the Iranian establishment.

Yet the prospect of renewed military action raises a deeper question: whether Trump and Netanyahu ultimately seek the same outcome.

Citrinowicz argued that while the two leaders might agree on military targets, their strategic objectives could diverge.

"Netanyahu seeks to topple the regime, and Trump seeks to reach a good agreement with the same regime that Netanyahu seeks to topple," he said.

"Operationally, maybe there will be eye to eye in terms of what to attack, but strategically, I'm not sure if they see eye to eye."

That divergence leaves a central question unresolved: even if Washington and Israel agree on another round of strikes, they may not agree on what those strikes are ultimately meant to achieve.

Iranian military officials warned of a stronger response to any renewed US attack on Monday, as Russia's foreign minister visited Tehran for talks and regional security concerns grew following Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia.

Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov met his Iranian counterpart Abbas Araghchi during an official visit, with talks also planned with President Masoud Pezeshkian.

The visit came as Iranian officials discussed the prospect of renewed fighting with the United States and the country's military capabilities.

The Revolutionary Guards said that Iran would respond more forcefully to any renewed US military action.

“The US entered the war with all its might, and it is certainly not in a position now to start a new conflict that would bring it any new gains,” Revolutionary Guards spokesman Hossein Mohebi said on Monday.

Mohebi said most US bases in the region were inactive and American forces had moved hundreds of kilometers away from Iran.

Revolutionary Guards deputy commander Mostafa Izadi said US naval forces had moved approximately 700 kilometers away to avoid Iranian missiles, according to the Guards-affiliated Fars news agency.

Senior Guards adviser Mohammadreza Naghdi separately said Iran's missile facilities had survived heavy bombardment and its strategic stockpiles remained intact.

Germany summoned Iran's ambassador on Monday over attempted attacks targeting Josef Schuster, head of the Central Council of Jews in Germany, and Volker Beck, chairman of the German-Israeli Society.

“Attacks on Jewish life and on those who defend it are something we will not tolerate - anywhere, and especially not in Germany,” the German Foreign Ministry wrote on X.

The ministry condemned Iran's activities and said the attempted attacks would have legal consequences.

Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar also criticized Araghchi after the Iranian foreign minister accused French President Emmanuel Macron of supporting US military action against Iran.

Sa'ar accused Iran of suppressing protesters at home while criticizing France over its response to unrest.

Saudi Arabia's Civil Defense said the danger had passed in the southern Najran region after an earlier alert over a potential threat.

The announcement followed a Houthi attack on a Yemeni government military camp in Shabwa province that killed at least 18 people, Reuters reported, citing government and medical sources.

The US State Department urged Americans across the Middle East to exercise heightened vigilance, warning that Houthi attacks could disrupt flights and airspace.

The US Embassy in Riyadh separately warned that Iran and groups supporting it could target American interests overseas.

The prospect of renewed conflict has also affected economic activity, according to an Iranian lawmaker.

“When conditions are unstable, no one can make decisions about their life and future; they cannot make a deal, invest or take action,” Mohammadmehdi Shahriari, a member of parliament's national security committee, said on Monday.

Shahriari said proposals for negotiations with Washington had been raised and officials should be allowed to formulate a response.

Another lawmaker, Mohammad Rashidi, rejected suggestions that Iran's economy was approaching collapse under US pressure.

Meanwhile, Iran Air chief executive Taher Abdolhay said the national airline had only six operational aircraft despite employing more than 9,000 people, down from a fleet of 40.

Abdolhay cited operational restrictions and air traffic difficulties, adding that the airline had faced obstacles to flights intended to bring medicine into Iran.

The developments featured the competing pressures facing Iran, with officials emphasizing military preparedness and diplomatic engagement as concerns over renewed fighting continue to affect regional security and economic activity.

US President Donald Trump on Sunday warned Washington could “soon finish the job” against Iran unless Tehran changed course, as Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Israel was prepared to strike Iran without US support and vowed to bring down Tehran’s government.

“Unless they change their ways, rapidly, we will soon finish the job,” Trump wrote in a post on Truth Social, after saying Iran had been “systematically destroyed, both Militarily and Financially.”

Addressing the people of Israel directly, Trump pointed to Tehran’s long-standing slogans of “Death to Israel, Death to America,” saying it had only been a matter of time before Iran sought to act on such threats.

He endorsed Netanyahu for re-election in Israel’s October 27 parliamentary vote, calling him a “Great Warrior Prime Minister” and an “even greater Partner for Peace in combatting the Islamic Republic of Iran.”

He said that if Israel were led by “anyone other than Bibi,” the United States would have to take on the work against Iran itself, adding that he was “not inclined to do so.”

Trump gave Netanyahu his “Complete and Total Endorsement” for re-election and praised him as “Strong, Brave, and Brilliant.”

Netanyahu thanked Trump on X, saying: “Together we will complete the mission!”

Israelis will vote on October 27 in the country’s first national election since the Hamas-led October 7, 2023 attack. The prime minister is not directly elected but emerges through coalition-building in the 120-seat Knesset.

Trump did not say what further action against Iran he had in mind. Earlier this month, he said the United States would not attack Iran before the November 3 US midterm elections and said Washington and Tehran were having “productive discussions.”

His latest comments come after he and Netanyahu discussed the possibility of a new military operation against Iran, according to Axios, which reported last week that the Israeli leader raised concerns about intelligence suggesting Tehran was trying to rebuild its nuclear program.

Netanyahu says Israel can strike Iran without US support

Separately on Sunday, Netanyahu said Israel was prepared to launch a preemptive strike against Iran without US support and that his objectives regarding Tehran did not depend on Washington’s approval.

“The objectives I set do not depend on American approval,” Netanyahu said as he presented an updated national security doctrine, according to Israel Hayom. “To the extent necessary, we will also act independently. We have done so before, and if necessary, we will do so again.”

Netanyahu described confronting Iran as his “life’s mission” and identified a nuclear-armed Iran as Israel’s greatest security threat. “We are prepared to take the initiative,” he said. “We must prevent the enemy from delivering the first blow.”

He said “90% of the job is done,” pointing to Iran’s economic crisis, recent protests and what he described as the government’s weakened position.

“We must bring this regime down once and for all,” Netanyahu said. “That is the directive I have given to all the security agencies.”

#35770. Saudi Arabia intercepts Houthi missiles, drones as Yemen fighting continues

Saudi Arabia intercepted drones and missiles over Riyadh and southern parts of the country on Sunday as fighting with Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis continued, the Saudi-led coalition said.

The coalition said two drones and a ballistic missile were launched toward Riyadh, while a cruise missile targeted Khamis Mushait in the south. It later said 10 ballistic missiles aimed at southern Saudi Arabia had also been intercepted.

Saudi civil defense authorities issued emergency alerts for Riyadh, Abha and Khamis Mushait before later saying the danger had passed.

Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport remained a “military target” and warned airlines, airport staff and travelers against using it.

The airport resumed operations at two terminals on Sunday after an October 10 attack, which the Houthis said they carried out, killed 13 people and wounded more than 300.

The Houthis also said they attacked the airport and Saudi oil facilities on Saturday. Saudi authorities did not directly confirm those assertions.

Fighting intensifies around Red Sea routes

Saudi Arabia has stepped up strikes against the Houthis after the group seized territory along Yemen’s Red Sea coast last month, bringing the fighting closer to the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a major global shipping route.

The renewed conflict has broken a UN-brokered truce that had largely held since 2022.

Saudi Arabia intervened in Yemen’s civil war in 2015 at the head of a coalition backing the internationally recognized government after the Houthis seized Sanaa the previous year.

Iran may be approaching a mental-health emergency as prolonged uncertainty over war, economic pressure and the future takes a growing toll on the public, the head of the country’s Psychology and Counseling Organization said on Sunday.

Asked by ILNA how far Iranian society was from a mental-health emergency, Alireza Agha-Yousefi said: “I don’t think we are very far from it.”

He pointed to marriage, divorce and birth rates as areas of concern and said authorities needed to act before psychological and social problems became more severe.

Agha-Yousefi said the prolonged state of neither full-scale war nor peace was itself becoming a major source of pressure.

“The overall condition of society in a situation of neither war nor peace can create significant psychological strain,” he said.

He said people normally try to meet their needs while also responding to threats, but when both are present at the same time, threats tend to dominate.

“Uncertainty about the future is one of the most difficult situations,” he said, adding that it deprives people of the ability to plan their lives.

Agha-Yousefi said prolonged uncertainty could produce severe anxiety and, over time, lead to both physical and psychological exhaustion.

He cautioned that the consequences of intense stress do not always appear immediately.

“The effects may show themselves one or two years later,” he said, citing depression, marital conflict and physical health problems as possible outcomes.

He also pointed to prolonged muscle tension, joint and spinal pain and gastrointestinal problems as conditions that can be associated with chronic stress.

President Masoud Pezeshkian last week also described the current “no war, no peace” situation as the worst position Iran could be in, as tensions with Washington remained unresolved.

Agha-Yousefi said the same economic conditions contributing to psychological strain were also making treatment less accessible.

He said demand for counselling had risen, but inflation and declining purchasing power meant many people could no longer afford psychological services.

“Psychological services are not covered by basic insurance,” he said, adding that official figures on the number of people seeking treatment could therefore give a misleading picture.

He said some people who need help simply do not seek it because of the cost.

A proposal to bring psychological services under insurance coverage had been submitted to the organization’s central council around four months ago but had yet to be approved, he said.

Pressure on families and social stability

Agha-Yousefi also said Iran appeared to be moving toward greater social dislocation.

“It seems our social situation is, to some extent, moving toward anomie or social normlessness,” he said.

He warned that as social stress rises, the effects can spread into family life and wider social behavior, including later marriage, addiction and greater instability within households.

“When problems enter the family, they can be a sign of deeper social damage,” he said.

He added that severe family pressures could, in some cases, contribute to extreme violence, including killings within families.

Agha-Yousefi said delaying preventive measures would make the psychological, physical and social consequences much harder and more expensive to address later.

His comments come as speculation grows over possible renewed US and Israeli military action against Iran.

Recent reports have said the US military has prepared options for further strikes after the November 3 midterm elections if President Donald Trump authorizes them.

That uncertainty has added another layer of pressure to an economy already strained by inflation, a weakening currency and declining purchasing power.

The war with Iran raises a familiar question for Israel: Can battlefield gains produce lasting peace? Its military history offers mixed answers, from unresolved victories to withdrawals and ceasefires that left adversaries armed.

Destroying Iran’s military capabilities and preventing their reconstruction are different objectives, requiring different measures of success.

Since 1948, Israel has fought conventional Arab armies and armed organizations such as Hezbollah and Hamas, and has increasingly confronted Iran directly through missile, drone and air attacks far beyond its borders. These forms of warfare have overlapped, posing different challenges for bringing the fighting to an end.

Their endings show how battlefield outcomes interact with diplomacy, outside pressure and arrangements for security after the fighting.

Fighting between Jewish and Arab communities followed the UN’s 1947 partition plan. After Israel declared independence in May 1948, neighboring Arab armies entered the conflict. Israel survived and gained territory beyond the boundaries proposed for the Jewish state.

In 1949, it signed separate armistice agreements with Egypt, Lebanon, Jordan and Syria. These established lines separating the forces, rather than permanent political settlements. The Egyptian agreement explicitly envisaged a subsequent peaceful settlement.

Israel’s survival did not resolve the territorial dispute or the displacement of Palestinians. The fighting ended without peace between Israel and its neighbors.

1956: Military gains, withdrawal under pressure

During the Suez crisis, Israel attacked Egypt in coordination with Britain and France, rapidly advancing across Sinai.

Pressure from the United States, the Soviet Union and the United Nations forced a withdrawal, completed in March 1957. Israel could not retain the territory it had captured, despite its battlefield success.

The outcome nevertheless brought security gains: Israel regained access to the Straits of Tiran, while a UN emergency force deployed in Sinai. The US State Department’s historical account distinguishes those gains from the territorial withdrawal.

The episode illustrates why withdrawal is not automatically evidence of military defeat, and why military superiority alone does not determine a war’s political outcome.

1967: Six days of fighting, decades of consequences

Israel’s opening airstrikes devastated Egypt’s air force. Within six days, Israeli forces had captured Sinai, Gaza, the West Bank, East Jerusalem and the Golan Heights.The war ended through ceasefires, without a formal surrender by the defeated Arab states. Israel’s decisive battlefield victory transformed the territorial balance but did not settle the conflict.

UN Security Council Resolution 242 subsequently established a framework linking Israeli withdrawal from occupied territory with an end to belligerency and recognition of states’ right to live within secure, recognized boundaries.

The military result was immediate. Disputes over occupation, borders and Palestinian rights lasted far beyond the fighting.

1973: From surprise attack to a peace treaty

Egypt and Syria attacked Israeli forces in Sinai and the Golan Heights in October 1973, initially making substantial gains. Israel counterattacked and crossed the Suez Canal before US-Soviet diplomacy and UN ceasefire resolutions helped stop the fighting.

The US State Department’s history describes the war as opening the way for Henry Kissinger’s shuttle diplomacy and, ultimately, the Egyptian-Israeli peace treaty. Egypt did not recover all Sinai through military action, but the war helped break the diplomatic stalemate.

The 1978 Camp David accords provided the framework for the 1979 treaty. Israel agreed to withdraw from Sinai in exchange for peace with Egypt. The main withdrawal was completed in 1982; the disputed Taba area was returned in 1989 following arbitration.

Egypt recovered territory through a combination of war and diplomacy. Israel exchanged territorial control for a political agreement with a major adversary.

Lebanon, 1982–2000: Initial success, prolonged conflict

Israel’s 1982 invasion drove into Beirut, where US-mediated arrangements secured the departure of Palestine Liberation Organization leaders and fighters. This was an evacuation from Beirut, not the elimination of every Palestinian armed presence in Lebanon.

Israel withdrew much of its force in 1985 but retained a southern security zone alongside the allied South Lebanon Army. Its remaining troops left in May 2000, following years of conflict with Hezbollah. UNIFIL’s historical account records both withdrawals.

The withdrawal was unilateral, without a peace treaty or formal Israeli surrender. Hezbollah portrayed it as a victory; Israel ended a prolonged deployment without resolving the underlying confrontation.

The departure of one armed organization’s leadership in 1982 had not produced a lasting end to fighting.

The 2006 war followed Hezbollah’s cross-border attack and capture of two Israeli soldiers. Israel launched extensive air and ground operations, but Hezbollah remained armed and continued firing rockets during the conflict.

Neither side’s survival or military performance alone explains the settlement. The operative mechanism was UN Security Council Resolution 1701, adopted on August 11, followed by a cessation of hostilities on August 14.

It called for Hezbollah to stop attacks, Israel to stop offensive operations, and Israeli forces to withdraw as Lebanese troops and an expanded UNIFIL deployed. It envisaged an area between the Blue Line and Litani River free of armed personnel and weapons other than those of the Lebanese government and UNIFIL.

Hezbollah was not disarmed. Nevertheless, UNIFIL says the arrangements helped sustain almost 17 years of relative calm before the escalation beginning in 2023. An incomplete settlement still had significant practical effects.

The Gaza wars of 2008–09, 2012, 2014 and 2021 ended without Hamas surrendering or losing all its military capabilities.

Scholars Efraim Inbar and Eitan Shamir described Israel’s approach as “mowing the grass”: periodically degrading an adversary’s capabilities and restoring deterrence rather than expecting a permanent political resolution through force. Their study appeared online in 2013 and in the Journal of Strategic Studies in 2014.

After Hamas’s October 7, 2023 attack, Israel set broader objectives, including dismantling its military and governing capabilities and recovering the hostages. Shamir argued that the attack marked a departure from the previous limited-campaign approach. That was his strategic assessment, rather than proof that eliminating Hamas was achievable.

The ensuing war devastated Gaza. The October 2025 ceasefire did not settle its future: a year later, the UN human rights office was still reporting killings despite the agreement.

Lebanon after 2023: Military damage and state authority

Israel’s 2024 campaign killed Hezbollah leader Hassan Nasrallah and other senior commanders, severely damaging its leadership. The fighting nevertheless moved toward a negotiated cessation of hostilities rather than formal surrender.

The US-French-brokered arrangement took effect on November 27, 2024, and again rested on implementing Resolution 1701, Lebanese state authority and Israeli withdrawal.

Disarmament remained contested. In October 2026, The Wall Street Journal reported that Hezbollah demanded the return of explosives seized by Lebanese authorities, illustrating the continuing struggle over weapons outside state control.

Iran: Ending operations or preventing reconstruction?

The June 2025 war involved Israeli attacks on Iranian military and nuclear targets and direct US strikes on Fordow, Natanz and Isfahan. US involvement therefore preceded the broader war of 2026.

Israel’s Foreign Ministry described the nuclear threat as “existential and imminent” in its account of the operation. That characterization was Israel’s stated justification, not an independently established finding that Iran possessed nuclear weapons. The same document records Israel’s acceptance of a US-proposed ceasefire on June 24.The broader confrontation in 2026 extended to shipping and energy supplies. By October, the US naval blockade and the standoff over reopening the Strait of Hormuz remained unresolved.

Netanyahu has explicitly advocated moving beyond containment. Addressing military cadets in February 2026, he declared there would be “no more containment of threats” and emphasized preemptive action. This supports describing a shift in his stated approach, without assuming a uniform doctrine across every Israeli institution.

Destroying launchers or facilities has measurable immediate effects. Preventing their reconstruction depends on industrial capacity, supply networks, political decisions and whatever monitoring or enforcement follows.

Within the approach of seeking to prevent Iran from rebuilding its military threat, two scenarios can be considered. Neither is a prediction or an exhaustive account of how the conflict might end.

The first is a military defeat sufficiently extensive to destroy much of Iran’s offensive capability and substantially constrain its reconstruction. Lasting results would depend on measures that prevent replenishment, rather than destruction alone.The second combines military defeat with the end of the Islamic Republic and its replacement by a political system that abandons hostility toward Israel and support for armed proxies.

That scenario depends on more than a change of leadership. It assumes a successor government both chooses and can enforce a different policy, including ending financial, military and operational support for allied armed groups. A government’s collapse would not itself establish those conditions.

The scenarios may overlap, but neither guarantees stability. Their outcomes would depend on political authority, security arrangements and the capacity to enforce commitments after combat ends.

Other possible outcomes include a negotiated agreement that constrains Iran’s capabilities without changing its government, or a prolonged armed standoff sustained by deterrence. Neither would necessarily eliminate the underlying hostility, though either could bring the current fighting to an end.

Israel’s earlier wars provide different benchmarks: territorial withdrawal under international pressure in 1956, land exchanged for peace with Egypt, unilateral withdrawal from Lebanon, and ceasefire arrangements that reduced fighting without disarming Hezbollah. Each ended a particular phase of conflict; only some produced a broader political settlement.

Tehran has offered to reopen the Strait of Hormuz if Washington lifted its naval blockade, Iran’s envoy to Pakistan said Saturday, while an IRGC-affiliated outlet rejected such an exchange and President Donald Trump raised the possibility of strikes as soon as “tomorrow.”

Iran’s ambassador to Islamabad, Reza Amiri Moghadam, said Tehran had conveyed through Pakistani mediators that it was prepared to reopen the strait if Washington ended its blockade of Iranian ports, the Associated Press reported.

Speaking at a seminar in Islamabad, Moghadam said Iranian officials had communicated that position during visits to Tehran by Pakistan’s army chief, Field Marshal Asim Munir. He accused Trump of rejecting the proposal by insisting the blockade would continue.

Moghadam said Iran remained open to negotiations under a Pakistan-brokered interim agreement reached in June, according to AP’s readout of his remarks.

Pakistan and Qatar helped broker that framework, which envisaged restoring shipping through the strait, lifting the blockade and beginning negotiations on a broader deal covering Iran’s nuclear program.

Al Arabiya separately reported Saturday, citing unnamed sources, that Iran had informed Pakistan it was willing to resume negotiations with Washington and reopen the strait in exchange for the blockade being lifted.

But the IRGC-affiliated Tasnim news agency quoted an informed source rejecting Al Arabiya’s account as “lies and fantasy” and saying Tehran had made no new proposal to Pakistani mediators.

“Iran fundamentally does not accept any equation of the Strait of Hormuz in exchange for the blockade,” the source said, adding that Iran would find ways around the blockade and ultimately break it.

The source said Tehran stood by seven conditions already formally conveyed through mediators. An earlier “seven-day plan” setting out its demands for reopening the strait had been passed to Washington, the source said, adding that insecurity would persist until all Iranian demands were met, including an end to disruption of its ports and shipping.

Tasnim’s denial explicitly targeted Al Arabiya’s report, rather than the ambassador’s remarks reported by AP.

Trump, meanwhile, kept open the possibility of both military action and an agreement, saying he wanted a permanent solution to prevent Iran from developing a nuclear weapon.

“Do you really think I’m going to tell you if I’m going to do it?” Trump told reporters Saturday. “There’s a possibility I will. There’s also a possibility we’ll have a nice big beautiful agreement.”

He said Iranian leaders wanted a deal but questioned whether they would abide by it.

“They want to make a deal. But the problem is, will they hold the deal?”

Trump argued that ending the military campaign after B-2 bomber strikes in 2025 would have allowed Iran to rebuild its nuclear capabilities and eventually develop a bomb.

“I’ve got to make it permanent. That’s the only reason I’m doing it as long as I’m doing,” he said.

The Hill reported Saturday, citing two sources familiar with the planning, that the US military had prepared options for renewed strikes on Iran after November’s midterm elections.

One source said US Central Command had follow-up strike plans ready pending White House authorization. Another said multiple options were being presented to War Secretary Pete Hegseth and that Trump would keep his options open until a final decision was required.

A Pentagon official told The Hill the department’s “job is to develop and present military options to the President.”

The Wall Street Journal reported earlier in the day that US naval forces are preparing for possible renewed strikes against Iran, with sailors loading munitions and readying aircraft aboard American warships.

The preparations include the USS George Washington aircraft carrier strike group, as Washington considers further military action against the Islamic Republic.

Baghdad’s pledge to stay out of renewed fighting is being tested by reported Israeli jet flights toward Iran through Iraqi airspace, suspected strikes on militia stores reportedly holding Chinese-made air defenses, and drone attacks on Iranian Kurdish opposition bases.

Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi says Iraq will not participate in any war, while Iran-backed factions describe supporting Tehran against the United States and Israel as a duty, raising questions over Baghdad’s ability to control how its territory and airspace are used.

“Iraq will not participate in any war,” Zaidi told state-run Al-Iraqiya television on Friday, saying Baghdad wanted to remain a meeting point for regional rivals and was working to ease the confrontation between Iran and the United States.

On Saturday, the Islamic Resistance in Iraq, an umbrella of Iran-aligned armed factions, declared that standing with Tehran was a moral duty and portrayed the conflict as a struggle between righteousness and falsehood, Rudaw reported.

The statement did not announce a resumption of attacks. It underscored the factions’ commitment to Iran at a time when Zaidi is promising to bring weapons and military decisions under state control.

Baghdad also faces economic and diplomatic costs from the conflict. Zaidi said disruption at the Strait of Hormuz had harmed Iraq and that his government had hoped its political, religious and popular ties with Iran would secure an exemption for Iraqi shipping.

He stressed the importance of relations with Saudi Arabia and other Persian Gulf states, saying some believed attacks against them had originated in Iraq.

Reports of Israeli fighter jet activity near the Iranian border have put Iraqi airspace at the center of the confrontation even as Baghdad seeks to avoid direct involvement.

Axios reported this week that dozens of Israeli fighter jets flew toward Iran’s border in a demonstration of military capability. The aircraft passed through Syrian and Iraqi airspace before turning back near Iran.

Hardline Iranian lawmaker Mahmoud Nabavian demanded that Iraq tale action against the flights, alleging they were preparations for an attack on Iran.

“The Iraqi government must explain why the Zionist regime’s fighter jets are training and preparing to attack Iran in Iraqi airspace,” Nabavian wrote on X.

“If no action is taken, the Iraqi people, Iraq’s resistance groups and the Iranian nation will fulfill their duty,” he added, without specifying what action he meant.

His warning invoked Iraqi armed groups as potential actors alongside Iran if Baghdad failed to respond.

The Islamic Resistance in Iraq has separately accused US forces of conducting 171 violations of Iraqi airspace between September 30 and October 23.

The umbrella group alleged on Saturday that the United States was using military bases in Jordan and Turkey to conduct flights over Nineveh, Duhok, Erbil, Salahuddin, Anbar and Kirkuk provinces.

It said it had detected 17 aircraft on Friday, including reconnaissance drones and specialized aircraft. The figures and allegations were the factions’ account.

The dispute over foreign military flights also complicates efforts to restrain militia operations. When Iran-backed Kataib Hezbollah announced a suspension of military operations on September 30, it excluded responses to what it called hostile aircraft and airspace violations until Iraqi government air defenses were fully established, Asharq Al-Awsat reported.

Iraqi officials suspect Israel attacked two sites storing Chinese-made man-portable air defense systems recently transferred from Iran to Iraqi factions, Awsat reported Saturday, citing unnamed sources.

The sources said a large shipment was destroyed shortly after arriving at the facilities.

On October 17, the Iran-backed Popular Mobilization Forces reported an explosion at an ammunition storage facility in eastern Baghdad that injured five people. Its initial account pointed to an internal malfunction.

The newspaper also quoted an Iraqi political adviser as saying intelligence officials were examining whether renewed US-Israeli fighting against Iran had already begun covertly on Iraqi soil, targeting weapons shipments to Tehran-aligned groups.

Israeli responsibility and the reported contents of the warehouses remain unconfirmed. The suspected strikes nevertheless raise the prospect that Iraqi factions could become targets in renewed fighting regardless of Baghdad’s stated position.

Zaidi presented his campaign to bring weapons under government control as a test of whether the Iraqi state could exercise sovereignty.

“Are we a state with factions, or factions with a state?” he said in the television interview.

He said his government had reached understandings with five factions, completing arrangements with three and working to finalize them with two others. Discussions were continuing with another two, he said.

Zaidi pledged that no weapons would remain outside state control by June 30, 2027.

That deadline represents an extension of an earlier September target, and some factions have disputed the government’s account of progress.

Rudaw reported on October 19 that Kataib Hezbollah had described negotiations over its weapons as remaining at “square one,” accusing Zaidi of failing to respond to a proposed agreement.

The group also demanded clarification of Baghdad’s positions on US sanctions against Iran and conflicts elsewhere in the region, tying the weapons dispute to issues beyond Iraq’s borders.

A separate drone attack on Saturday highlighted the exposure of Iraq’s Kurdistan Region, where Iranian Kurdish opposition groups have repeatedly come under fire.

An explosive-laden drone struck a camp northeast of Erbil, Reuters reported, citing security sources.

The Kurdistan Komala Party of Iran said one of its bases in the Alana Valley was hit, causing material damage but no casualties. The available account did not establish who launched the drone.

Iran has repeatedly launched missile and drone strikes against Iranian Kurdish opposition groups based in northern Iraq, accusing them of organizing attacks and fueling unrest inside Iran.

Baghdad agreed in 2023 to disarm the groups and relocate them away from the Iranian border.

The groups also figured in discussions about a possible ground offensive after the US-Israeli war began in February. Reuters reported in March that Iranian Kurdish factions had consulted Washington about attacking Iranian security forces in the country’s west, although it could not establish the extent of CIA involvement or whether US weapons had been supplied.

Trump initially welcomed the prospect of Kurdish fighters crossing into Iran, telling Reuters on March 5 that it would be “wonderful.” Two days later, he said he had told them to stay out.

“They’re willing to go in, but we really—I’ve told them I don’t want them to go in,” Trump told reporters. “The war is complicated enough without having, getting the Kurds involved.”

Nazanin Sharifian, an Iran-born former Mossad officer running for Israel’s parliament with Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar party, told Iran International that Israel should step up military and economic pressure on the Islamic Republic’s leaders and work to end their rule.

“We must do everything we can to bring down the leaders of the Islamic Republic, so this regime is gone and the people of Iran are free,” she told Iran International’s Babak Eshaghi.

Sharifian, a Persian speaker who was born in Iran in 1982 and lived there until she was seven, is a candidate for the Knesset in Tuesday’s election. If Yashar joins the next coalition, she could hold a role in government.

Sharifian called the Islamic Republic Israel’s greatest enemy and an enemy of Iranians as well. Iran’s wealth, she said, goes to Hezbollah and the Houthis instead of to the people it belongs to.

Asked what Yashar’s policy toward Tehran would be, she said it would continue the course set by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, Eisenkot’s main rival.

“We must intensify this pressure on the leaders of the Islamic Republic,” she said. “We do not want to put pressure on the people of Iran. The people of Iran are the last hope of Iran.”

She called for every available means to be used to end the Islamic Republic’s rule. “I have great faith in the people of Iran,” she said.

Her emphasis on pressure differs from her party leader’s. Eisenkot, a former military chief, said this month that the Islamic Republic’s fall is necessary but cannot be achieved by military action, and that it must come from within Iranian society.

Sharifian was born into a Jewish family. After the 1979 revolution, some relatives left for the United States and Israel, but her father, who ran businesses in Tehran and Isfahan, refused at first to leave. The family fled when she was seven.

In Israel she served in the army, then in the Shin Bet internal security service and the Mossad, Israel’s foreign intelligence agency. Her Persian, she said, was one reason she was moved to the Mossad. She has since taught Persian and Middle East strategy to hundreds of Israeli students.

“I am very proud that my being is Iranian,” she said. Representing Iranians in Israel would be a great honor, she said, adding: “I expect to speak Persian in the Israeli parliament in the future.”

She hopes to bring more people of Iranian origin into Israel’s state institutions, she said, and that one day Iran will be returned to its people.

The trickiest part about making a tart like this one is sticking the landing on the crust. Timing is everything. #35772. Best Dashi Packets to Buy in Japan

Dashi packets are the simplest way to make Japanese soup stock. Steep one in simmering water, and in about five minutes, you have the base for miso soup, hot pots, rolled omelettes, and more. This guide covers which type to choose, where to find them, and what to cook once you get home.

This post may contain affiliate links. Please read my disclosure policy.

I know how overwhelming a first trip to Japan can be, especially when it comes to food. What’s worth buying? How do you use it once you’re home?

My Souvenir Cooking series is here to help. This series rounds up the best Japanese food souvenirs and teaches you how to use them in your own kitchen. This first post is all about dashi packets.

Dashi packets (だしパック) are one of my top souvenir recommendations for anyone visiting Japan. They’re light, shelf-stable, easy to pack, and the savory backbone of countless Japanese recipes. Think of dashi as Japan’s answer to beef or chicken stock.

I use these packets to add deep, savory flavor without simmering stock from scratch. I find them far better than instant dashi powder since most are additive- and salt-free for a flavor that’s close to homemade. Here’s what makes them worth the suitcase space:

Dashi packets are available in nearly any Japanese grocery store, but a few spots are especially worth seeking out.

Walking into any of these stores, whether a specialty shop or an all-purpose supermarket, will feel overwhelming but in the best way. Use this list to choose the right dashi packet for your desired recipes back home.

Shopping Tip: Look for the characters 無添加 (mutenka) on the package. This means “no additives.” These packets skip the MSG and preservatives, for a flavor closer to homemade dashi.

Once you are back home, replicating all the dishes you loved in Japan will be at the top of your list. Here is how to use a dashi packet—about five minutes start to finish:

Store leftover dashi in the refrigerator for up to 4 days.

For the video, a printable card, and the packet Nami buys herself, see her Dashi Packet recipe.

Once you’ve stocked up, try these recipes to put your dashi packets to use right away.

Keep unopened packages in a cool, dry pantry. Once opened, transfer to an airtight container such as an OXO container. Add the desiccant (silica gel) that comes with the dashi package to keep the packets dry.

Use within a few months for best flavor. Most packets have a best-by date (shōmi kigen, 賞味期限) printed on the package, usually 8 to 12 months out.

Once you’ve worked through all the dashi in your suitcase, look for more dashi packets at most Japanese grocery stores and Asian markets. Kayanoya and Yamasan packets are available on Amazon.

Yes. I recommend declaring them. Sealed, commercially packaged dashi is exactly what customs expects to see, and APHIS does not regulate most seafood, so bonito-based packets are fine. Declaring costs nothing; failing to declare is what causes problems. This is US guidance. Please check your own country’s rules.

Yes. Reuse it for a lighter second steep, ideal for cooking rice or a delicate vegetable soup. But it won’t be as flavorful as the first steep. A used packet is wet, so use it on the same day.

Most contain bonito or other dried fish, so they are neither vegan nor vegetarian. Look for kombu dashi or shiitake-based shojin dashi for plant-based options.

To make dashi broth, you do not open the packet directly into the boiling water. Some packets can be opened and used as a dry seasoning for dishes like fried rice, omelettes, and stir-fries.

Dashi packets steep like tea bags and produce a cleaner, more nuanced flavor. Dashi powder dissolves instantly but tends to taste flatter and saltier. If you have five minutes, the packet is worth it.

If you take one thing home from your trip to Japan, make it dashi packets. They’re inexpensive and light, and they’ll quickly transform your Japanese cooking into the real thing.

#35773. Blue Cheese Dressing

This is my classic Blue Cheese Dressing, a great all-rounder that I use for “everything”. It’s a dip, it’s a dressing, it’s a sauce! It’s loose enough to toss through your favourite salads, yet thick enough to cling to anything you dip into it. I can’t wait to show you how I make a big steak salad with this!

I know blue cheese is a little divisive but I’m firmly in the love-it camp! Especially in dressing / dip form. Not because the bold blue cheese flavour is mellowed, but because it becomes endlessly useable, beyond just cutting off huge hunks of cheese to balance on bread.

In this dressing form, it is thick enough so it clings to anything you dip in it (veggie sticks, buffalo wings, wedges), creamy enough for tossing through salads, and saucy enough for spooning over steak and drizzle over pizza.

Just give me an excuse to use it and I will!

Here’s what you need to make this. If you’re a seasoned blue cheese eater, I recommend roquefort for its bold, beautiful blue cheese flavour. If you’re a newbie feeling a bit nervous, start with Blue Castello. Blue cheese training wheels!

Blue cheese – Any creamy blue cheese will work, just don’t use the hard crumbly sort as they won’t melt into the dressing. As for strength of blue cheese flavour, here’s a list of common ones from the strongest to mildest:

Roquefort – Sharp, tangy, salty, creamy and complex. My favourite!

Stilton – strong, rich and savoury, but rounder and less sharp than Roquefort.

Danish Blue / Danablu – classic blue-cheese flavour. This is a good value easy to find choice.

Gorgonzola Piccante – fairly strong and spicy, though creamier and less salty.

Bleu d’Auvergne – medium-strong, creamy and earthy.

Gorgonzola Dolce – mild, creamy, sweet and buttery with gentle blue flavour.

Blue Castello – most mild, good one for beginners! This is also easy to find, sold at grocery stores an suburban corner stores here in Australia. We love a Blue Castello!!

Buttermilk – This is the main liquid in the dressing that thins it into a dressing consistency. Thicker than milk, thinner than sour cream, with a lovely tangy flavour. 🙂 If you’d rather not get a whole carton just for this recipe, you can use a 50/50 mix of milk and yogurt instead.

Mayonnaise and sour cream – These add richness and keeps the dressing a nice thick, creamy consistency. Whole-egg mayonnaise is best, the flavour is smoother and not as sweet or tangy as regular mayonnaise can be. Kewpie is also great here!

Garlic powder – This is the only flavouring I use in blue cheese dressing, I personally feel that anything more is unnecessary as the blue cheese already adds so much flavour. I prefer using powder to fresh as it’s more earthy and suits the blue cheese flavour better. If you substitute with fresh, leave the dressing for a few hours to let the flavour mellow.

Apple cider vinegar – Just a touch of acidity. We don’t need too much as the buttermilk already provides some. You can substitute with lemon juice.

Worcestershire sauce (OPTIONAL) – Just a small 1/2 teaspoon (do not want to taste it), I personally feel it’s not needed if using a blue cheese with strong flavour but I’d add it if using a mild blue cheese (like blue castello).

Blue cheese dressing is supposed to have some little lumps of blue cheese in it. But if you prefer to make it completely smooth, you can use a stick blender instead.

Mash the blue cheese with a fork until it sort of becomes crumbly. Best to use a fork rather than fingers as it’s creamy (unless you’re just looking for an excuse to suck your fingers clean of blue cheese!).

Whisk with the remaining ingredients until it becomes a thick creamy dressing. Whisk vigorously for 10 to 15 seconds until most of the blue cheese blends into the dressing. As mentioned above, it won’t be completely smooth, there will be some little lumps of blue cheese which is normal – everybody loves the little pops of blue cheese!

And that’s it. Your blue cheese dressing is ready to use!

Its uses extend far beyond the basic role as a salad dressing! Here are just a few ideas:

Salad dressing – Toss it through salads or drizzle over iceberg lettuce wedges, like pictured above!

Dipping sauce – Buffalo wings, veggie sticks, crackers, potato chips (plain), potato wedges, chicken fingers, Fish Fingers, Popcorn chicken, bread.

Drizzle – on pizza (especially Buffalo chicken pizza!), fries, baked potatoes, roasted potatoes, smashed potatoes, roasted vegetables, a big show-off Tomahawk Steak (or a regular one)

Fellow blue cheese lovers, tell me – what are some other ways to use blue cheese dressing?? I wanna know! – Nagi x

PS No video today because this is a quick-flick recipe. 🙂

These iced sesame noodles have become my summertime bestie. Is it hot out? If so, there’s a good chance this is going to be on the table. I'm here to share the details before we run out of summer. Imagine a rotating cast of long, slurp-able noodles (soba, pici, somen, spaghetti, etc.) tangling with a creamy sesame sauce, topped with 4-5 easy toppings. That’s the basic formula. The noodles are served family-style in a large bowl of ice water. Everyone mixes up their own individual, custom portions. So good, so fun. Definitely a Japanese-inspired concept, dovetailing, in our house, with whatever is popping up at California farmers’ markets. I encourage you to incorporate whatever your family loves and the ingredients shining at your local markets.

Aside from boiling the noodles, nearly everything else here can be prepared ahead of time. It’s part of what’s great about this and what makes it a weeknight-friendly meal. I like to toss some chopped veggies (whatever is on hand - broccoli, asparagus, etc.) in the pasta water after the noodles come out, keeping the cooking to a single pot. To summarize, here are the main components of the meal:

I’ve done fantastic versions of this meal with all of the following. Think long and slurp-able on the noodle front. I also check my noodle labels to make sure they're not wildly salted, to be honest, I've been caught off guard  on a number of occasions.

Choose 4-5 different toppings. I feel like grated ginger is a non-negotiable here. So good. And I leave any spicy component out of the base sesame sauce so that each person can light up their bowls with whatever level of spicy they can handle.

And as we move into later summer and early fall, and the weather is still hot enough for cold noodles, but the seasonal ingredients are shifting, here are a few other ideas:

Broccoli florets, asparagus tops, green beans, yellow beans, corn - these are just a few of the vegetables I’ve cooked in a flash after cooking the noodles for the bowls. Boil for a mint or so, strain under cold water and serve on the side. Everyone loves to work the vegetables into their noodle bowls as well.

#35775. Miso Eggplant Stir-Fryナスの味噌炒め

Miso Eggplant Stir-Fry is a quick, classic Japanese side dish ready in 20 minutes. Tender eggplant soaks up a sweet and savory miso-ginger sauce, creating a rich, glossy glaze. Serve it over warm rice, alongside grilled fish, or as part of a bento.

This post may contain affiliate links. Please read my disclosure policy.

Miso Eggplant Stir-Fry is a classic home-cooked Japanese side dish. It pairs tender Japanese eggplant (nasu, 茄子, ナス) with a rich, sweet-savory miso sauce made from pantry staples. A quick sear gives the eggplant a silky texture that soaks up the deep miso flavor.

What readers say“I made this last night with freshly harvested Japanese eggplant from my CSA and white miso from Trader Joes. It was quick, simple, and very delicious. I don’t get eggplant often, but I’ll keep this recipe for the next time!”

I didn’t like eggplant growing up, and I always wondered why my mom cooked it so often. Now that I’m a mom, I’m doing the exact same thing, and my kids keep asking why I always cook eggplant. Well, they haven’t learned to love it yet, but I know the day will come. Eggplant is delicious, especially when it’s cooked right!

If you love Japanese stir-fries, try my Miso Pork and Eggplant Stir-Fry, Stir-Fry Vegetables, and Japanese Lotus Root Stir-Fry next!

You’ll need Japanese eggplants, green onion/scallion, toasted sesame oil, and neutral oil, plus a quick sauce of miso, sake, mirin, soy sauce, and ginger.

Find the printable recipe with measurements below.

Here are my go-to cooking tips for tender, glazed stir-fried miso eggplant.

To store: Refrigerate leftovers in an airtight container for up to 3 days. Freezing is not recommended, as frozen eggplant becomes watery upon thawing.

To reheat: Warm in a skillet over medium heat for 2 minutes with a splash of water to revive the glossy glaze. Alternatively, microwave in 30-second bursts until warm, taking care not to overheat so the eggplant retains its shape.

Feel free to mix and match based on what you have on hand.

Add these colorful and nourishing sides to make a complete meal.

Yes! A large skillet works well. A carbon steel pan is the best substitute for a wok because it’s much lighter than cast iron, handles high heat, and develops a natural nonstick patina. However, any well-preheated skillet will give the eggplant a great sear.

White miso offers a sweeter, milder flavor from a shorter fermentation. Red miso ferments longer for a deeper, saltier umami kick. If your miso contains added dashi stock, taste your sauce first and slightly reduce the soy sauce.

Yes. If you cannot find Japanese or Chinese eggplants, globe eggplants are a good substitute (they just have a thicker skin). Keep the skin on and cut the pieces into uniform wedges so they hold their shape without getting mushy.
