#35817. Introducing full transaction detection for Cloudflare WAF

Daniele Molteni,Â Elie Roudninski,Â andÂ Nick Downie

This post is also available in Deutsch, EspaÃ±ol, FranÃ§ais, æ¥æ¬èª, íêµ­ì´, ç¹é«ä¸­æ, andÂ ç®ä½ä¸­æ.

Today, we are expanding our web application firewall (WAF) by adding two new capabilities: full transaction detections and response rules. Full transaction detections evaluate each HTTP request alongside its response to identify evidence of exploitation. It helps answer both "Does this request look malicious?" and "What happened when the application handled it?" Response rules can then block the originâs response before it reaches the requester.

These are valuable protections because the latest frontier models are uncovering vulnerabilities buried deep in widely used software, giving defenders clarity on what to fix â and attackers new paths to exploit. The recent php2shellÂ vulnerability shows the stakes: a flaw in a common software component can put applications across the Internet at risk. AI agents scanning for vulnerabilities can be extremely persistent, adapting payloads using feedback, and chaining vulnerabilities, credentials, and permissions. An application's response can reveal whether an attempt worked and give an attacker information that helps them go deeper.

Inspecting incoming requests remains essential for stopping recognizable attacks before they reach an application. But some threats become clear only when the request is considered alongside what the origin returns. A suspicious input followed by a response exposing sensitive information tells a different story from the same input followed by a rejection or an error.

With these new capabilities, customers can use Cloudflare-managed protections or build their own policies combining request and response properties. This extends our always-on application security framework, with detection results available in Security Analytics to support investigation. Our first managed protections using this capability address the recently disclosed php2shell vulnerability.

And the best part? We are making these new capabilities generally available to all Cloudflare customers, including Free plans.

Cloudflare WAFÂ protects websites and APIs with managed rules, custom rules, and rate limiting. Managed rules provide protection for known attack techniques and vulnerabilities while custom rules let teams create their own policies using parameters such as an IP address, URL path, headers, and request body. These controls operate at the request level to stop exploits or unwanted traffic from reaching the origin.

For many threats, this is the right place to act. However, treating every suspicious request as a confirmed exploit creates a difficult choice. Broad request signatures can catch more potential attacks, but they can also show âfalse positivesâ, such as matching legitimate traffic â which then breaks the applications. Deploying only rules that do not trigger false positives reduces that risk, but can leave more room for more ambiguous traffic to reach the server.

The response provides the missing evidence. Cloudflare can now correlate it with the request that produced it, so detections can account for the outcome of the entire HTTP transaction.

As an illustrative example, consider an application that lets users download files. An attacker manipulates the file parameter to request a private configuration file outside the permitted directory:

Request inspection can recognize this path traversal attempt and block it before it reaches the application. The request alone, however, cannot establish whether the application would expose the file. It might reject the request, ignore the traversal, or return an error. If the request reaches the origin, a response like this provides additional evidence:

Full transaction detectionÂ provides a missing piece: it can correlate the attempted file access with response content characteristic of a private configuration file. Configuration-like text can legitimately appear in documentation or example downloads; combining it with a traversal attempt provides stronger evidence of sensitive data exposure than either signal alone. A response ruleÂ can then replace the origin response with a Cloudflare WAF block page and HTTP 403 before it reaches the requester, effectively blocking the exploit by preventing sensitive information from reaching the attacker.

Full transaction detection extends the always-on detection frameworkÂ we introduced earlier this year. Detections analyze traffic and attach metadata to the request and response, rules then decide what to do with those results.

Separating those jobs gives customers visibility before they design a policy. Security teams can inspect detections in their own traffic, understand which endpoints and signatures are involved, and choose the response that fits their application. Similar to the approach for the request-based Attack Signature Detection, the outcome of the detections are stored in fields that can be accessed in the response custom rules or used in managed detectionsÂ to block traffic.

Mirroring the request detection fields, the following new fields are added to our platform:

Confidence values associated with matching signatures

Categories associated with matching signatures

The first full transaction detections focus on exploit confirmation for high profile vulnerability. It correlates suspicious input with response signals that indicate an exploit may have succeeded.

We will expand coverage over time by supporting other use cases, including detecting data exposure and exfiltration signals. This is important for the Internet beyond any one application: defenses can distinguish probing from evidence of impact, while detection of exposed data and services can reach customers that do not have a dedicated security team tuning every WAF rule.

Detecting evidence of exploitation is most useful if you can act on it in real time. Response custom rules turn full transaction detections into inline protection by blocking a matching origin response before it reaches the requester, although it cannot undo actions already performed at the origin.

Security teams can now combine request and response properties with detection results to decide which responses to block. When a blocking rule matches, Cloudflare replaces the origin response with a WAF block page or a custom response.

Response phase controls are available in the Cloudflare dashboard at the bottom of the Security > Security Rules page, with both managed protections and custom rules.

We haveÂ released both managed and custom rules to all plans, including Free plans. Over time, we will follow the same approach we use for request detections, where managed detections for free plans focus on high-profile vulnerabilities, while paying customers get a richer catalog of detections.

All customers get the protection of the full array of transaction detections through the Cloudflare Managed Response Firewall DefaultÂ ruleset, which is designed for a simple one-click deploy and simplified configurability. When a signature matches, the managed detection will block the response and return a standard WAF block page.

You can edit the Cloudflare Managed Response Firewall DefaultÂ scope to run detections only on a portion of their applications, for example by excluding or restricting the detection to a specific path. Paying customers can use detection fields in custom responseÂ rulesÂ to create more tailored policies.

Custom response rules are designed to give customers full control of the rule logic. A useful rule can stop an administration interface from being exposed when an authentication gateway has not marked the request as internal. For example:

http.request.uri.path starts_with "/admin" and not http.request.headers["x-internal-user"][0] eq "true" and http.response.code eq 200 and http.response.headers["content-type"][0] contains "text/html"

This blocks only when an unauthenticated request targets `/admin` and the origin actually returns a successful HTML administration page. It does not block ordinary authentication failures, redirects, or non-administration traffic.

All customers can create up to three custom response rules supporting LogÂ and BlockÂ actions. The fields and functions available in response to custom rules mirrors what your plan gives you access to in request custom rulesÂ already. Creating rules on the response body is not yet available.

Following the Attack Signature DetectionÂ approach, paying customers also have access to the outcome of attack detections through the cf.waf.signature.response.*Â  fields listed above. These fields can be combined with other parameters (such as a hostname, URL path, source IP, request header) to enable protection on a single path, or limit the policy to application-specific context. We are currently rolling out the response fields to all our accounts. If you donât have access to them yet, please contact your account team.

When a managed or custom response rule logs or blocks a transaction, the event is available in Security Events. This means responders can trace any detection back to the full context of the request and the specific rule that took action.

At the moment, both request-only rules and full-transaction rules are shown together in the same analytics page. In Security Events, the events generated by response rules are part of the Managed Rules or Custom Rules service. You can filter events belonging to a specific rule ID in the relative rule list section.

Full transaction detection is generally available for all zones proxying traffic through Cloudflare. To verify that youâre protected, go to Security > Security RulesÂ in the Cloudflare dashboard. If you want to customize your policy, start by reviewing full transaction detections in Security Analytics, then create the response phase policy that fits your application.

#35818. Measuring the Impact of Personalized Recommendations

By Kevin Zielnicki, Guy Aridor, Aurélien Bibaut, Allen Tran, Winston Chou, and Nathan KallusIntroductionPersonalization is everywhere on the internet. It shapes the products we discover, the stories we read, the music we hear, and the movies and TV shows we watch. At Netflix, personalization has been central to the member experience for decades — from the Netflix Prize to our modern recommender system that helps members navigate a large and constantly changing catalog.But personalization is not only an algorithmic problem, it is also a measurement problem. How do we know how much value personalization creates? More precisely, how do we separate the appeal of a title from the value created by recommending that title to the right member at the right time?In a new article in the International Journal of Industrial Organization — which we are also presenting at this year’s ACM Conference on Economics & Computation (EC ‘26) — we develop a model of member behavior, title choice, and personalized recommendations. The model lets us estimate how recommendations affect both whether members choose to watch and, if so, which titles they choose. In this post, we summarize our approach and main findings.The Measurement ChallengeA natural first attempt at valuing recommendations is to ask: what share of viewing comes from titles that were recommended? This is an intuitive metric, but it fails to answer the causal question at hand.The problem is that recommendations are not randomly assigned. A title appears on a member’s homepage precisely because the recommender system predicts that the member might want to watch it. If a member watches that title, was it because the recommendation caused the member to watch it? Or would she have watched it anyway because of her underlying preference for that kind of title? This is the core measurement challenge: recommendations are targeted to demand, so viewing a recommended title combines the effect of personalization with the member’s underlying preferences.One way to solve this would be to run a large experiment that replaces Netflix’s personalized experience with an unpersonalized one. That would create clean variation — but it would also be a poor member experience. Personalization is a central part of how members locate valuable titles in a large catalog, so turning it off broadly is not an acceptable measurement strategy.Instead, we take a hybrid approach. We build a behavioral model that separates members’ underlying preferences from the incremental effect of recommendations. The model uses the natural variation in the recommendation system, for example due to algorithmic exploration, to estimate how recommendations affect choice. Then, to validate the model predictions about title substitutability, we use small-scale A/B tests that “nudge” the salience of a handful of titles exogenously, generating ground-truth substitution patterns for a subset of titles. This lets us combine the scale and richness of modeling with the credibility of experimental evidence.A Model of Member ChoiceTo measure the value of personalization, we need a model of what members would watch under different recommendation systems. Our model treats Netflix viewing as a day-by-day choice process. On each day, a member chooses among the titles available in the catalog, or she chooses not to watch anything. This gives us a concrete target to estimate: the probability that a member watches each title on a given day, as a function of their preferences, their viewing history, and the recommendations they see.A simple version of this model would be too restrictive. It might assume, for example, that removing one title from the catalog shifts viewing toward all other titles in roughly proportional ways. But that isn’t how member choice works. If a member is considering a romantic comedy, the closest substitutes are likely other romantic comedies, not every title on Netflix equally. For similar reasons, two members may react very differently to the same recommendation.To capture this complexity, we use a low-rank choice model. The model learns a representation of each title and a corresponding representation of each member’s current preferences. These representations are not limited to manually specified features like genre, cast, or language. Instead, they are learned from viewing behavior itself, allowing the model to capture nuanced similarities between titles that may be difficult to describe with coarse features, such as genre or release date, alone.Our Model Attributes Choices to Dynamic Member-Title Affinity and the Effect of RecommendationsMember preferences are dynamic. What someone wants to watch today depends on what they have watched recently. A member who just finished a crime thriller may be in a different preference state than the same member after watching a stand-up special or a kids’ movie. Rather than estimate a fixed preference vector for each member, the model summarizes each member’s past viewing history into a current preference state. This lets us capture heterogeneous and time-varying tastes while also scaling to millions of members.Our Model Architecture Allows Us to Scale to Millions of Members EfficientlyThe key component for our purposes is that the model explicitly parameterizes the effect of recommendations. When a title is recommended, the model gives it an additional recommendation effect, or “bonus,” that increases its probability of being chosen. This bonus is a reduced-form way to capture two related mechanisms. First, recommendations can create awareness by helping members discover titles they may not have known about. Second, recommendations can provide information by signaling that a title is likely to be a good match.Once estimated, the model becomes an engine for predicting counterfactuals. We can ask what would happen if a title were not recommended, if a different set of titles were recommended, or if the current recommender system were replaced with simpler alternatives. Because the model separately represents member preferences, title appeal, and recommendation effects, it lets us estimate not only how recommendations affect total viewing, but also how they change which titles are watched.The model is only useful, however, if it captures real substitution patterns. The next step is therefore validation: comparing the model’s predictions to randomized experiments that directly perturb, on a small scale, the visibility that each title receives.Validating the Model with Randomized ExperimentsThe model relies on an important assumption. After conditioning on the member, title, and state information available to the recommender system, we treat the remaining variation in whether a title is recommended as if it were randomly assigned. In our setting, this assumption is reasonable: we observe all of the information available to the recommender system, so we should be able to model its behavior accurately. But it is still an assumption. A useful model should not only fit historical viewing patterns; it should also predict what happens when recommendations change for external reasons.Thus, to validate the model, we used randomized experiments that introduce variation in title visibility exogenously. These experiments mirror the kinds of variation that occur routinely when recommendation algorithms are updated: some titles receive more impressions, while others receive fewer. The key difference is that, in the validation experiment, this variation was prespecified so that we could estimate clean experimental benchmarks.Specifically, we randomly assigned members to treatment arms that slightly nudged recommendations towards and away from different categories of titles. This let us measure diversion ratios: when a set of titles becomes less visible, how much viewing shifts to other titles, and how much shifts out of Netflix viewing altogether?We then asked whether the model could reproduce those experimentally measured substitution patterns. We estimated the model on the control group, simulated the same recommendation changes, and compared the model-implied diversion ratios to the experimental ones. The agreement was strong: the model’s predicted diversion ratios had a correlation of 0.86 with the experimental estimates and an R-squared of 0.73.Our Model Predicts Out-of-Sample Experimental Diversion Ratios WellThis validation gives us confidence that the model captures counterfactual substitution patterns accurately. Subsequently, we ask what would happen under more dramatic changes, such as different recommender systems.Counterfactuals: Aggregate Consumption and DiversityWith a validated model in hand, we can move from measurement to counterfactuals. Instead of asking only what happened under the current Netflix experience, we can ask what would have happened if members had seen recommendations generated by a different system.We compare the current recommender system to three baselines:The first is random recommendations: every member receives titles selected uniformly at random from the catalog. This is not intended as a realistic product experience, but it helps isolate the value of having recommendations that are relevant.The second is popularity-based recommendations: every member receives broadly popular titles. This is a natural non-personalized benchmark.The third is a basic matrix factorization model, a classic personalized recommendation approach and a useful baseline for older generations of recommender systems.In each counterfactual, we replace the recommended titles while keeping the rest of the choice environment fixed. This lets us estimate how much viewing would change if the recommendation policy changed, holding constant the catalog, members, and model of member choice.The results show that the current recommender system generates substantially more engagement than each benchmark. Relative to the current system, random recommendations reduce engagement by 16%, popularity-based recommendations reduce engagement by 12%, and matrix factorization reduces engagement by 4%. These are large differences at Netflix scale. Even the comparison to matrix factorization — a personalized baseline — suggests that continued improvements in personalization translate into meaningful gains in how effectively members find titles they want to watch.Personalized Recommendations Increase Engagement and its DiversityEngagement is only part of the story. A recommender system could increase viewing while concentrating attention on a narrow set of already-popular titles. That would be a worse experience for members whose tastes are not well represented by those titles, and it would make poorer use of a broad catalog.We therefore also examine consumption diversity: how broadly viewing is distributed across titles. The current system performs well on this dimension too. Popularity-based and matrix-factorization recommendations both substantially increase concentration, meaning that fewer titles receive meaningful viewership. Random recommendations produce slightly more diversity, as expected, but at a large cost to engagement.Taken together, these counterfactuals show that the value of personalization is not just that members watch more. It is also that members are matched to a broader set of titles. The current recommender system increases engagement while preserving a wide distribution of viewing, reflecting the diversity of member tastes across the Netflix catalog.Decomposing the Impact on TitlesThe aggregate counterfactuals show that personalization increases engagement while maintaining broad consumption across the catalog. We can also use the model to ask a more granular question: why does a recommended title get watched?There are three conceptually distinct channels:The first is exposure: simply showing a title to a member can increase the probability that the member watches it. This captures the basic value of surfacing a title that may otherwise have been hard to find.The second is selection: recommended titles are shown to members who already have a relatively high baseline probability of watching them. This channel doesn’t lead to incremental engagement, but it can smooth the discovery experience and help users feel that the recommender system understands their preferences.The third is targeting: the recommender system may identify members for whom the recommendation itself is especially effective, meaning members who are much more likely to watch the title when it is recommended than when it is not.The distinction matters because not all recommendation-driven viewing should be interpreted the same way. If recommendations worked only through exposure, then any reasonably visible surface could generate much of the same value. If they worked mostly through selection, then recommendations would mainly be finding members who were already likely to watch a title. Targeting is different: it captures whether the system is placing titles in front of members for whom the recommendation changes the decision.Decomposing the Impact of Recommendations into Selection, Exposure, and TargetingOur model lets us estimate these channels title by title. For each title, we can compare the predicted probability that a targeted member watches it when recommended to the probability that an average member watches it when not recommended. We then decompose that difference into selection, exposure, and targeting.We first show that exposure is meaningful: showing a title to an average member roughly triples its consumption probability relative to the baseline. Exposure is not the main driver of differences in consumption, as mechanical exposure explains only about 7% of the gap under the current recommender system, while selection and targeting account for the vast majority of the difference and the targeting effect is nearly seven times larger than the exposure effect.This pattern is especially informative when compared with simpler recommendation systems. Random recommendations are dominated by exposure because they do not personalize: differences in consumption mostly reflect differences in what titles are shown. Matrix factorization changes this by making recommendations personal, reducing the role of exposure and leaving exposure, selection, and targeting to contribute nearly evenly to consumption differences. The current recommender system goes further: its gains come less from mechanical exposure, but more from targeting the right titles to the right viewers.Targeting is also not uniform across the catalog. It is strongest for mid-popularity titles: titles with enough potential audience to be broadly relevant, but not so much mass appeal that everyone already knows about them. Very popular titles need less help from targeting, while very niche titles may have too small an audience to target effectively. The largest gains come from the middle of the catalog, where personalization helps connect specific titles with specific member tastes.Personalized Recommendations Give the Strongest Boost to Medium-Popularity TitlesConclusionPersonalized recommendations are valuable because they help members navigate a large catalog and find titles they want to watch. They are also valuable to Netflix because they make the service more useful, more engaging, and better able to serve a wide range of tastes.But measuring that value is not straightforward. Recommendations are targeted by design, so we cannot simply compare recommended and non-recommended viewing. At the same time, turning off personalization at scale would create a worse member experience.Our approach combines a large-scale model of member choice with true experimental validation. The model lets us separate underlying title preferences from the incremental effect of recommendations, and the experiments verify that the model captures real substitution patterns.Using this framework, we find that personalization affects both how much members watch and which titles they watch. The value of recommendations comes not just from exposure, but from matching the right titles to the right members.Measuring the Impact of Personalized Recommendations was originally published in Netflix TechBlog on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

#35819. Il ristorante in Sardegna con piatti strepitosi e menù a 44 euro

Nel cuore della Marmilla, dove il paesaggio della Sardegna si fa rurale e collinare, il ristorante Arieddas si impone come modello d’avanguardia della cucina territoriale. In tavola, infatti, arriva tutta l’essenzialità di un menù che traduce la biodiversità locale in un linguaggio gastronomico contemporaneo. Attraverso una rete di micro-fornitori locali, lo chef Francesco Vitale dimostra manico e mente nel rendere concreta la visione di Pier Giorgio Parini, già chef dello stellato Povero Diavolo e consulente della struttura. Quindi, piatti raffinati ma capaci di conservare aspetti rustici.

Il menu è un condensato di sapori della Marmilla, in cui il “tempo dei ricordi” non è rievocato in chiave nostalgica, ma declinato da Francesco Vitale in una visione contemporanea. Che rende onore alla sfida di portare in tavola una tradizione che non tradisce la memoria, ma resta collegata al futuro per affermare la propria identità. Via dunque inutili esercizi di stile per dar voce ad ingredienti di indiscussa qualità e ad un pensiero di cucina “netta”, fatta di estrema pulizia, di equilibrio tra rigore filologico e precisione tecnica.

Arieddas sa creare una elegante liaison tra cibo e cultura, memoria e futuro, antichi saperi ed evoluzione. E lo fa in un ambiente avvolgente e coinvolgente con una cucina che rifugge dall’iper-inflazionato binomio tradizione /evoluzione. Preferisce trasformare le peculiarità agroalimentari dell’entroterra sardo in un’esperienza d’alta cucina rigorosa e alla portata di molti.

La conferma arriva dal menù degustazione “Viaggio in Marmilla” (44 euro), un percorso di 7 assaggi (5 antipasti, un primo e un secondo) che permette di gustare la Sardegna autentica ed il pensiero dello chef ad un prezzo super accessibile.

Ma anche i piatti alla carta offrono un ottimo rapporto qualità – prezzo. Oltre a quelli assaggiati e di cui vi racconto ecco qualche esempio.

— Pane lentu e gallina, 13 €— Pan brioche, fegatini, agrumi e alloro, 12 €— Lorighittas e ragù di cortile, 16 €— Coniglio al Vermentino, 16 €— Sanluri-Brest, 9 €

Con questi prezzi, un pasto completo con 3 piatti salati vi costa in media 45 euro. Difficile fare meglio.

L’entré, pane di semola e farine macinate a pietra con testa in cassetta, è un goloso biglietto da visita che ben predispone all’inizio della degustazione.

Gli antipasti, pensati per essere condivisi, vengono serviti in contemporanea per favorire l’interazione a tavola e quel tanto rimpianto dialogo tra i commensali.

La tartare di pomodoro arrosto con olio all’origano, fichi, mandorla e agrumi (12 euro) è un atlante di colori, profumi e paesaggi di macchia mediterranea. È l’esempio concreto di come una cucina ragionata d’entroterra possa declinare l’ingrediente vegetale con rigore e originalità. Un vero e proprio manifesto di sostenibilità e intelligenza gastronomica che denota l’abilità dello chef nel nobilitare materie prime povere attraverso un’esecuzione tecnica d’autore. Nulla da aggiungere ad un boccone inclusivo e rassicurante al tempo stesso.

Medesimo costrutto per l’anguria al bbq con pesto di basilico ed erbe aromatiche (12 euro), che stravolge la percezione comune attraverso una cottura ancestrale, ma di grandissimo impatto emozionale e di “gola”. Lo chef sa impreziosire la dolcezza del frutto con una piacevole e inattesa tridimensionalità, giocando sui rimandi aromatici del pesto che allunga oltremodo la persistenza. Un bite che rende omaggio alla filosofia agricola, cui conferisce spessore culturale, senza risultare banale. Qui la mano di Parini è evidente anche per ricordo storico.

La Kofta – lo spiedo di pecora e maiale con semi misti, spezie e salsa allo yogurt (13 euro) – è un compendio di eleganza, tecnica e conoscenza della materia. Un piatto che, pur conservando un’anima sarda, strizza l’occhio alla cultura mediorientale, senza mai perdere di vista l’obiettivo. Francesco conferma dunque di saper giocare con dosate contaminazioni e dimostra maturità professionale nel rendere omaggio al genius loci, ampliandone l’orizzonte in maniera ponderata.

L’uovo della festa all’occhio di bue con pomodoro arrosto, pecorino e basilico (12 euro), tra i signature del ristorante, è un inno alla cucina golosa ingentilita dal know-how dello chef. Un boccone rotondo, capace di regalare la purezza strutturale dei sapori “di casa” attraverso consistenze millimetriche e una studiata freschezza.

La zucchina brasata con fondo di carne, riduzione di vino, erbe aromatiche e pecorino (12 euro) è la combinazione tra grandi classici e nuove vibes. Qui da Arieddas i colori vivi e intensi raccontano le colline, la Marmilla, i frutti della terra. Un antipasto che dà continuità alla alla filosofia no-waste in modo leggibile e diretto.

I lorighittas fatti a mano con ragù di cortile e uovo di gallina marinato (15 euro) sono omaggio alla tradizione e esaltazione di un pensiero di cucina in cui la tecnica è a servizio dell’ingrediente. Un primo piatto che compie il miracolo di dar spessore a pochissimi ingredienti, divertendosi a stuzzicare il palato in un crescendo di sensazioni. La texture da manuale di una pasta dai ricami complessi, il ragù perfetto nella cottura e il tocco dell’uovo marinato, rendono questo piatto una felice, golosa versione POP di un classico senza tempo. Una forchettata che nasconde dietro un apparente “così com’è” il lavoro di ricerca dell’armonia.

I filindeu in brodo di pecora (15 euro) sono l’essenza di una cucina testarda, di quella resilenza sincera tra campi e fornelli a tutela della salvaguardia della biodiversità territoriale. Un gusto che va in crescendo, arricchendosi di un pot-pourri di sfumature gustolfattive, ad ogni cucchiaiata. Eclatante per maestria e studio maniacale di dosi e ingredienti. Un piatto che sa asciugare la tradizione portandola a livelli di finezza inattesa e che arriva dritto al cuore di molti nostalgici.

La pecora di Sanluri (12 euro) è in tre diverse cotture, ognuna riservata ad uno specifico taglio. Contemporaneità della mano e della tecnica per questa felice espressione di una cucina riduttivamente etichettata come “di casa”. Ma che è un profondo e atavico insieme di gesti innati della cultura gastronomica locale. Impossibile resistere a questo grande classico sardo che stupisce per cotture e lavorazione.

Il gelato di Arieddas alla crema, accompagnato da ciò che la stagione e il territorio offrono (9 euro) è un piacevole gioco di gusto che incuriosisce l’ospite, invitandolo a comporre il proprio abbinamento ideale, attingendo dal territorio. Un’idea fresca per ritoccare un tipico “fine pasto”.

La winelist dà giustamente spazio ai vini della Cantina Su’Entu, che ospita il locale, cui si affianca una corretta selezione di bottiglie sarde, nazionali ed internazionali. Una carta che sa parlare tanto all’appassionato quanto al tradizionalista, senza far sentire in difetto nessuno.

A rendere più piacevole l’esperienza è un servizio di sala, professionalmente informale, che sa accogliere l’avventore e il cliente con sorriso e savoir-faire.

Arieddas – La Cucina della Marmilla. S.P, 48/Km 1,8, 09025 Sanluri VS. Telefono: 070 705 0418. Instagram

Dall’economia ai campi di ulivo, il mio percorso è una ricerca continua di qualità e sostenibilità. Ho trasformato la passione in professione diventando una figura poliedrica nel settore: dalla critica enogastronomica a "naso" professionista, provo a sintonizzarmi con vini, oli extravergine, pizze, cucina e molto altro. Il mio approccio? Un insolito mash-up tra rigore strategico ed esperienza sensoriale pura. Sempre in viaggio tra l'Italia e l'estero, esploro le filiere con il mantra imprescindibile della sostenibilità, in vigna così come nei bilanci. Quando non sono impegnata in un panel di assaggio o in un'azienda agricola, mi trovate immersa tra i numeri o tra le pagine dei classici della letteratura.

#35820. Inside Prometheus: Meta’s Journey to a Gigawatt-Scale Supercluster

Right now, in New Albany, Ohio, Meta is undertaking its most ambitious AI infrastructure project to date. Prometheus, our gigawatt-scale supercluster, is an advancement in our infrastructure that is training the next generation of foundational models that will bring new AI experiences to billions of people.

Two years ago, New Albany was a conventional data center site running web traffic. With advancements in hardware, networking and building design, we reworked this site to be home to training programs for frontier models. We’re building the supercluster in phases. The first phase has already been completed and was used to train our Muse foundational models, including the Muse Wonder models, our new frontier models that deliver state-of-the-art performance on personal and professional agentic tasks.

Large training jobs require everything to work optimally to sustain their performance; an issue on a single host can slow down or stop the entire job, lowering its ‘goodput’. By focusing on improving our systems’ stability and reliability we were able to achieve more than 85% goodput for pre-training runs and more than 90% goodput for reinforcement learning (RL) runs of Muse Wonder. During these training runs, we were able to achieve an overall wall-clock mean time between interruptions (MTBI) of ~47k GPU hours. Since then, we have landed further changes across our fleet including firmware fixes to increase MTBI to more than 54K GPU hours, and we are constantly improving it.

Now, we’re continuing to scale Prometheus with our next frontier models from Meta Superintelligence Labs in mind.

The Prometheus supercluster is housed in Meta’s New Albany, Ohio, data center.

Today, Prometheus comprises an array of hundreds of thousands of GPUs across multiple interconnected buildings, including traditional and AI-optimized data center buildings and rapid deployment structures, all tightly interconnected by miles of fiber and functioning as a single machine.

This capacity allows us to pursue larger models and longer context windows than were previously practical. At full scale, Prometheus will comprise roughly 1 million distributed GPUs, all functioning in lockstep.

Prometheus currently deploys two NVIDIA GPU platforms, with a third (based on NVIDIA’s Vera Rubin NVL72) arriving soon. Each represents a generational leap in performance and efficiency, leveraging our NVL72 rack architecture where 72 GPUs act as a single accelerator within the same network fabric.

Our first platform, Catalina, leverages the NVIDIA GB200 NVL72. We deploy the Ariel variant, a two-rack configuration in which 36 GPUs per rack are interconnected via NVLink to form a unified 72-GPU domain. Catalina provides improvements in raw compute and memory capacity compared to Grand Teton H100. It leverages our Open Rack V3 (ORv3) high-power rack (HPR) structure, an open hardware design contributed to the Open Compute Project (OCP).

The Ariel variant of GB200 NVL72 pairs each NVIDIA Blackwell GPU with an NVIDIA Grace CPU and 2x NVIDIA ConnectX-7 400G NICs at a 1:1 CPU-to-GPU ratio, letting us deploy 800G of I/O per GPU earlier than the rest of the industry. We chose Ariel because the GB200 NVL72 scaled up nearly every other dimension relative to the NVIDIA H100: FLOPS, HBM bandwidth, scale-up bandwidth, and scale-up domain size, while scale-out bandwidth per GPU would have stayed at 400G. We expected that imbalance to cost performance, so we opted for a configuration that delivers 800G of scale-out per GPU. This also gave us more uniformity of spec as the region expanded over time and 800G scale-out became available.

Our second platform, Clemente, moves to the NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 and improves on Catalina at both the GPU and the platform level. GB300 raises HBM capacity per GPU by 1.5x, from 192 GB to 288 GB, and dense FP4 throughput by a similar factor, while roughly doubling attention (softmax) acceleration. At the platform level, scale-out is no longer the constraint it was on the GB200 NVL72: NVIDIA ConnectX-8 SuperNICs deliver 800G per GPU natively, so the capability we deployed early on Ariel becomes the baseline. That, together with a 2:1 GPU-to-CPU ratio, allows Clemente to pack the full 72-GPU domain into a single rack, streamlining our physical deployment. Clemente can be deployed with our modular Air-Assisted Liquid Cooling (AALC) or use Facility Liquid Cooling (FLC) in our newly designed data centers. Serviceability also improves substantially, with reduced cabling.

In traditional web services, the data center network transports requests and responses between services whose instances typically don’t require high bandwidth, high performance, and tight, lock-step coordination across many servers. Large-scale AI training requires all these, meaning the network that connects them is now an important part of AI workloads. To best address this, in addition to the standard data center network connecting servers, several years ago we added a second dedicated data network based on Ethernet, called the Back-End (BE) network, to enable direct GPU-to-GPU communication both within and across data center buildings.

Large pre-training jobs partition the training into data-parallel model replicas, creating a hierarchy in network usage: Latency-sensitive and bandwidth-sensitive operations concentrate within a replica, while traffic that is more tolerant of higher latency and less bandwidth is scheduled between replicas. Our network is designed to match this hierarchy, with low-latency, high-bandwidth fabrics within buildings and an aggregation network connecting the building fabrics.

We work closely with Meta Superintelligence Labs to ensure the parallelism design, traffic patterns, and communication algorithms and software are optimized to minimize exposure of any network communication. This keeps the GPUs as busy as possible and not waiting on the network.

The Meta team has employed these networking concepts in earlier building-scale, 24K GPU clusters and our region-scale, 100K+ GPU cluster over the last several years, and we took them to a new level of scale and distance in Prometheus.

At the building level, each Ethernet-based fabric interconnects up to 20,736 GPUs through a high-bandwidth, low-latency multi-layer topology. Our initial design used a Disaggregated Scheduled Fabric (DSF) to mitigate the network congestion caused by training collectives that typically have a small number of large, long-lived network flows that collide under traditional load-balancing techniques; it does this by utilizing sub-packet-level multipath routing and packet re-ordering in the fabric along with virtual output queues and credit-based end-to-end flow control.

As Ethernet NIC technology advanced, enabling packet re-ordering at the endpoint, we were able to update to a Non-Scheduled Fabric (NSF) utilizing shallow-buffer 51.2T Ethernet switches, such as Minipack3 with Dynamic Load Balancing and the NVIDIA Spectrum-4 switch ASIC-based Minipack3N with NVIDIA’s Adaptive Routing on ConnectX NICs. Both DSF and NSF are based on Meta’s FBOSS networking stack, giving us the control to rapidly iterate on and optimize the fabrics in Prometheus, and the visibility to operate these clusters at scale.

The Backend Aggregation (BAG) network is a multi-layer hub-and-spoke network that connects building-level fabrics across the Prometheus cluster, spanning 2 km to over 100 km. It is built with Arista 7800-series chassis running deep-buffered Broadcom Jericho3 silicon, delivering multiple Pbps of bandwidth per region pair.

Running pretraining over this network required a dedicated optimization effort with Meta Superintelligence Labs to ensure training was not slowed down, especially given speed-of-light constraints at these distances.

Pulling this all together, the complexity of the Prometheus network involves millions of miles of fiber strand, tens of thousands of switches, and millions of optics — from 2×400G FR4 LITE short-reach, low-cost pluggables inside the buildings to 800G-ZR coherent optics for links beyond ~10 km.

At Prometheus’ scale, every component needs to be monitored for reliability. A single fault anywhere can halt an entire training job and waste valuable compute resources.

Maintaining reliability at this level requires a co-engineering model with NVIDIA that goes beyond a traditional vendor dynamic. Teams are deeply embedded at our data centers, sharing real-time telemetry and running joint triage sessions to decompose every system halt by its root cause.

This attribution-driven accountability model ensures both sides are focused on targeted improvements. While Meta optimizes scheduling and infrastructure, NVIDIA addresses firmware, signal diagnostics, and memory handling. This transparency eliminates ambiguity and drives faster fixes across both organizations.

The transition from the H100 generation’s NVL8 architecture to NVL72 has fundamentally redefined our approach to infrastructure resilience. In the NVL8 era, the scale-up domain — the group of GPUs tightly coupled via NVLink for tensor parallelism — was limited to eight units. With NVL72, that domain expands to 72 GPUs, increasing the fault blast radius by 9X.

The larger scale-up domain is what gives NVL72 its bandwidth advantage, but it also makes the 72-GPU rack the unit of allocation we plan capacity around. Training parallelism maps most efficiently onto power-of-two group sizes, so each NVL72 domain runs a 64-GPU slice and keeps its remaining eight GPUs as in-rack spares. When a GPU fails, a spare takes its place immediately, so the job restarts from its last checkpoint instead of waiting on hardware repair, and the rack stays in the job. The in-rack redundancy pushes the effective rack fault rate down to the floor set by failures that can remove an entire pod; for rarer whole-rack faults we hold roughly 2% additional racks in reserve. For a 32,768 active-GPU training run, this means provisioning 523 NVL72 racks, or 37,656 GPUs, about 13% above the active footprint. Most of that margin (11%) falls out of the 64-of-72 slice geometry rather than being an absolute reliability tax.

Physical complexity further intensifies these reliability requirements. A single NVL72 domain incorporates 5,184 tuned differential-pair signaling links operating at 200 Gbps, each traversing multiple potential points of failure, including GPU SerDes, compute tray PCBs, cable cartridges, and switch tray interfaces. Maintaining consistent signal integrity across this dense fabric — at 200 Gbps per lane — represents an unprecedented engineering challenge at this scale.

Fault recovery addresses how we react to faults to minimize the impact on training time. Depending on the scope (i.e., blast area) of a fault we address it through two mechanisms:

Parallelism-Aware Fault Tolerance (PAFT): When a fault can be isolated to a data-parallel model replica, we reduce the impact of a hardware failure by allowing a single faulty replica to be taken offline, while the remaining cluster repeats that step and continues productive training. The compromised slice simply restarts on available spare hosts and resynchronizes, converting a potential total system halt into a minor, temporary reduction in aggregate throughput.

Checkpointing: When a fault blast area is larger than a data-parallel model replica, the entire job is restarted back to the last checkpoint; frequent checkpointing reduces the amount of work lost in these events. Our distributed checkpointing architecture asynchronously saves the model state — including gradients and optimizer data — to multi-tier storage. We use delta checkpointing and in-memory staging to ensure these saves happen with minimal impact on training throughput.

These two fault recovery mechanisms combine with a sparing strategy that utilizes pre-allocated spare GPU trays within a rack, as well as spare racks, to minimize the time to bring up replacement hardware and reduce the amount of work lost to hardware failures

When training frontier models, infrastructure reliability requires a perspective beyond simple availability. The fundamental challenge lies in maintaining training momentum without frequent system halts. Within Prometheus, we classify an interruption as any fault — from GPU silicon defects and network fabric anomalies to storage bottlenecks or thermal limits — that forces a job to pause and initiate a recovery cycle.

These interruptions introduce a large operational overhead because our workloads are tightly interdependent; a single fault within a 72-GPU domain can affect the entire cluster’s aggregate throughput. This performance loss directly impacts our engineering iteration speed, resulting in less effective compute and longer timelines for delivering advanced AI experiences to billions of people.

During the initial phase of Prometheus in mid-2025, our interruption rates reached a peak of nearly 1,000 events per 8K GPUs daily. Through a year of rigorous cross-functional engineering, we have achieved a 99% reduction in interruptions, enabling the cluster to sustain multiple training jobs of tens of thousands of GPUs in parallel.

Attaining this stability required a granular decomposition of every interruption source, followed by the deployment of targeted engineering solutions for each failure category:

NVLink Signal Integrity: initially the primary bottleneck for GB200 deployments. With over 600,000 NVLink connections, even marginal signal degradation triggers frequent NVLink recovery cycles. We implemented continuous telemetry and automated flagging, utilizing L11 diagnostic burns to isolate weak links before production. Our classification tools distinguish transient faults from persistent signal integrity failures, guiding targeted repairs and component replacement, and we validate repaired systems before returning them to production.

Memory Reliability (HBM and LPDDR): Memory-related faults became a major source of interruptions as we scaled GB300 with higher memory capacities. Working closely with NVIDIA, we used fleet telemetry and detailed error analysis to identify recurring failure signatures, which are mitigated via refined HBM firmware settings, memory scrubbing, an improved error correction algorithm for LPDDR, and pattern-based predictive detection to retire degrading devices before they impact job throughput. We are deploying these changes across the fleet and measuring their impact on interruption rates and hardware replacement demand.

NVLink Switch and Fabric Health: A single switch fault can compromise an entire NVL72 domain. We monitor fabric health at millisecond resolution, utilizing automated recovery paths to isolate faulty components and rebalance traffic across the remaining infrastructure without a job interruption.

Backend Network Events: At the BAG super-spine layer, link events are managed transparently via hardware-based fault detection. Our planar topologies ensure that individual fiber or port failures are rerouted without interrupting the synchronized GPU traffic bursts.

Sustained improvement is driven by our operational infrastructure: A colocated triage team at the New Albany site, a comprehensive stability sprint in March that synchronized fixes across the stack, and a rigorous attribution-driven accountability framework. Every repair undergoes a mandatory quarantine to validate system integrity before returning to the compute pool.

Our reliability north star remains two interruptions per 8K GPUs per day, which is ~100k GPU hours MTBI. Driving a 99% reduction from our peak interruptions rate demonstrates that, at Prometheus’ scale, stability is an engineering challenge with solvable engineering outcomes.

Deploying hundreds of thousands of first-generation accelerators reveals quality issues that are hidden at lower volumes. The GB200 deployment has transformed hardware maturation into a primary engineering discipline for our teams and partners.

Each new platform architecture — from Blackwell to Vera Rubin — incorporates these real-world operational insights, tightening our screening and design specifications at every step.

Maximizing throughput for a given power envelope, minimizing stranded power, and synchronous distributed training introduces a power delivery hurdle. When tens of thousands of GPUs execute compute-heavy phases and communication cycles in unison, they trigger large power transients — sudden load fluctuations of 30-40% within the cluster. Initiating or pausing a major training job can shift loads of more than tens of megawatts in just seconds.

We address this with Dynamo Dimmer, our cluster-wide power management framework that enables intelligent power capping. Instead of hard-stopping workloads, Dimmer gradually adjusts GPU power limits as the cluster nears its electrical ceiling, ensuring training continues uninterrupted. This system is reinforced by rack-level battery backup (BBU) modules that handle immediate spikes, capacitor trays (CBUs) for peak smoothing, facility-level battery energy storage systems (BESS), and deep coordination with utility providers to manage these unique AI profiles.

While our distributed approach has allowed us to build Prometheus quickly, it has also meant navigating site-specific power and cooling constraints across different locations.

Our physical infrastructure incorporates multiple cooling generations to deliver the liquid cooling required by these high-power racks. Prometheus runs on a mix of modular air-assisted liquid cooling (AALC), including our free-air data center buildings and our rapid-deployment structures. Our purpose-built AI-optimized building now uses facility liquid cooling (FLC) for maximum power density.

By integrating leased capacity from strategic partners in addition to our own buildings, we accelerate our deployment timelines and total deployable capacity. Meanwhile, our industrial-grade rapid-deployment structures have redefined the construction playbook, delivering production-ready compute with faster timelines.

In New Albany, we’ve long partnered with local utilities to ensure we are paying the full cost of energy for our site and not adding any unnecessary strain to the local grid. We’ve also partnered with energy developers to match our energy use with new clean and renewable energy.

Meta’s newest AI-optimized data centers use closed-looped, liquid cooling as it is the most efficient way to cool GPU servers, and supports efficient use of water. Direct-to-chip, closed-loop liquid cooling helps save space by allowing us to fit more GPUs on a server rack. We also work to extend our sustainability work by sharing designs for systems like IcePack, our liquid-cooled network rack, with the wider industry through OCP.

We’ll continue to work closely with NVIDIA to expand Prometheus’ capacity with a mix of NVIDIA GB300 NVL72s and NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72s.

NVIDIA’s next-generation Vera Rubin NVL72 platform will be a generational leap in per-GPU performance and will integrate directly into Prometheus’s existing network fabric. As the cluster matures, it will deliver even more compute per watt by augmenting its capacity (primarily interconnected GB300s) with Vera Rubin via our upcoming San Miguel platform.

The San Miguel Vera Rubin NVL72 will feature:

The technological accomplishments within Prometheus have helped establish the blueprint that will inform how we approach the complexity of supercluster design going forward. Hyperion, our upcoming supercluster in Richland Parish, Louisiana, is being designed from the ground up with insights from Prometheus in mind. It will feature closed-loop liquid cooling, full grid connectivity with our utility partner Entergy, for which Meta pays the full cost, and next-generation network designs.

Learn more about our community efforts in New Albany.

Meta believes in building community through open source technology. Explore our latest projects in Artificial Intelligence, Data Infrastructure, Development Tools, Front End, Languages, Platforms, Security, Virtual Reality, and more.

Engineering at Meta is a technical news resource for engineers interested in how we solve large-scale technical challenges at Meta.

#35821. Cloudflare deploys protections against php2shell vulnerability

Daniele Molteni,Â Dan Jones,Â andÂ Kuber Nandwani

Update - On October 23, the PHP project published an informational advisory for a related vulnerability, CVE-2026-115560, in PHP's session upload progress feature. It affects fully patched PHP releases, including 8.5.12, and will be fixed in PHP's next regular release.

All Cloudflare WAF customers are protected against known exploit attempts if their site uses PHP's default upload progress field name. Customers who have changed session.upload_progress.name are not covered by the WAF rule.

The existing rules "PHP Remote Code Execution Attack (CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619) #6" protects against this vulnerability.

October 21, Calif.io, Wiz, OpenAI and Quarkslab disclosed twoÂ vulnerabilitiesÂ in PHP, tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 and known as php2shell.Â The vulnerabilities affect all web servers running PHP 5.4 or later and they may allow an attacker to cause denial of service, remote code execution, and data exposure when an application processes specially crafted HTTP traffic.

Cloudflare has been part of a coordinated effort to deploy mitigations to protect the Internet, working with PHP foundation, OpenAIÂ and WizÂ among others. Cloudflare has developed and deployed web application firewall (WAF) protections since early October 2026, which were deployed about 9 hours ahead of public disclosure. Starting on October 21 3:02 am UTC, Cloudflare customersÂ using our free or paid WAF were protected by default against php2shell.

CloudflareÂ successfully deployed multiple mitigations for all its customersÂ while the vulnerability was leaked before the official release date and we observed attack traffic targeting our customers.Â We observed how attackers were mutating the attack payload to try to bypass our protections by tracking the volume of matches and cross-referencing with the rule logic.

Protecting against php2shell required more than standard request-based rules. Request data alone does not always provide enough evidence to distinguish an exploit from legitimate traffic. The originâs response adds context, helping identify whether an exploit succeeded while reducing the risk of false positives.

To deliver this protection, we developed full transaction detection, a new Cloudflare WAF capability that combines signals from the request and response within the same HTTP transaction. Response rules can then block a matching origin response before it reaches the requester. The php2shell protections are the first managed detections we have released using this capability.

Customers should patch their PHP repos even with WAF protections providing an additional layer of defense-in-depth mitigation.Â Our security analysts continue monitoring attack activity and update the rules when and if new techniques and variations emerge in the hours and days ahead. You can track new rules in the changelog.

The protections are available and deployed automatically on all plans with WAF deployed, including Free users.

PHP is used by almost 70% of websites. The php2shell vulnerabilities affect the PHP runtime itself and can allow attackers to execute malicious code on vulnerable servers, expose customer data, or disrupt services. Because PHP underpins widely used platforms such as WordPress and Magento, these flaws could potentially affect a large number of applications across the Internet.

The two vulnerabilities involve how PHP handles memory when something goes wrong while processing a HTTP request. Normally, PHP allocates memory to store the data it needs to process a request, then releases it when that work finishes. If processing stops unexpectedly, for example because it runs out of memory, PHP fails to clean up the memory safely. These vulnerabilities arise when PHP handles an error and then tries to use data that was not fully set up or memory that has already been released.

An attacker can send specially crafted HTTP requests to trigger these conditions. Large requests are one way to put memory under pressure, but the problem goes beyond consuming server resources. By manipulating the data PHP encounters in this invalid memory, an attacker may be able to crash a PHP process, expose sensitive information, or execute code provided by the attacker.

The two vulnerabilities differ in when the unsafe memory access happens:

PHP runs out of memory and interrupts its work before some internal data has been properly initialized. During cleanup of that request, PHP may use this unfinished data as though it were valid.

A fatal error interrupts a request, leaving PHP holding references to memory that is released when the request ends. When the same PHP process handles a later request, it may follow those outdated references and access memory that is no longer valid and expose sensitive data.

These flaws are in the PHP runtime, so updating website code or a plugin(s) alone does not fix these vulnerabilities. Administrators need to update the PHP software running their applications. If a hosting provider manages PHP, ask the provider to apply the security update.

Administrators can follow the PHP advisory for affected versions and remediation instructions. Keep Cloudflare WAF protections enabled while patching. Restricting unnecessary uploads and limiting upload sizes can also reduce exposure, but these measures do not replace the PHP fix.

For Free customers, new rules have been released under the Cloudflare Managed Free Ruleset (Ruleset ID 77454fe2d30c4220b5701f6fdfb893ba). Free customers donât have to take any actions to enable the protection. To override the ruleset behavior, you can refer to our documentation.

To better identify exploit attempts, Cloudflare developed full transaction detection, a new WAF capability that analyzes both sides of the same HTTP transaction. While some malicious payloads can be identified using the request alone, the response contains useful signals that can be used to create rules with higher confidence, reducing false positives. A matching full transaction rule can block the origin response before it reaches the requester. Learn how it works in our full transaction detection blog post.

The new Cloudflare Managed Response Firewall Default has been automatically deployed for customers on all plans, including Free. To verify that the response rules are active, you can visit the Security > Security Rules page. Read the full transaction blog to learn how to customize its deployment.

To analyze blocked requests, visit Security > Security Analytics > Events. Filter by the rule IDs in the table above and inspect the matched request, action, and path. Events identify whether the action came from a managed or custom rule. Customers who need to tailor the protection can update the scopeÂ of the Managed Ruleset to the parts of an application where it is relevant.

Cloudflare customers using our Managed Ruleset are protected by default. We recommend following the advisoryÂ recommendation and applying the vendor update to your PHP reposÂ as soon as possible while keeping the WAF protection enabled as an additional protection. Our WAF analysts will continue to update protections as new techniques emerge.

#35822. TimeSeries Tiered Storage Journey: Kafka/Flink Streams to Native Cassandra Cold Reads

By Oleksii Tkachuk, Rajiv Shringi, Chris Lohfink, Abe Ratnofsky, Kartik SathyanarayananIntroductionIn an earlier post, we introduced the TimeSeries Abstraction, our high-throughput, low-latency platform designed to store and query temporal event data at scale. It has since become the operational backbone for Netflix’s largest datasets, which now span multiple petabytes.However, managing such large datasets in hot storage, tuned for low-millisecond latency access, is not cheap. At Netflix, cost-efficiency is a continuous discipline rather than a temporary initiative. This post shares two solutions that significantly reduce storage costs by continuously moving older, less frequently accessed data into cheaper object storage:Solution 1: Uses Apache Kafka and Flink to stream data directly to S3Solution 2: Leverages Cassandra backups in S3 and pluggable Memtables to read data directly from S3We’ll start with the Kafka/Flink-based design, then describe how we evolved to a native Cassandra-based cold tier.ChallengesAs Netflix’s TimeSeries datasets have expanded, we’ve encountered several compounding challenges:Growing retention demands: Users often push for increasing data retention to serve a broader range of use cases, which in turn increases the storage costs.Escalating costs: Maintaining massive, dense clusters for infrequently accessed historical data is prohibitively expensive.Sparse historical access: Most queries target recent events, but older data must remain readily available for occasional audits and investigations.Operational strain: High storage density on hot nodes complicates scaling, deployment, and cluster stability.Latency requirements: Even historical data sometimes requires sub-second query performance for internal tooling and analysis.This creates a clear opportunity: keep the most recent data on fast storage and migrate older, rarely read data to cheaper storage while preserving a consistent API. Done well, this can meet user and operational needs while greatly reducing our infrastructure spend.TimeSeries AbstractionBefore we dive into the cold storage solutions, here is a quick recap of how TimeSeries partitions its dataset into multiple tables, each covering a window of time we call Time Slices.Time Slices and Immutable WindowsThis enables several key optimizations, most notably allowing a table to become immutable once it crosses the write boundary, which lets us safely apply further optimizations. For more details, refer to our previous post.This slice information is critical and is maintained in a dedicated metadata table:Time Slice Metadata StorageCreating new Time Slices and maintaining their metadata is a primary responsibility of the TimeSeries control plane. The TimeSeries data plane uses this information to correctly route the read and write traffic to the provisioned tables.TimeSeries Data and Control PlaneWith that background, let’s look at the different solutions we built for data tiering.Solution 1: Streaming with Apache Kafka and FlinkOur first solution followed a familiar streaming pattern using Apache Kafka and Flink, where we streamed data to S3 in realtime while simultaneously persisting it to Cassandra.Streaming with Apache Kafka and FlinkGetting Data Into S3 EfficientlyTo optimize data streaming to S3, the system hash-partitions Time Series IDs into buckets. This partitions the stream and lets dedicated Flink tasks handle each bucket, ultimately batching and reducing the write throughput to S3. Flink workers batch events into Parquet files grouped by event time within the hour. These files are great for high-throughput streaming writes, but not for low-latency reads.Enter the Compaction job.Compaction Job to Optimize ReadsThe compaction job runs daily and merges small Parquet files into a single, optimized daily Parquet file per namespace.The job further optimizes the Parquet files in the following ways:Small Row Groups: Creates small (4–8 MB) row groups to minimize lookup cost. We can then use the Parquet Java library to perform range reads of row groups from S3. This is intentionally well below Parquet’s recommended row group floor — smaller groups were better because our reads are dominated by point/range lookups rather than full scans.Event Sorting: Sorts events within a row group by time, eliminating brute-force scans when querying for a time range.Bloom Filters: Caches Bloom filters and file metadata in EVCache, allowing the TimeSeries query planner to efficiently skip unnecessary reads from S3.Compacted and Sorted Parquet File LayoutOnce the compaction job completes, all compacted files per partition are recorded in the TimeSeries control plane, and the hot storage slices can now be truncated!On some of our largest datasets, this job typically takes about 12 hours, prioritizing lower compute costs over execution speed.Compaction Burndown Per DayStreaming Cold Tier ReadOnce compacted files are optimized in cold storage, they are ready to be read. The TimeSeries data plane fans out a given query across both the hot and cold tiers and merges their result. The users still use the same query interface:TimeSeries Tiered Storage Read PathThe Cold Tier Data Plane uses compaction metadata for aggressive planning and pruning, which dramatically reduces the S3 query fan-out. As a result, retrieving a full day of data requires at most three sequential S3 reads, even in the uncommon case where an ID spans two row groups. This yields a p50 latency of ~150 ms and a p99 latency of ~500 ms per read.Cold Tier Read Latency in SecondsAt the time of writing, the streaming cold tier implementation was processing up to 1,250 reads per second from cold storage globally:Cold Tier Read Requests Per SecondWhy not stop here?The streaming cold tier has delivered real savings, shrinking both Cassandra’s EBS footprint and the Cassandra backup footprint in S3. But the streaming infrastructure itself is expensive and adds moving pieces that widen the team’s on-call scope:Additional Infrastructure and Operational CostWe wanted to improve this further and asked ourselves:Can we avoid streaming data into the object store and the associated data transfer costs?Can we reduce the compute and operational overhead of new components?That led to a more radical question: Can we read directly from existing Cassandra backups in S3?Solution 2: Cassandra Cold Storage for Immutable DataAt Netflix, we back up Cassandra data into S3 at regular intervals for disaster recovery. The idea for tiering is simple:Read directly from these S3 backups instead of paying a separate data transfer cost to S3.Once TimeSeries marks a hot Time Slice as ready for cold storage, we can customize Cassandra to read directly from its backups, allowing us to delete the on-disk data copy. This would also incur minimal changes to the TimeSeries read path!New TimeSeries Read PathTo make this viable in production, we had to answer a series of “How…?” questions.How Can We Read the Backups Efficiently?We introduced a new compaction strategy in Cassandra, which we call ReadOnlyCompactionStrategy (ROCS). Here is how it works:Once a time slice crosses the user-configured cold-tier boundary, TimeSeries stops accepting writes for that time slice making it immutable. This immutability unlocks significant optimization opportunities:SSTable overlap: Standard strategies (LCS, TWCS) often produce SSTables that overlap in the token space, and so a single partition key may exist across multiple files.Read fan‑out: Because a read must touch every SSTable covering the key’s token range, this overlap turns a single point-read into multiple lookups, increasing latency across all tiers.ROCS re-compacts all SSTables once, aligning them precisely with token ranges:ROCS SSTable BoundariesROCS applies more broadly to all TimeSeries use cases, driving tail latency down on all storage tiers by reducing the SSTable fan-out during read operations:Tail Latency Improvement in Reads after ROCSOnce the immutable Time Slices have been optimized, it is time to trigger backups.How Would We Leverage Backups?Cassandra backs up every node in the cluster, organizing each backup on S3 as a declarative manifest, along with the SSTables backing the keyspace’s tables: {bucket}/ └── {prefix}/ ← cluster identity (env_backup/hash_app) └── {token}/ ← node identity (ring token) ├── META_V2/ ← manifests, one per snapshot │ ├── {snapshotInstantMs}.json │ ├── {snapshotInstantMs}.json │ └── ... └── SST_V2/ ← actual SSTable files └── {backupTimestamp}/ ← snapshot timestamp └── {keyspace}/ └── {table-with-uuid}/ └── {compression}/ └── {encryption}/ ├── {component-file} └── ...The backup manifest orchestrates the backup, listing the paths to all its SSTables:manifest.json ├── info │ ├── appName "cass-cluster" │ ├── region "us-east-1" │ ├── snapshotInstantMs 1748908800000 │ ├── backupPathPrefix "prod_backup/1234_cass/token" └── data[] └── [0] ├── keyspaceName "ks" ├── columnfamily "tbl-a1b2..." └── sstables[] └── [0] └── components[] ├── na-1-big-Data.db ├── na-1-big-Index.db ├── na-1-big-Filter.db ├── na-1-big-Statistics.db ├── na-1-big-Summary.db ├── na-1-big-CompressionInfo.dbAlongside the large Data.db file, backups include a compact set of index, metadata, and integrity files. This structure allows us to quickly locate, validate, and restore specific partitions or data ranges without scanning the entire dataset. Furthermore, since the manifest catalogs every S3 path, we can download most of these components directly to the Cassandra node (excluding the Data.db file) where they occupy negligible space. These local components enable efficient query planning before any data is read from S3.How Would Cassandra Read From Backups?Cassandra reads typically pull data from two sources: the Memtable, which holds recent unflushed writes, and flushed SSTables on durable storage. As of Cassandra 4.1, we can leverage pluggable Memtables to redirect reads from “cold” tables directly to the backup storage in S3.-- create table for a given Time SliceCREATE TABLE data_20260616_00_04 ( ... ..., PRIMARY KEY ((time_series_id, time_bucket, event_bucket), event_time, event_id, key)) WITH CLUSTERING ORDER BY (event_time DESC, event_id DESC, key DESC) ... AND compaction = ... AND compression = ... AND memtable = 'backupmemtable:timestamp=1781953200000' ← Custom memtable ...The timestamp marks the point at which the backup is guaranteed to cover the full table, and the table is guaranteed to be immutable.Opening a backup Memtable kicks off a state-machine initialization that pulls the index data from S3 onto the node once:State Machine for Cassandra Backup Memtable InitializationThis process ensures all SSTable components are downloaded reliably through several resilience mechanisms:Retries and backoff: All S3 operations and file-system cache writes use retries with exponential backoff.Resource isolation: Initialization runs on a dedicated thread pool, isolated from normal Cassandra operations.Partial download protection: If a downloaded component’s size doesn’t match the manifest, it is deleted and re-downloaded.DDL change protection: A .timestamp file marks completed initialization and ties it to the backup timestamp. If the table’s backup timestamp changes, this file is removed and initialization restarts for the new timestamp.Read protection: Memtable initialization is asynchronous; reads to an initializing memtable block for at most half the read RPC timeout.Once initialization has pulled every SSTable component (except Data.db) from S3 onto the local disk, the Memtable is ready to serve reads. Here is what the read process looks like:Reading from Cassandra Backup MemtablesTo minimize latency, the system parallelizes S3 reads across requests, SSTables, and individual chunks. A shared cache deduplicates fetches and prefetches data, so chunks are ready before they are needed.We further optimize cluster and table settings to reduce the number of S3 calls:Larger compression chunks: Reduce S3 calls per partition by reading fewer, larger chunks (accepting some over-fetch on small reads).Read repair disabled: Avoid expensive, unnecessary repair traffic against immutable, pre‑repaired backup data.Speculative retries disabled: Prevent S3’s higher latency from triggering redundant, overlapping reads.How Would We Know When It Is Safe To Read From Backups?However, before the Memtable can point to a backup, we must confirm two things across the whole ring, and we use Cassandra Virtual Tables to do that.First, that ROCS re-compaction succeeded:cqlsh> SELECT * FROM netflix_views.cluster_view WHERE keyspace_name = 'system_views' AND table_name = 'sstable_tasks';keyspace_name | table_name | host | value --------------+---------------+----------+------------------------------------------------system_views | sstable_tasks | 10.0.0.1 | [{"table_name":"<.>","kind":"compaction", ...}]system_views | sstable_tasks | 10.0.0.2 | [] <---- no active compactionssystem_views | sstable_tasks | 10.0.0.3 | []And second, that backups were fully captured (denoted by uploaded=True):cqlsh> SELECT * FROM netflix_views.complete_backups WHERE keyspace_name = 'my_ks' AND table_name = 'my_table';keyspace_name | table_name | timestamp | num_tokens | num_uploaded | uploaded --------------+------------+---------------+------------+--------------+----------my_ks | my_table | 1765211400000 | 3 | 3 | Truemy_ks | my_table | 1765213200000 | 3 | 2 | FalseHow Would We Automate This Entire Flow?The TimeSeries control plane automates the entire transition as slices cross the immutable boundary:Automating Time Slice Lifecycle TransitionsEach slice can be in any lifecycle stage at any time without impacting system availability, and the system remains resilient to delayed backups or lagging compactions.How Would Cassandra Handle The Additional Load?Serving data from S3 is much more CPU-intensive than reading from local storage. A sudden spike in read requests can overwhelm the Cassandra cluster and affect the hot path, turning a cost-saving feature into a reliability risk.To avoid this, cold reads can optionally run on a separate Cassandra cluster that points its backup Memtables at the hot cluster’s backups:Isolated Cold Tier Cassandra TopologyThe cold Cassandra cluster must match the original cluster in topology but need not match it in hardware! We can run the cold cluster on much smaller, cheaper, storage-light instances.Real World PerformanceCassandra Cold Tier was rolled out to the most storage‑intensive TimeSeries Abstraction clusters. It currently stores over 15 PB of compressed data in Cassandra cold storage and has allowed us to cut attached storage significantly on all affected clusters:Storage Reduction During Rollout: from 80% disk usage to 7%At the same time, it serves thousands of reads per second from cold tier storage in any given region:Cold Tier Read Requests Per SecondCassandra Cold Tier improves p90 latency by ~30% over the previous cold storage implementation, thanks to more efficient S3 access patterns and smaller read sizes, while keeping p99 latency under ~500 ms. Cassandra already handles bursts of cold reads gracefully via its chunk cache, so this design preserves that same resilience for the S3-backed cold tier:Cold Tier Read Latency: blue — p90 latency, brown — p99 latency; latency measured in seconds)Acknowledgements: Special thanks to our stunning colleagues who contributed to the TimeSeries Abstraction’s success and collaborated with us on the cold storage solutions: Kaidan Fullerton, Matt Lehman, Sumanth Pasupuleti, Carlos Matias Herrero, Nick Pavlakis, Bryan Keller, Francesco Di ChiaraTimeSeries Tiered Storage Journey: Kafka/Flink Streams to Native Cassandra Cold Reads was originally published in Netflix TechBlog on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.
