Caching is a super important aspect of system design, especially for large-scale systems. You can use a cache to store some data that is expensive to calculate so that it can be reused later without paying the same cost. For example, a website might cache the result of a database query instead of running that query every time someone opens a page.

The same is the case for large language models. Just like normal systems, caching in LLM applications also means storing stuff calculated as part of earlier requests so that we can reuse it later. This helps bring down processing costs and response time, especially when requests contain the same instructions, documents, or questions.

However, there are two types of ways we can cache stuff in LLMs: prompt caching and semantic caching. Both have the same general aim of reducing repeated work, but they work at different stages of a request. They also follow different rules.

In this article, we’ll look at how LLM caching works in detail. Here’s what you’ll learn:

Where to place the shared content in prompt caching

How prompt and semantic caching can work together

Disclaimer: This post is based on publicly shared details from various sources. References at the end. Please comment if you notice any inaccuracies.

When you send some text to an LLM, the LLM processes that text and generates a response. During processing, the text is divided into tokens. Each token is a small piece of text. A token can be a word, part of a word, or punctuation.

These tokens directly impact the cost. For a typical text-generation API, the cost has two main components:

Output tokens often cost more for obvious reasons. However, the input tokens can also cost a lot because of the size. Input can include much more than just the user’s latest question. For example, let’s say you have a customer-support application. Along with the current question, this application can also send a bunch of instructions telling the model how it should behave. It might also send examples of good answers. Relevant product documentation. Earlier conversation messages. In other words, a 10-word question can be part of a request made up of 1000s of input tokens.

Let’s say you have another application that sends a long product manual with every user request. This product manual is like an encyclopedia of all the information that the user might be looking for. One user might ask about the installation procedure. Another asks about troubleshooting. Maybe a third user asks about account settings. While their questions happen to be different, the answers are all there in the same long product manual that is part of every request.

There is another type of repetition as well. 100s of users might ask how to change their profile picture. But each user might write the query using slightly different words. In such a case, the model may end up generating the same rough answer again and again.

As you can notice, we have two opportunities to reduce this repetitive work and bring down costs:

What if the application can reuse the input information that has already been processed once? For example, the product manual.

What if the application can reuse a previously generated answer if it is suitable? For example, similar questions asked again and again.

Prompt caching is used to exploit the first opportunity. Semantic caching is for the second one. Let’s look at both in detail.

To make caching effective, you need a rule to decide whether something is fit for reuse. This rule is the most important part of building an effective cache setup.

For prompt caching, the rule is to match the beginning of the model’s input.

A typical text-generating transformer model works in two stages:

First, it processes the input. This stage is called prefill.

Second, it generates new tokens. This stage is called decoding.

When processing the input, the model converts text to numbers. This numeric representation helps the model use information it read earlier to generate output tokens down the line. Some of these representations are called keys and values. Or KV states.

Keys help the attention mechanism find out which earlier information is useful. Values are the actual representations of that information. A KV cache stores these intermediate results so that they can be reused. This is all part of the ordinary text generation flow in an LLM.

Prompt caching piggybacks on this reuse setup. It extends the whole thing for all the compatible input requests that share the same beginning. Let’s say you have the following two requests:

Request A: Support instructions + product manual + “How is installation configured?”Request B: Support instructions + product manual + “How are diagnostic logs enabled?”

As you can see, the support instructions and the product manual are shared across both requests. They are known as the shared prefix. The actual question is part of the suffix that keeps changing for each input request.

After the model processes Request A, the system can store the KV states for the shared prefix. When Request B arrives, the model can reuse those same KV states to process the new question and generate the answer. We’ve reused the intermediate computation for the common context. No recalculation. No reprocessing.

More AI-written code means more CI minutes. On default runners those minutes are slow and expensive.

Half the cost, so the bill shrinks as usage grows

Teams at Braintrust, Raycast, OpenRouter, Comcast and Jane Street trust WarpBuild with their GitHub Actions.

The switch is one runs-on change. Use code START50 for $50 in free credits.

For prompt caching to work, we need to put the shared content at the beginning of the request. Basically, the prefix position. The word “prefix” is important here because a token’s internal representation depends on the information that comes before it in the input.

In a typical causal language model, the tokens that come earlier in the prompt can’t look forward at the question that might appear later in the request. This is why a model can reuse the shared stuff from the beginning even when the final user question is completely different.

However, when you place a different question before the manual, it changes the way the manual is processed. The question impacts the representation of the text in the manual. The manual’s text is the same. But the processed version is completely different.

This is the reason we have to place fixed, stable instructions or any shared reference material before the request details that can change. Even if you place a seemingly unimportant timestamp or random request ID at the beginning of the input, it can stop the model from reusing a large chunk of shared stuff.

To be clear, even the instructions need to be “exactly” similar. Even if you have two instructions that might mean the same thing, you cannot use them interchangeably for prompt caching. There should be no change in wording. No change in document order. No change in request settings.

Simply caching the shared prefix doesn’t make the cost zero. Most LLM providers usually charge it at a discounted rate. Also, the output token charges stay the same because the model still generates a fresh answer.

For reference, Anthropic’s standard prompt-cache pricing uses a cache-read rate of 1/10th of the ordinary input rate. There are some exceptions for particular models. Its standard 5-minute cache write costs 1.25 times the ordinary input rate, while a 1-hour write costs twice that rate. These are total rates for the affected tokens, rather than additional charges on top of their ordinary input cost.

As an example, if processing a prefix normally costs $1, that five-minute pricing schedule makes the initial write cost $1.25 and a subsequent read cost $0.10. Therefore, one write followed by one read costs $1.35 instead of $2. The more the number of reads, the greater the savings. But if a cached prefix is never reused, you don’t get any benefit.

LLM provider and model rules also determine minimum eligible lengths, expiration, and cache-write pricing. Even if we repeat a prompt, it doesn’t guarantee a cache hit if the cache record has expired or is unavailable.

To summarize, prompt caching mainly reduces input-processing work and can reduce the wait time before we generate a response. You cannot use it to eliminate the work that goes into generating a long answer.

Semantic caching is usually part of the application that surrounds an LLM. It can also be a separate service that the application calls before it goes to the LLM for an answer. Consider a couple of example questions that you might ask an LLM:

“Where is the setting for dark mode?”“How can I switch the app to its dark theme?”

As you can notice, the same answer may be able to satisfy both questions if there’s no change to the application features in a major way. But a simple text comparison would consider them as two separate questions with two different answers. However, a semantic comparison can identify that they are essentially the same query asked in slightly different words.

To implement semantic caching, you need an embedding model. This type of model converts text into a list of numbers called a vector. These numbers represent features of the text in a way that makes it easy to compare two pieces of text.

The embedding model creates an embedding for the incoming question.

It searches question embeddings that are already stored for suitable candidate answers.

It checks whether a candidate answer is similar and valid for the current question.

If accepted, it returns the stored answer. Basically, a cache hit.

On a miss, it calls the LLM to generate a fresh answer. It may store the answer for future reuse.

As you can see, if there’s a cache hit, we don’t have to call the LLM to generate a fresh answer. No input and output charges in that case. However, tasks like embedding generation, lookup, and cache storage still use resources. So it’s not all free. Also, if we have a cache miss, we pay for the preliminary tasks as well as the LLM request. So a miss ends up being more costly.

The most difficult part with semantic caching is to find out how similar two separate questions are.

In a semantic cache, we calculate a similarity score and compare it to some threshold. You can think of this threshold like a cutoff for accepting that the questions are similar.

If we keep a very strict threshold, we end up rejecting many more answer candidates. While this can improve accuracy and reduce inappropriate reuse, it also rejects a lot of legitimate paraphrases of the question. However, if we go for a loose threshold, more answer candidates get accepted. This increases the overall cache hit rate. But it also increases the possibility of returning an unsuitable answer. There is no single, universal threshold that works perfectly for every application. You need to decide the threshold on a case-by-case basis.

Let’s say a user asks two questions about cancelling an order before it gets shipped and after it gets shipped.

As you can see, both questions are almost the same. Except for one critical word that changes the meaning. Both questions deal with cancellation and shipping. Their embeddings may also be quite close. But a short answer of “Yes, cancellation is available” could be the correct answer for one, but totally incorrect for the other.

Data types like numbers, negation, dates, product editions, and eligibility conditions can cause similar problems while determining similarity. For example, “Does the Basic plan include backups?” cannot automatically reuse the answer to a question about the Pro plan.

Also, we cannot consider a similarity score the same as the probability of an answer being correct. For example, even if you get a similarity score of 0.92 between two questions, it doesn’t mean there is a 92% chance that the cached answer is suitable for both. The way we interpret the score depends on the embedding model and comparison method. Some systems expose a distance score instead, in which smaller values indicate closer matches.

Therefore, we need to have an evaluation process to find out the effectiveness of a semantic caching implementation. This evaluation process has to find out if a particular stored answer can satisfy a new request correctly. For testing purposes, the development team can collect a bunch of requests, identify candidate answers, and label whether reusing a specific answer is the right way. The test suite should have examples that cover legitimate paraphrases as well as difficult near-matches. This way, we have a better chance to find out the optimal threshold value.

Lastly, we need to measure the proportion of requests answered from cache and the proportion of those answers that are actually appropriate. We cannot celebrate just by achieving a high hit rate. We can also have an additional verifier that checks border cases. However, such a verifier also contributes to costs and latency.

You can ask the same question multiple times. But every time, you might expect a different answer. For example, a question like “What is my order status?” depends on the customer and the current status of the order. Similarly, a question such as “Does it support offline access?” depends on what the word “it” means in the conversation’s context. Also, if the user requests an answer in a different language, we can’t automatically respond with a cached answer generated in English.

Therefore, for a semantic cache to work, we need information beyond just the question to make the right decisions. Depending on the application’s use case, we may need to include stuff about the customer or organization, access permissions, product version, language, relevant conversation state, and source-data version.

Also, we need to enforce these conditions as part of the application. You cannot expect an embedding model to find the details of a customer just because the user included a customer identifier in the input question. Typically, semantic-cache implementations need to have metadata filters so that searches can be restricted to an appropriate scope.

There is another example that shows a specific complication. If the user asks questions such as “What’s the weather in NYC?” and “NYC weather today?”, they might look like suitable matches. But their answers depend on whether the user is looking for current conditions or a daily forecast. While generating an answer, we need to consider location, date, forecast period, units, and freshness.

There are chances that a cached answer might appear like an excellent match for a new question. But the answer might still be wrong because the source information behind the answer may have changed.

Let’s say you have an application that allowed product returns to take place within 30 days. Now the company has changed the policy. The product return time period has been reduced to 14 days. However, a cached answer might still talk about the old time period of 30 days. In this case, you might ask the same question and get the cached answer, which is no longer valid.

This is why we need to have a strategy for invalidating the cache.

Invalidation means making a cache entry unavailable for reuse. We can use multiple approaches to build an ideal invalidation setup.

The first approach is to define a TTL value. A TTL (time-to-live) adds an expiration time to a cached record. Deciding the TTL value is the key. If we keep a short TTL, we place a strong limit on how long stale information can stay eligible within the system. But there is still some gap that will always remain. TTL cannot guarantee freshness of data before expiration. For example, if a policy changes immediately after an answer is cached, that answer can be stale till the TTL expires.

The second approach is to use versioning. You can allow reuse of data based on a specific version. For example, an answer cached under policy_version=12 is ineligible when the application expects version 13.

It’s much easier to have a version that contains the entire knowledge base. But there’s a disadvantage. One small update can make the entire knowledge base invalid. All the cached answers are suddenly stale. However, if we invalidate only those things that have changed, it’s much more efficient. Much more selective. But to make it work, we need to track which answers depend on which documents or records.

The third approach that can impact cache invalidation is the overall settings we have used to generate answers. Things like high-level instructions. Output formats. Model behaviour guidelines. And so on. These settings matter a lot when deciding when to invalidate a cache. If these settings are changed, we should invalidate the earlier answers.

Invalidating a prompt cache is different from its cousin. If the application sends an updated policy in the prompt, the modified prefix cannot reuse an incompatible old version from the point at which the policy changed. However, if there is an unchanged earlier portion, it might still be reusable. Also, if the application keeps providing the old policy as part of every input, prompt caching cannot automatically find out if the actual business rule has changed somewhere. It’s the application’s responsibility to fetch the current policy information and feed it to the model.

You can use prompt caching and semantic caching in the same setup. They are complementary. For example, you can have the application first look for a valid existing answer using semantic caching. If no such answer is available, only then does the application call the LLM and take advantage of any reusable prompt prefix.

If we get a semantic-cache hit, we don’t need to go for the main generation request. On the other hand, prompt caching reduces the cost of requests that still reach the LLM. We can also have an exact-answer cache that is checked before any semantic lookup happens. It can handle repeated identical requests cheaply.

It’s not necessary that we have a cache lookup at the very beginning of the flow. For example, if the application must retrieve current source versions to validate an answer, that particular check should happen even earlier.

Prompt caching is a natural choice in scenarios where you need to generate fresh answers for different questions. But those answers have to be generated from a shared context. This common context could be a general product manual, a set of instructions, stable tool definitions, or a long conversation history.

Semantic caching is great for cases where the same answer is good enough for many different requests. For example, product FAQs. Stable support instructions. However, semantic caching doesn’t work well when you want to generate highly personalized answers. Or if the answer depends on rapidly changing facts. Also, when there is a need for fresh creative output.

We need to have even greater care for action requests. For example, a cached message saying “The subscription has been cancelled” cannot be a substitute for making a real cancellation.

For a practical implementation of these caching strategies, we need to have some measurements. In the case of prompt caching, we need to measure how many input tokens are reused. This is because there is a major cost difference between serving a request that reuses a tiny prefix and one that reuses a long manual. For semantic caching, we need to evaluate metrics like accepted answers, freshness, and scope. Only those answers that satisfy the application’s quality requirements should be turned into reusable entries.

The ultimate goal with either approach is to lower cost and provide faster responses while preserving answer quality.

The distinction between reusing a KV prefix and reusing an answer is especially clear here.

In a RAG pipeline, semantic-cache invalidation becomes a provenance problem: a cached answer can depend on several retrieved chunks, each with its own version and access scope. How would you record that dependency set and test that a changed or revoked chunk cannot leak through a still-similar cache hit without flushing the entire cache?

I honestly don't think the cancelled-subscription case is a huge problem in practice. A decent setup routes anything that triggers an action around the cache, so only true repeat questions ever get a stored answer. Telling a new request apart from an old one is pretty easy at that routing step.

#35859. Introducing Clairic, a new System One class of extraction models

Alex Reneau,Â Michelle Chen,Â andÂ Kevin Flansburg

Today, we're announcing aÂ previewÂ of a new class of System One-style models: extraction models. Our first one, Clairic, is available hosted on Workers AI as @cf/cloudflare/clairic.We intend to release the model open-weights soon. Clairic is an extraction model that is able to extract, compute, estimate, and forecast values from unstructured inputs â all at a significantly higher accuracy, faster latency, and cheaper costÂ than traditional LLMs.

When System One models were announced by TypeSafe a month ago, it took the industry by storm. As referenced by TypeSafe in their blogÂ and defined by Daniel Kahnemanâs book Thinking, Fast and Slow, a System One model should be fast and precise, which contrasts a System Two model that is capable of deliberate reasoning (like LLMs). With this, TypeSafe introduced Jev â a model that is purpose-fit for a specific use case, and priced accessibly given its niche domain. It excelled where LLMs failed, helping users make decisions based on probabilities and well-typed outputs. The introduction of Jev prompted people to start thinking about a new class of models that were not LLMs and how to integrate them into their workflows.

We were inspired by the concept of System One models and started thinking about other tasks where LLMs are inefficient. There are many structured-output calls going to frontier LLMs today with the same shapes again and again: What's the invoice total? When was this delivered? How many days late is it? What will this repair cost? What will traffic look like over the next 24 hours?Â None of these have answers you can list out in advance, which is needed for a decision model to give probabilities against. That led us to the class of models we're introducing today: System One extraction models.

Until now, every System One model has been a decision model: Jev and ClefÂ take an input state and a list of questions and give probabilities against the inputs and your listed questions. ClairicÂ is the first model in a new class: System One extraction models. It is still fast, typed, and cheap, but it answers with valuesÂ directly extracted from the input, computed from it, or predicted beyond it.

Most model tasks ask for one of three kinds of output: a number, a choice from a fixed set, or open-ended text. Clairic handles the first, returning numbers with an 80% range, and also pulls typed values like names, dates and lists out of the input. Clef handles the second: it picks among options and returns a probability for each. LLMs handle the third. We call Clairic and Clef System One models because they answer in a single pass, without reasoning or generating tokens. They charge only for input and typically respond in under a second, while an LLM that reasons through the same step takes several seconds.

And because it generates no tokens, it can't produce a mistyped answerÂ or âhallucinateâ in the same way as an LLM (though it can, of course, make mistakes). Outputs are a value of the type you asked for, or null when theÂ model fails to find an answer in the input. It also comes with confidence scores against the outputs to help you evaluate if it is appropriate to trust the model or to take a second look.

Hereâs how extraction models fit into the landscape of System One and System Two models:

Typed values: spans, numbers, dates, times, lists, distributions, with calibrated probabilities

Typed decisions: options with calibrated probabilities

Continuous, but typed and bounded by your schema

What's the amount? When does it happen? How much will it be?

Which category is it?Â Is it legitimate? Which action should we take?

Why did it happen? How should we approach it? Can you fix it?

Yes: every answer is a value of its declared typeÂ (or null), inside your bounds

Yes: answers are always one of your options

Together, these models can work together in unison to help you get closer to parsing through real-world data, making decisions on inputs, and then taking actions. Extraction models turn raw input into typed values, decision models turn values into decisions, and LLMs turn decisions into words.

Clairic is designed differently than an LLM. Similar to a decision model, it only processes input tokens with a single forward pass, and thus has no charge for output tokens. It is much faster, cheaper, and more accurateÂ than an LLM for certain use cases.

A request is a stateÂ (the text to read, plus up to four optional images) and a map of typed fields. You name each field, give it a type and optional plain-language instructions, and get back one typed answer per field, all from one parallel pass. There is no reasoning and no output tokens â everything computes in a single forward pass, which means it is both fast and cheap.

A specific span of the input, with its offsets

A number read orÂ computed, honoring integerÂ and decimals

Calendar dates and valid times, in ISO form

Matching text, number or date, in input order

A distribution inside your [min, max], on your stepÂ grid, linear or log scale.

Every scalar answer comes with p_nullÂ (the probability that the value isnât in the inputs) and confidence. Every estimateÂ answer comes with a median and an 80% interval (p10Â to p90), plus all 99 percentiles on request.Â There's no limit on the number of fields: if they don't fit beside the input in one pass, the server splits them into parallel passes that each see the whole input, then merges the answers.

Here are some examples to illustrate the modelâs features. Of course, using these features in a workflow would require appropriate inputs.

Extraction is probably the most common job handed to LLMs today: "return the invoice number, vendor and due date as JSON." It works most of the time, but the failure modes are hard to catch. The output may not be valid JSON, a digit can be misreadÂ as it's generated, and once a text excerpt comes back, there's no way to trace it to where it appeared in the source. Most people build extraction pipelines to combat this, with multiple layers of parsing, schema validation, retries and spot checks. On top of that, you pay for reasoning and output tokensÂ on every field of every document.

Clairic operates differently; it doesnât generate text answers. Instead, you get:

Letâs walk through an example to illustrate the ways Clairic can extract values from unstructured data and make estimates. Take a customer support email:

Hi, order A-88412 arrived on Sept 28, 2026Â with a cracked screen and a dented corner. I paid $649.00 plus $52.10 tax. It's now Oct 9, 2026 and I'd like this fixed or refunded. Thanks, Dana

From a Worker, you would make a request to Clairic to process this data:

Clairic returnsÂ the extracted values, spans in the input, probability that it is null (p_null) and confidence score:

Hereâs a real-life photo of a receipt â the text is not perfect and the angle of the image doesnât help its legibility. We passed this image to Clairic to see what it could extract:

As you can see, it was able to extract all the values from the images, alongside a confidence score. It also correctly stated that there was no discount shown in the receipt, giving the value as null.

Some values aren't in the input at all, but the input carries evidence for them. For example, values might not be in plain text but can be discerned from values around it. If you ask an LLM for an estimation, you usually get a single number with no sense of how sure the model is. It will make safe guesses or hallucinate, or reason its way around the answer. If you land on an estimate, any downstream processing can't tell a confident $180 from an unconfident $180, so it can't help you decide what is appropriate to automate in the circumstances.Â It is also a lot slower and more expensive to do reasoning through LLMs.

A decision model can approximate an estimate by choosing among buckets ("under $100", "$100â500", â¦), but buckets are coarse, every bucket adds input tokens, and each new category adds more sources of confusion for the model during its decision making process.

Clairic returns a distributionÂ over the range you declare: a point value, a median, an 80% interval, and every percentile on request. The estimate is designed to fall inside your bounds, so there's nothing to clamp or round afterward. The width of the interval reflects data confidence: a narrow range signals high certainty, while a wide range indicates low certainty, information you can use to route another check.

Hereâs another example, where Clairic looks at historical home prices and comparable sales, to determine an estimate :

Values always fall inside your bounds, and the width of the interval shows how much the input informs the prediction: price is narrow ($370,000-$470,000), days on market is wide (24-148). Because fields are unlimited and answered in parallel, you can score many items in one call (one estimate per candidate, lead, or listing) and sort them in code.

Forecasting values in a time series is quite hard for generalized models â it usually means you have to either build a specific pipeline per metric (parse the data, fit a model, tune it, deploy it), or you paste 36 months of numbers into an LLM and ask for the next three. The first is accurate but really expensive and time-consuming to set up for every new series. The second is easy, but you get point forecasts with no intervals, forecasts that shift depending on how the prompt is worded, and answers with limited confidence.

Clairic sits between the two â it is not claiming to replace a dedicated time-series model, but it is a little faster and cheaper than your regular LLM.Â A forecastÂ field takes the history as plain text in stateÂ and returns, for every step ahead, a value and an 80% interval, inside the bounds you declare. It reads the history the way you already have it, whether that's a CSV export, a pasted dashboard, or rows mixed with notes, and may often work with no need to clean up your data beforehand.

To see how that holds up on real data, we used a public series: the number of people the Transportation Security Administration (TSA) screens at U.S. airport checkpoints each day. Each morning we asked Clairic for the next day's count, given the real counts so far, for 21 days in a row:

In actuality, TSA screened 2,419,474 people that day, which is right around the median 2,419,283 that Clairic predicted.

Data: TSA checkpoint travel numbers, accessed Oct. 15, 2026.

Across the 21 days, Clairic's forecasts were off by 3.3% on average, and 17 of the 21 actual counts landed inside its 80% interval, which follows what an 80% interval should do. It picked up the weekly rhythm from the numbers alone: quieter Tuesdays and Saturdays, busier Thursdays, Fridays, and Sundays.

The misses are also interesting: three of the four days outside the interval fall on the Columbus Day weekend, when more people flew than the previous weeks suggested. Clairic forecasts from the patterns in the series but doesn't account for events the series doesn't show, like holidays.

These models are designed to fit alongside your existing agentic workflows. An extraction model predicts values, a decision model decides what to do with these values, and an LLM takes action with them. It is a perfect marriage between System One and System Two models. It bridges the existing gap, where you either have to manually extract data for LLMs, or have an LLM parse through messy data (which is costly, time-consuming, and can lead to hallucinations). With System One extraction models, you can work with real-world data with more speed, efficiency, and precision.

Here's an example of the damaged-product claim from earlier, illustrating how all the models can work together. Â We built this into a live demo you can try here.

Each step gets cleanerÂ input than the one before. Clef decides from a five-line summary of typed values instead of a free-form email, which can also be susceptible to prompt injection. The LLM never sees the email, only the decision and the predictions it needs, so there are fewer numbers for it to misuse. Every step is typed and auditable, and only one step generates text. In the all-LLM version of this pipeline, all three steps are generative calls, and every value in the reply has to be checked by hand.

We ran this pipeline against an all-LLM version with GLM-5.3 writing the reply in both. In the all-LLM version, GLM-5.3 also does the extraction and the decision, from the same email, policy and prompts:

The cascade finished in 19.3 seconds against 61.7 seconds: 69% less time, or about 3.2 times faster. Clairic and Clef handled extraction and the decision in under a second combined, where GLM-5.3 took 38 seconds for the same two steps. It also costs 49% lessÂ to use the cascaded pipeline vs the all-LLM pipeline. With GLM, both pipelines got the facts and the decision right in every run, but Clairic's repair estimate was identical each time, while GLM-5.3's changed on every run ($250, $250 and $220, with different ranges each time).

Notably, under the all-LLM pipeline both Gemma 4 and Qwen failedÂ at this task, as they were unable to deduce values like repair_cost from the inputs, showing how LLMs are not great at data extraction tasks.

Today, we're releasing a hosted endpoint for Clairic on Workers AI. We intend to release the model with open weights soon. We wanted to take the time first to introduce the concept of a System One extraction model, so you can start thinking about how this class of model would fit into appropriate workflows.

The current endpoint is an early checkpoint and we expect it to get better. Here are our early impressions:

We'll keep working on the arithmetic, estimation and forecasting sides of the model with each checkpoint. After some more work, we plan to releaseÂ the model open-weights for everyone to play around with as well.

Clairic is available as a preview on Workers AI as @cf/cloudflare/clairic. Call it from a Worker with env.AI.run(), or from anywhere with the REST API. We have full model docs here, as well as a new docs explainerÂ on how the extraction model API looks.

P.S. Since you liked the etymology of the name Clef, hereâs how we landed on the name Clairic.Â We started with a desire to keep the name of the model thematically and sonically similar to Clef. Clair came to mind, sharing the same âclâ sound, as well as roots in music (âClair de Luneâ). More importantly, we wanted the name to be descriptive to the nature of the model. The Clairic model should be able to help you with clericalÂ tasks like extracting data clearlyÂ from a corpus of inputs and upholding accuracy in tasks like bookkeeping. The prediction aspect of the model leans into the âClairâ root â allowing you to estimate and predict future values, similar to clairvoyance. Lastly, we like the idea of having this be [Cl]oudflareâs [AI R]egression model. Thus, Clairic was born into the world. We hope you enjoy it.

#35861. Why Shopify Migrated From React Native

Most teams record session replays at a flat sample rate, then spend the next incident scrolling through hundreds of sessions that have nothing to do with the bug.

This hands-on Sentry workshop shows you how to capture the replays that matter:

In 2020, the Shopify engineering team decided to go all in on React Native. It saved them a ton of time and money. By using React Native, the developers didn’t have to implement the same feature in both Kotlin and Swift to make it work on Android and iOS. Sure, the framework came with its requirements. But the idea was very successful at the time.

However, in 2026, AI coding agents have made a huge difference to the economics of building mobile apps. Earlier, if you implemented something with React Native, you could justify the savings that came because of it. But now, AI agents have become so good at coding that building the same feature in Swift and Kotlin is much cheaper.

In this article, we’ll look at how Shopify decided to move out of React Native and how they migrated to native mobile development. Here’s what we’ll cover:

Disclaimer: This post is based on publicly shared details from various sources. References at the end. Please comment if you notice any inaccuracies.

As you might be aware, an iPhone runs Apple’s iOS, and Android phones run Android. Both these OS provide a bunch of facilities to display the UI, handle notifications, and talk to the device hardware.

In native mobile development for a particular OS, you build an application directly using the languages, frameworks, and tools for that platform. This means Swift for iOS and Kotlin for Android. To be clear, a programming language is different from a UI framework. For example, Swift and Kotlin are programming languages. However, Apple’s SwiftUI and Android’s Jetpack Compose are frameworks. These frameworks give developers the tools to create the real UI with various components like text, buttons, lists, layouts, and animations.

To build natively for both platforms, you need to maintain two implementations of the mobile application. One for Android. Another for iOS. Sure, you can share the backend services for both platforms, but the client code will still be separate.

However, React Native lets you share much of that implementation across both iOS and Android. It’s a framework for building mobile apps using React and JavaScript (or TypeScript). The main benefit of React Native is that many components and application code you write using this framework can work with both iOS and Android. You don’t need to implement every screen independently in Swift and Kotlin. This is because React Native sits on top of the native UI components that are backed by their respective platforms. For example, if you make a component in React Native, it can create the appropriate iOS or Android views without the need for developers to write any platform-specific code.

To be clear, sharing code doesn’t mean that every platform difference is completely gone. You would still have some features that might need platform-specific coding. Also, you need to build, test, and release the application for each OS.

Right now, you’re your agent’s context engine. You write the rules files, maintain the skills, and paste in the Slack thread it missed.

But hand-curated context goes stale. And when there are conflicting answers, your agent can’t tell which is right. You pay for it in higher token bills and longer reviews.

The 8-levels of AI maturity and where teams get stuck

How a context engine curates context and resolves conflicts before your agent writes a line of code

Live demo: token savings in the same coding task, and use cases beyond code gen

Bonus: 2 open source tools you can use today.

The Shopify engineering team went with React Native in 2020. They wanted to solve three problems that were more or less linked.

The first problem was that you had to implement every feature two times with native development. One time for each platform. The second was that you couldn’t share developers between platforms. A developer was confined to their tech stack. An iOS developer couldn’t work on the Android version. Neither could the Android developer work on the iOS version. Not a great way to utilize the developers in a team.

The third problem was that you had to maintain feature parity across both versions. Feature parity is when every version of the app has the same features and capabilities. Let’s say, if you have a cool feature that works on iOS, but it takes another month to be available on Android, you can say that the two versions are out of parity. If you don’t maintain this parity, you risk alienating the user base of the platform that usually runs behind.

Also, when you have two versions of the app, you need to change both versions whenever there’s a change in any requirements. Even if the change is something as small as a text change. As you can see, this is a continuous cost problem that is present throughout the life of the application. You also need to have more coordination between the different platform teams while planning releases, announcements, and so on.

By going with React Native, Shopify reduced the impact of these problems in a big way. No need to implement every feature twice. No need to coordinate changes across multiple platform teams. It also made mobile development easy for developers already familiar with React and TypeScript. This is great because you could easily move people between projects. Plus, you also get to select developers from a much bigger TypeScript or JavaScript talent pool.

As a framework, React Native has a lot of benefits. We have seen that already in the earlier section. But the framework also needs maintenance. This means additional costs.

The Shopify engineering team had to spend effort on optimizing the framework’s performance. They made improvements to the React Native foundations and contributed to framework upgrades. They also had to deal with changes to external dependencies. You can think of a dependency as a piece of software that the application relies on. If there’s a change in the dependency, you need to make changes to the application as well.

Native development is different from using a framework. The application has greater synergy with the platform and first-party tooling. You can use the tools provided by the platform’s own developers. Also, you have fewer dependency layers between the application code and the platform (iOS or Android).

Shopify was already using native code for some features. For example, widgets and watch applications. Also, for some background processing. You could say that React Native and native development coexisted within the application for several years. Of course, the benefit equation tilted more towards React Native.

However, the rise of coding agents made big changes to the equation. As you know, a large language model (LLM) can generate code quite easily. A coding agent combines an LLM with special tools that can read code files, edit code, and run tests. It could also check why things are failing and make changes to handle those failures.

By 2025, these agents had improved so much that Shopify had to take another look at its mobile strategy. To test the waters, the Shopify engineering team rebuilt some core parts of its application in Swift and Kotlin. These prototypes proved that the coding agents could take an implementation on one platform as a reference and write the equivalent code for the other platform.

For example, you can have an iOS feature that provides all the details about the UI elements, actions, and error conditions. An agent can use those details and build an Android equivalent. Sure, developers had to check whether the outcome was good enough and followed the conventions of Android and the overall architecture. However, suddenly, you had developers who could use these agents to code stuff outside their primary stack without a lot of effort.

Of course, with native development, two implementations would still be there. Both will need to be maintained. But Shopify claims that coding agents have reduced the work to such a level that concerns about duplication are no longer as important for making decisions as they were in 2020.

To carry out the migration to native, Shopify had to choose the best pathway to migrate the existing applications. You have two ways to do so.

First, we have brownfield migration. In this approach, you change an existing application gradually. New and old implementations run together as individual parts are replaced. While the risk is lower, the migration takes more time. Also, you have to manage the integration between the new and old implementations.

Second, we have a greenfield approach. In this approach, you create a fresh implementation. Developers get more freedom to design a new architecture. However, you need to build an almost complete replacement before getting rid of the existing product. There’s no incremental change.

Shopify had used the brownfield approach earlier for some of its large applications. The development methods at the time would have taken too long. However, when they tried the new prototypes, the team found out that a fresh native implementation would be faster. The existing React Native application was a solid reference point for how things should work.

Therefore, Shopify chose the greenfield approach.

They first shipped the Shop app. This app was used by shoppers. The larger Shopify app, which is used by merchants, was migrated later. For reference, the Shopify app has more than 300 screens. Also, many features, such as widgets. And an Apple Watch application.

When planning the migration, the Shopify engineering team found that if you asked a model to rebuild a large feature in one attempt, you got mediocre results. The output code was difficult to maintain. Also, it was very difficult for developers to properly review big features.

Therefore, Shopify built Helix to support the migration. Helix breaks the migration into small steps that can be reviewed. With Helix, you can have a developer select a screen, and Helix proposes small pieces of migration in the best possible order. Each migration piece has to go through the review process. Only then does it become the foundation for the next piece.

For example, let’s say you have an order detail screen. An initial checkpoint can finalize the structure of the screen and how navigation should work. Later checkpoints will deal with other features such as order summary and customer information. Each checkpoint is small enough that developers can review it properly.

Four types of checks are done to make sure everything works as intended.

First, you have the behavioural tests. You take expected actions on the app and check what happens. Second, you have the visual review. In this, we check how the new UI looks compared with the old reference application.

Next, you have adversarial code reviews. Two reviewers look for problems in the code. They try to find issues that might stay hidden behind a normal workflow. Lastly, we have another developer review where we check the results of the previous tests. If everything meets expectations, things proceed further.

The best part about Helix is that the team gets continuous feedback while the change is still small.

Shopify has a design philosophy that separates app logic from the UI.

For example, you can have a form with rules about valid or invalid inputs. To test them, you don’t need a visible text box. They can receive an input value and return a result.

Shopify’s architectural principle is to keep the business logic independent of the UI. The idea is that the business logic can run headlessly. You can expose the application state and actions through a CLI. This way, the agents can check state, navigate between sections, and perform actions.

While navigating like this without a UI might sound strange, it makes it easy to check how things work. You can have an agent take an action and check the state. There’s no need to make sense of screenshots and find out where a button is located. This is why behavioural checks can be made quite fast.

The Shop app was live on the app stores as a native application in 12 weeks. There were many interesting stats.

The app startup time on iOS went down from 3200 ms on React Native to approximately 2400 ms on the Native version. The startup time on Android had even greater gains, going from around 4400 ms to 2200 ms. Almost half. The crash-free sessions went up. Also, the app size on Android was down from 293 MB for React Native to 184 MB for the native version.

All in all, these results have been quite encouraging for the Shopify engineering team. Of course, their approach combines a lot of things that make it successful. For starters, you have direct use of platform tech. You also have an existing application, which can act as a strong reference point. Also, the migration process is made smooth with small implementation checkpoints and quality checks.

The main thing we can take away from Shopify’s case is to have a fast feedback loop that can check if the code generated by AI agents is good enough. This is the key to making big migrations like this safe for the users.

React Native is the Future of Mobile at Shopify

Helix: The internal tools powering Shopify app’s native migration

Migrating Shop app from React Native to native

The headless CLI is the part I'd steal. Once agents can read app state and trigger actions directly, behavioral checks become assertions on state instead of screenshot parsing, which is much cheaper and less flaky than a computer-use loop. I'm curious how the visual review step worked, though. Was it automated screenshot diffing against the React Native reference, or people comparing by eye? That's the one check the CLI can't cover, and across 300+ screens it seems like where small drift would hide.

Well, the question is how long would shopify continue being relevant

#35862. What smart people are saying about Anthropic's IPO paperwork

Anthropic is ready to IPO. Analysts and onlookers are weighing in.

On Monday, the AI lab filed its hotly anticipated S-1 paperwork. The prospectus offered an inside look at Anthropic's financials: a net loss of about $42 billion in 2025 and revenue of $4.6 billion. It plans to trade under the ticker symbol ANT.

The S-1 sets the stage for a blockbuster IPO. Here's what smart people are saying about Anthropic's filing:

Venture capitalist Sarah Guo opened her X post with a big "CONGRATS" to Anthropic on the S-1 filing.

Guo shared her first takeaways: the inflection in operating profit, the focus on novel discovery, the mismatch between consumption-based revenue and long-term compute obligations, and more.

"I am curious to see how 1) a company with strong mission changes - or doesn't - how it operates under quarterly public inspection and 2) how public opinion may change when retail owns a piece of the upside," Guo wrote.

Gary Marcus, one of the AI industry's most outspoken critics, wrote on X that Anthropic provided financial statements through June 30 — but omitted a full Q3 update.

He predicted that the company's economics had not improved, and alleged that Anthropic was "trying to skirt the truth."

Earlier this month, Business Insider reported that Anthropic told investors it generated $16.8 billion in third-quarter revenue, up 45% from the prior quarter.

Add BI in Google so our reporting is easier to find when you’re searching for what matters.

Ann Bordetsky was a partner at New Enterprise Associates' technology practice before founding her own firm, Elora Capital. She wrote on X that the S-1 was a "juicy read."

The filing will set "a (high) bar for how capital markets evaluate AI startups," Bordetsky wrote.

In a note sent to Business Insider, Harrison Rolfes said Anthropic's filing shows just how fast the company is growing — and just how expensive that growth is.

His main positive highlight: the $11.6 billion in revenue in the second quarter. His big worries: the $321.4 billion in future lease payments that haven't begun yet, and the $265.6 billion in fixed minimum purchase commitments.

"The compute commitments are enormous, and the suppliers are also lenders," Rolfes wrote, pointing to financing arrangements with Google, Amazon, and Broadcom. "The price range, Q3 revenue and the total compute commitment are still blank, so the next amendment should fill in a lot."

Finally, Rolfes said it's important for investors to note that Anthropic's founders retain outsize voting power. Put plainly, "public shareholders won't control the company," he wrote.

Sam Ro, a financial journalist and former Business Insider reporter, wrote in his Substack that Anthropic's longwinded AI risk section shouldn't make investors fret.

If AI really does create an existential catastrophe, he wrote, "having money might not be your biggest concern."

He also said it's anybody's guess whether Anthropic's stock price will rise or fall after it opens on the market.

The company hasn't been consistently profitable, he said, but "a company's valuation depends less on what it earned (or lost) in the past and more on what it's expected to earn in the years to come."

On X, Gavin Baker wrote that Anthropic's annual recurring revenue has "likely gone vertical," even after the company cut prices on its AI tokens.

"I am shocked, absolutely shocked," he wrote. "$100b plus in year-end ARR looks possible again."

Jacob Bourne, an analyst at EMARKETER, a sister company to Business Insider, wrote in an email that Anthropic's filing comes as investors are increasingly wary of debt-fueled AI infrastructure projects.

"Anthropic's decision to press ahead is particularly noteworthy given its own warnings about AI risks, signaling a willingness to face heightened public scrutiny," he wrote.

Bourne also said the S-1 comes as the cost of developing frontier models remains "eye-watering." It's all evidence that companies are turning to public markets for fresh investments "to remain at the cutting edge of AI development," he wrote.

SemiAnalysis, the research firm founded by Dylan Patel, posted the "most mind blowing stat" it had seen in the S-1. It cited Anthropic's raised capital, compared to its cash and investments.

Anthropic is "growing at a rapid pace" and "profitable on an operating income basis as of the June quarter," SemiAnalysis wrote.

"This is likely the most efficient scaling of a business in the history of capitalism," the firm wrote.

Brad Gerstner heaped his praise on Anthropic. He congratulated the team on "another important milestone!"

Altimeter will partner with Anthropic through "major participation in the IPO on top of our existing ownership," Gerstner wrote. He used an American flag and a rocket emoji.

Gerstner's venture capital firm is a longtime investor in Anthropic, co-leading the AI lab's Series H in May.

During an interview on CNBC, Matt Murphy, one of Anthropic's earliest investors, said he's increasingly bullish on the AI lab.

"You wait your entire 25-year career to find a technology wave like this," he said. "To be able to have invested in the leader early is just phenomenal."

Vivek Gopalan is an investor at 8VC, the venture capital firm cofounded by Joe Lonsdale. He posted a graph from Anthropic's S-1 showing rising revenue per dollar of compute.

"You need to believe that this is monotonic and increasing," Gopalan wrote.

Dan Shipper had "big news" to share: a joke about Anthropic's ever-present safety focus. He celebrated that the S-1 "doesn't say 'or it might kill / unemploy everyone' in the first paragraph!"

The CEO of Every, an AI agent startup, called it a "win for humanity."

Dadisi Olutosin said on LinkedIn on Monday that Anthropic’s IPO filing raised a question for potential investors: “When does an extraordinary company become an overpriced investment?”

Olutosin wrote that at a reported valuation of $1.5 trillion to $2 trillion, buyers would pay about 101 times the company’s trailing revenue, compared with roughly 20.5 times the revenue pace at which Series H investors bought in.

“Innovation can transform an industry,” Olutosin said. “That doesn’t make every entry price attractive.”

Sinan Aral said Anthropic’s potential valuation could make it one of the world’s most valuable companies, but that its infrastructure commitments also pose a “tremendous economic risk.”

Aral told CNBC's "Squawk Box" show on Monday that he has questions about what the AI lab’s margins and profitability would look like as it spends hundreds of billions of dollars on infrastructure. Aral also said there are many risks described in the company’s S-1, including the possibility that its products could act on their own.

“The question is, where is the enduring value?” Aral said. “And I think the enduring value is going to come from companies that can demonstrate enterprise profitability, productivity, and actual value add rather than just providing intelligence.”

Nick Moran wrote on LinkedIn said Anthropic’s $80.7 billion loss in the first half of 2026 was largely an accounting story.

“Anthropic lost $80 billion on paper mostly because it became more valuable,” he wrote.

Moran said the bigger question for investors is the price they’ll pay. While Anthropic’s revenue growth remained “spectacular,” Moran wrote, it slowed from the second quarter to the third as the company sought a higher valuation.

“The loss is an accounting story. The multiple is the real one,” Moran wrote. "Institutional and retail demand is real. I wouldn't be surprised to see it end up on the higher end of the range."

Brian Sozzi wrote on LinkedIn that he has three takeaways from Anthropic’s IPO prospectus: the banks leading the offering, the AI lab’s adjusted profits, and its warning about risks to humanity.

Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley are the lead underwriters and “will be cleaning up here on fees,” Sozzi wrote on LinkedIn, adding that Anthropic was profitable on an adjusted operating and net basis in the first six months of the year.

Venture capitalist and "All-In" podcast host Chamath Palihapitiya praised Anthropic in a brief X post after the S-1 dropped.

"Ant is an amazing business…," Palihapitiya wrote in a Monday noon X post.

The VC has previously been critical about Anthropic, advising consulting firms not to deploy Anthropic and OpenAI's products.

"If you are running a consulting business and you are deploying Anthropic or OpenAI directly into your organization (I'm looking at you PwC and Accenture) you are letting the fox into the hen house," Palihapitiya wrote on X in May.

Anish Acharya, a general partner at Andreessen Horowitz, said his earlier predictions about Anthropic's financials have largely held true, calling it a gross-margin-positive profile and "obviously a tremendous business."

Acharya's post on Monday was a repost of a September post, in which he laid out some predictions for Anthropic.

He said in the earlier post, "Overall I think the market underweights how sophisticated anthropic has been in aligning its business interests with its technical and mission interests."

Aaron Levie, the CEO of enterprise cloud company Box, said the industry is still in the early stages of AI adoption, as most companies have not started using AI agents in full force.

As deploying agents increases token consumption, the average Fortune 500 customer's spending on Anthropic products could rise, he said in a Monday X post.

"This S-1 gives you a sense of both the strength of the frontier lab business model - even amidst massive competition - and how early we are in the build out of AI," Levie wrote.

#35866. Beyond the patch: Protecting your NetScaler gateway against future vulnerabilities

The recent disclosure of a major vulnerabilityÂ in Citrix NetScaler pointed to a widespreadÂ weak point: a login page is an attackÂ surface that can be used to compromise and access an application server. Indeed, the disclosuresÂ included an actively exploited flaw that allowed attackers to execute commands on affected gateways without signing in. As with any emergency patch, admins had to weigh cutting off or disrupting their usersâ access with the risk of delaying a critical security update.

If youâre a NetScaler customer and you havenât patched your instance, stop reading and go do that. This was a bad one.Â Once youâve finished the patch, weâll explore how to avoid a future fire drill by laying additional security controls.

This issue extends beyond NetScaler and can be applied to any internal application available on the Internet. Remote desktop portals, administrative consoles, and other publicly accessible authentication pages all deserve the same scrutiny: Does the intended audience require unrestricted Internet reachability? And can an attacker bypass this authentication check to reach the application's server?

Citrix released software updates to address the flaw, and Cloudflare followed with an emergency web application firewall (WAF) ruleÂ on October 1. But having a patch available does not guarantee safety: every instance has to be identified, updated, and tested. Applying updates across a production deployment is painful â it can result in downtime or cause disruptions to employees who still need their desktops throughout that process. Customers, patients, and others dependent on users of a remote desktop definitely donât care about your security patch.

Using a web application firewall (WAF) can buy some additional time before a patch can be fully rolled out, but itâs reactive and does not account for the next exploit thatâs discovered. Cloudflare and other security vendors do their best to cover variations and similar attacks. But AI is hastening how rapidly attackers can discover new and novel variants. Thatâs why it is crucial to build defense in depth, to ensure that no specific software failure or exploit will lead to a critical security issue.

Cloudflare combines access policies, web application security, and restricted origin connections to protect the authentication service before a new vulnerability is disclosed. Access controls limit who can reach the application server; WAF inspection evaluates web requests for attacks; origin restrictions prevent direct connections from bypassing those defenses. These reduce exposure without waiting for a new exploit signature or replacing the existing desktop platform.

Citrix's September 27, 2026 bulletinÂ reported observed exploitation of CVE-2026-88771 and CVE-2026-88772. The first allows unauthenticated command execution on affected appliances, including in their default configuration. The second affects configurations using Datagram Transport Layer Security, or DTLS. Further advisories on October 3Â and October 8Â addressed additional vulnerabilities in SAML configurations. These exploits allowed attackers to execute arbitrary scripts on target machines and also execute denial of service attacks.

CISA's alertÂ and Mandiant's technical investigationÂ cover the vulnerabilities, observed exploitation, and response guidance in more detail. For details of the available web application protection, see Cloudflare's emergency WAF release for CVE-2026-88771.

In a typical Citrix deployment, the user authenticates through NetScaler Gateway, which then uses a secure ticket authority to pass through to the StoreFront, which presents the applications and desktops available to that user. The native-installed Citrix app then uses that information to establish a separate connection using Citrix's Independent Computing Architecture (ICA) protocol. The gateway validates the ticket before proxying the desktop connection. Citrix documents these as distinct stages of the connection workflow. The entire exploit stems from the fact that the Gateway has to be publicly accessible on the Internet, otherwise users would not be able to initiate their desktop connection.

The best thing that you can do, after patching all your instances, is move any publicly accessible login pages or applications behind single sign-on before the request ever hits the target server. Cloudflare AccessÂ can enforce an independent access policyÂ before the request reaches the existing gateway server. The Citrix environment continues to determine which desktop the user may launch and to validate the resulting session ticket. The additional boundary ensures that an attacker could never get to the Gateway server to try running specific exploits. They would only see the Cloudflare Access login page.

That decision no longer depends on recognizing an exploit signature and blocking that way, but rather on a set of Zero Trust policies that determine if someone should even be there to begin with. More attacks like this are coming, and adopting Zero Trust controls throughout your network is the single most important thing you should do next.

This follows the principle described in Cloudflare's own architecture as customer zero: reduce exposure and use independent defenses so that one flaw does not become a compromise. Here, the practical starting point is the service that users reach before they enter their applications.

Protecting the web authentication path adds a boundary in front of the existing Citrix controls. It does not automatically extend that boundary to other gateway services, including DTLS-enabled listeners. Those interfaces still need their own exposure review and applicable security updates, even when the desktop sessions they support already require authentication.

Changing a DNS record and enforcing Access policies are not enough. If an attacker can connect to the original address or an alternate hostname, they can avoid the controls placed in front of it. Access enforces a specific hostname: if the authentication server can be reached via an IP address or alternative hostname, then the Access policy enforcement is worthless. Itâs important to take steps to ensure that all traffic comes from a request that was validated by Access. There are a few different approaches to accomplish this, based on your internal architecture.

Cloudflare TunnelÂ is the most commonly used approach. It establishes an outbound only tunnel from your application server and allows you to close all inbound IP traffic. This means that you wonât have a public IP for the server that can be reached by anyone.

When a public origin IP Address must remain or connector software cannot be run, network restrictions and origin authentication need to constrain the connections it accepts. For example,Â Dedicated CDN Egress IPsÂ give an account dedicated source addresses for traffic from Cloudflare to its origins. The application serverâs firewall can allow those addresses and reject other sources. This makesÂ the network restriction specific to the account's traffic, rather than broadly allowing traffic from Cloudflare's shared address ranges.

Authenticated Origin PullsÂ can add further depth with mutual TLS to verify the Cloudflare-to-origin connection.

An origin that supports it can alsoÂ validate the Access JSON Web Token, including its signature, issuer, expiry, and intended application audience. This is the best way to guarantee that a request was authenticated by Access.

If you're unsure where to start,Â speak with a Cloudflare expertÂ to review your architecture and identify which controls fit your environment.

Cloudflare Access determines who may reach the web application; Cloudflare'sÂ web application firewall (WAF)Â inspects HTTP requests to that same protected service. The WAF runs before any Access authentication checks, which gives you the ability to completely block known malicious IPs, specific countries, ASNs, or other attributes you know definitely shouldnât be accessing your applications. The firewall runs continuously on all requests and will also identify users who managed to authenticate attempting to run exploits with known CVE signatures.

Alongside managed CVE signatures,Â WAF Attack ScoreÂ uses machine learning to identify potentially malicious requests that do not exactly match a known rule. Administrators can use the score in rules that block or challenge requests. The WAF attack score is powered by network observations from Cloudflare's global network traffic and Cloudforce One investigations feedÂ Cloudflare's shared threat-intelligence platform.

Customers with a Cloudforce One threat intelligence subscription can alsoÂ use live threat indicators in WAF policies. That adds context about known malicious sources alongside inspection of the request itself.

Reducing exposure does not remove an attacker who already has a foothold. Seriously: go patch your system if you havenât, and follow Citrix'sÂ suspected-compromise guidance. They lay out how to preserve evidence, revoke credentials and certificates, investigate connected systems, and rebuild or restore from a known-good state.

Protecting web authentication can be an initial step without making it the final architecture. Cloudflare'sÂ Zero Trust architecture for virtual desktopsÂ also supports controlling access to the desktop infrastructure itself. With the Cloudflare One Client and private-network connectivity, teams can restrict who and which devices may reach the endpoints carrying desktop traffic, including an existing Independent Computing Architecture (ICA) path. This requires its own routing and policy design; it is not a capability supplied by the browser authentication proxy alone.

Some workflows can remove the ICA dependency instead. For supported Windows workloads, Â Cloudflare's browser-based remote desktop accessÂ connects users to a Windows host through Cloudflare Tunnel,Â without a local remote desktop client. If users only need a desktop to open web applications, Access and Browser Isolation canÂ replace that web-access use caseÂ without a full virtual desktop.

Start by protecting the authentication service and existing desktop connections. Then replace virtual desktops used only for web access, and move supported Windows workflows to browser-based remote desktops. Reducing exposure does not have to wait for a full desktop migration.

The same assessment applies beyond virtual desktops. An employee portal or management console may need to be reachable by approved users from anywhere, without needing to accept application requests from everyone.

Not every authentication page can require a prior employee identity. Consumer login pages and the identity-provider endpoints required to establish an initial session may need to remain publicly reachable. Protect those intentionally, and avoid introducing circular authentication dependencies. The point is to make reachability a design decision rather than an inherited default.

Start with one restricted service. Map the web and non-web paths into it, then put the access decision ahead of its authentication surface. Before expanding the rollout, validate the boundary in your own environment:

Check the relevant policy, firewall, and origin logs rather than relying only on what the browser displays. Repeat these checks when routing, identity, or failover settings change, so the next configuration update does not quietly reopen the path you closed.

The full architecture brings the access decision, web inspection, and availability controls in front of NetScaler, with restrictions on the connection to the origin. The public origin and Tunnel paths are alternatives. The native desktop connection remains separate, with an optional Zero Trust network access layer around that traffic.

Speak with a Cloudflare expertÂ to plan the right controls for your environment. Download the solution briefÂ and sign up for the upcoming webinar.

Andrei Migia, Nathan Sackett, and Doug Shepherd contributed to this post.
