#35869. This AI startup raised $300 million to build digital versions of consumers

Companies could soon have a new way to find out your shopping habits — by asking your digital clone.

Joon Sung Park, Co-Founder & CEO of Simile, an AI startup, told show host Molly O'Shea on the Sourcery podcast released on Monday that the company is building simulations of people that businesses can quiz about everything from products to marketing campaigns.

Park said the company is "creating a foundation model of human behavior that basically can take as input a description of a person or a group of people and then simulate what these people might do in different contexts," Park said.

"So they get access to this web interface where they can basically come in and define two things," Park added of existing users. "They can say who they want to talk to and what questions they want to ask. And really they can ask anything, and right now they can ask any number of questions."

Park said Simile raised $300 million in total at a $2 billion valuation.

Simile’s pitch comes as retailers turn to AI to get shoppers to spend. Amazon and Walmart have rolled out AI shopping assistants that answer questions, compare products, and recommend items, while retailers use customer data to personalize what shoppers see. Executives at both companies have said their AI tools are helping boost online sales.

Park said CVS has worked with Simile to better understand consumers, including their responses to store layouts and messaging. The startup also works with financial institutions and entertainment companies, Park said.

Simile maintains simulated panels for different industries and collects additional data when customers want to understand a specific population. Park said Simile's partnerships with organizations, including Gallup, which have access to actual humans who have agreed to participate, provide it with data from more than 40 million people globally. He said the company also uses behavioral information, such as transaction and mobility data, to train its models.

“If we can create simulations of people and be able to ask any questions at any time," Park said, "That becomes a superpower for these companies."

#35870. How Uber Built a Genie to Answer Questions Correctly

Right now, you’re your agent’s context engine. You write the rules files, maintain the skills, and paste in the Slack thread it missed.

But hand-curated context goes stale. And when there are conflicting answers, your agent can’t tell which is right. You pay for it in higher token bills and longer reviews.

The 8-levels of AI maturity and where teams get stuck

How a context engine curates context and resolves conflicts before your agent writes a line of code

Live demo: token savings in the same coding task, and use cases beyond code gen

Bonus: 2 open source tools you can use today.

Genie is Uber’s internal AI assistant for answering engineering support questions. It finds relevant information in Uber’s documentation, uses a language model to explain that information, and gives engineers a way to continue the conversation or ask a human for help.

The interesting part about Genie is how Uber has connected multiple capabilities into building a working support system that fits seamlessly into an engineer’s workflow.

In this article, we will understand how Genie prepares knowledge, retrieves it, and generates answers. Here’s what we will cover:

The problem that Genie is trying to solve

How Genie finds specific information from that knowledge

What does a typical Genie workflow look like

How Genie makes sure the answer is correct

What if Genie isn’t able to answer something

Disclaimer: This post is based on publicly shared details from various sources. References at the end. Please comment if you notice any inaccuracies.

The problem starts with how engineering teams support one another.

In a large software-driven company, many teams build platforms that other developers use to perform their jobs. A platform might provide tools for various activities such as software deployment, data processing, or working with ML workflows. Developers from other teams making use of these platforms inevitably need help with configuration, errors, or understanding unfamiliar features.

In a typical setup, the team responsible for managing a platform assigns an engineer to handle incoming issues during a particular period. This responsibility is commonly about providing on-call support. Although on-call work can definitely involve urgent production incidents, the problem Genie is trying to solve is geared towards everyday tech support that developers on platform teams provide through Slack channels.

For example, a developer from a product team might ask how to configure a platform feature. The on-call engineer reads the question and requests more details. The person asking responds, then waits again. Eventually, the on-call engineer identifies the relevant documentation or explains the required steps. Even a relatively straightforward question can involve several rounds of back-and-forth conversation and waiting.

Uber reports that its internal support channels received approximately 45K questions each month. At that volume, repeated questions consume considerable engineering time that the platform teams could utilize for better stuff.

Much of the information needed to answer such questions already exists somewhere. However, it is often scattered across Engwiki, which is Uber’s internal engineering wiki, or its internal Stack Overflow, and other documents. Finding the right information becomes difficult enough that it is much easier to ask another person.

Genie is designed to make that existing knowledge available through the Slack channels where developers already ask for help.

Genie combines finding information with explaining it.

A large language model (LLM) can produce readable explanations and answer technical questions. However, its general training doesn’t automatically give it knowledge of Uber’s private platforms, internal procedures, or documentation.

Therefore, Uber needed a way to connect a language model to its internal knowledge base. Two approaches help with this: fine-tuning and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG).

Fine-tuning means further training an existing model using examples selected for a particular purpose. Uber explains that this approach would require a collection of high-quality, varied training examples, along with sufficient computing resources to update the base model as new examples come up.

On the other hand, RAG supplies relevant information when a question is asked. The system first searches a knowledge collection, retrieves useful passages, and then gives those passages to the LLM along with the question. The model uses all this information to generate its answer.

For example, suppose a developer asks how to change a setting in an internal platform. A RAG system searches the platform’s documentation, finds the passage explaining that setting, and gives it to the model. The model turns the retrieved information into a response appropriate to the question.

Uber chose RAG for Genie because it could begin with existing documentation and be ready for launch sooner without the need to first assemble a fine-tuning dataset. This still needed a lot of work to collect, prepare, and evaluate the documentation. It also meant that updating the external knowledge collection could improve the information available to Genie without retraining the model for every change in documentation.

Preparing knowledge happens separately from answering questions. Before Genie can retrieve useful information, Uber must turn its scattered documents into a searchable collection. This preparation happens using an ETL pipeline.

ETL stands for extract, transform, and load.

Extraction means fetching content from internal sources.

Transformation means preparing that content for retrieval, including breaking it into pieces and generating numerical representations.

Loading means making the resulting data available to the search infrastructure.

Uber engineering team uses Apache Spark to run this work. For reference, Spark is a system for processing data across multiple workers, allowing a large preparation job to be divided into smaller pieces of work.

The pipeline fetches content through interfaces provided by sources such as Engwiki and Uber’s internal Stack Overflow. It places the results into a Spark DataFrame. Think of it as a table with rows and columns.

At this stage, a row contains information such as the document’s source URL, its text, and additional metadata. Here, metadata is information that describes the document rather than the content of that document.

Keeping the source URL alongside the text is important throughout the system. This is because Genie needs to eventually connect an answer back to the real documentation that supports it. Preserving this relationship during the preparation phase makes it easy to perform source attribution later on.

Embeddings allow Genie to search for related meaning within its knowledge base. Once Uber has collected all the documentation, the next challenge is finding the passages that relate to a user’s question.

The system first divides documents into smaller pieces called chunks. For example, a long document might contain installation instructions, configuration options, and troubleshooting guidance. However, a question about one configuration option may only need a small part of that document. Chunking makes those smaller passages available as individual retrieval candidates.

Uber uses LangChain to chunk its wiki content. It then uses an OpenAI embedding model to generate an embedding for each chunk. An embedding is a list of numbers that represents aspects of a piece of text’s meaning. An embedding model is designed so that related texts have representations that can be found through similarity search. This helps a system find relevant information even when a question and a document use different wording. For example, a question might refer to a job “taking too long,” while a relevant document discusses an “execution time limit.” These phrases are just examples, but they show why searching for related meaning can be a game-changer when exact keywords differ.

The resulting data keeps each chunk associated with its embedding and source information. The original text still remains essential. The embedding simply helps the search system locate a passage. The passage itself supplies information for the language model to read.

Uber generates embeddings using custom Python functions executed through Spark. This lets embedding generation fit into the same data-processing pipeline as document collection and preparation.

Uber prepares the search infrastructure to serve questions. Creating embeddings produces searchable data, but that data still has to reach the systems that handle live requests. This is handled through the Pusher stage.

Sia: This is Uber’s internal vector database solution. A vector database supports searching numerical representations such as embeddings.

Terrablob: This is Uber’s blob storage, which holds stored data and files used by the pipeline and serving infrastructure.

A bootstrap job ingests data into Sia, followed by Spark jobs that build and merge an index that organizes data for efficient searching.

The resulting index data is stored in Terrablob. Serving machines, called leaves, download the base index and synchronize snapshot data. These leaves handle searches against the loaded index when requests arrive.

This separates the work of building searchable knowledge from the work of answering an individual question.

Document preparation and index construction happen through the ingestion pipeline.

Live requests use the index made available to the serving machines.

Each incoming question goes through retrieval before generation. Once the knowledge collection is ready, Genie can answer questions. The central backend component for this is Uber’s Knowledge Service.

When someone posts a question in Slack, the Genie bot sends it to Knowledge Service. The service converts that question into an embedding.

It then searches the vector database for document chunks with related embeddings.

The search returns relevant passages associated with their source information. Those passages become part of the material sent to the LLM, together with the user’s question and instructions for answering.

Next, the model generates a response, which is returned through Genie to Slack.

There are two distinct model responsibilities in this flow.

The embedding model produces numerical representations that support retrieval. On the other hand, the LLM reads the retrieved text and produces the written response.

This difference is useful when dealing with failures. Genie might retrieve unsuitable passages, or it might retrieve useful passages and still generate an inadequate answer. Improving the system requires checking both stages.

Uber gives the model explicit boundaries for generating its answers. An LLM can generate a plausible statement that is incorrect or unsupported. This behavior is commonly called hallucination. In an internal support system, an invented instruction could send a developer in the wrong direction.

Uber addresses this partly through how it constructs the model’s input.

Each retrieved result is presented as a separate sub-context, together with its source URL. A sub-context is simply a clearly identified piece of supporting material within the larger prompt. The model is instructed to answer using the provided sub-contexts and to provide source URLs as citations. This gives it explicit evidence to work from and gives the user a way to check the supporting documentation. For example, if several passages discuss different parts of a configuration process, preserving each passage’s source helps the generated explanation remain traceable to the actual source.

These measures reduce the risk of unsupported answers, but a source link doesn’t guarantee that every statement is correct. The retrieved passage must be relevant, the underlying document must be accurate, and the model must represent it faithfully. This is why evaluation remains an essential part of the architecture.

Uber also restricts the knowledge available to Genie. The team preselects sources that are broadly available to Uber developers because some internal information would be inappropriate to expose through model processing or Slack responses.

The conversation includes a clear path to human support. A support interaction often continues after the first answer. Someone may need clarification, discover that the suggested information doesn’t quite address their situation, or require an action that documentation cannot provide.

Uber redesigned Genie’s interaction flow to deal with these possibilities. Its responses include action buttons that let users ask a follow-up question, mark the issue as resolved, or contact human support.

If Genie lacks enough information to answer, it tells the user and directs them to the on-call developers responsible for the platform. When a user escalates an interaction to human support, the human developer takes over while Genie stays muted. This keeps the conversation focused while an engineer handles the issue.

This feature is really important because successful support involves more than producing a paragraph of text. The user needs to understand what to do next. An answer that helps only partially can still be valuable if it leads smoothly into clarification or human assistance.

User feedback measures the impact of the answer. Uber collects feedback directly in Slack, where users can select a response category.

Resolved: The answer completely resolved the issue.

Helpful: The answer provided some help, but more assistance is needed.

Not Helpful: The answer was wrong or didn’t address the question.

Not Relevant: The request requires human help that Genie cannot provide, such as a code review.

The differentiation between these categories is very important. Partial help differs from complete resolution. Similarly, an incorrect answer differs from a request that falls outside what a documentation assistant can accomplish.

When a user submits feedback, a Slack plugin collects it together with relevant metadata. It sends that information through a Kafka topic, which acts as a stream of events, into a Hive table, where it can be stored and analyzed in the future. Uber then displays the resulting metrics in a dashboard.

This creates a record of how Genie performs in real use. Without such a record, a system could answer many questions while its operators had little visibility into whether those answers actually helped anyone.

Uber evaluates both the answers and the documents behind them. User feedback provides direct evidence of Genie’s usefulness. However, Uber also supports custom evaluations of qualities such as hallucination and answer relevance.

For these evaluations, a separate pipeline retrieves Genie’s recorded context and responses from Hive. It combines them with relevant information such as Slack metadata and user feedback, then prepares the data for an evaluator.

The evaluator uses an “LLM as a judge” approach. This means a language model receives an evaluation prompt that tells it how to assess the material. Its task is to examine an existing answer against the chosen criteria. For example, an evaluation prompt could ask whether an answer addresses the question and whether its claims are supported by the supplied context.

The evaluation results are processed into metrics and published in a report available through the interface. Uber says these evaluations can help plan improvements to both retrieval and generation steps.

The evaluation can also extend to the source documents themselves. This is a particularly useful part of the design because answer quality depends on the material available for retrieval. If a document is unclear, incomplete, or inaccurate, retrieving it successfully may still produce a poor support experience.

Uber’s document evaluation pipeline represents each document as a row in a Spark dataframe. It sends the document and a custom evaluation prompt to an LLM judge. The model returns a score, an explanation of that score, and actionable suggestions for improving the document. These results are published in a report that is also accessible through the Michelangelo interface. For example, a document might describe a procedure while leaving prerequisites unclear. Improving that document can give Genie better material to retrieve and explain, while also helping developers who read the documentation directly.

To summarize, the two evaluation processes examine different parts of the system. Answer evaluation checks what Genie produces in a particular interaction. Document evaluation checks the quality of the knowledge from which future answers will be constructed.

Genie was launched in September 2023. Within a year, Uber reported 154 Slack channels using Genie. More than 70K questions were answered during this time. The overall helpfulness rate was 48.9%, which is like a full-resolution rate, with engineering time savings of around 13000 hours.

This cost tracking is generated by following calls through the system. Running a model-backed service across many support channels also requires visibility into its costs. Uber provides that visibility by carrying an identifier through the request flow.

When a Slack client or another platform calls Knowledge Service, it passes a UUID. Knowledge Service forwards this identifier in request metadata to Michelangelo Gateway. The identifier can be included in an audit log and used to track costs associated with it.

Genie is a cutting-edge bot with the goal of streamlining on-call management, optimizing incident response, and improving team collaboration. It has the potential to change the entire experience of how users and on-call developers of any platform interact and engage within the respective platform’s Slack channel.

Meet Michelangelo: Uber’s Machine Learning Platform

Checking answers before showing them to the user is the hard part in these text to SQL style systems. Did Uber use a separate validator step?

The judge scores whether claims are supported by the retrieved context stored in Hive, not by the wiki page as it stands when someone reads the report. A doc can be edited after that row was written, and the score still looks fine. I'd keep the document id and revision on the Hive row with the answer, so a later document-eval suggestion and the answer score refer to the same version rather than mixing a stale retrieval into the 48.9% helpfulness number.

#35872. 世帯年収1100万円で夫が主夫の50代女性「税金がバカ高いです」

この記事の見出しと要約は、ライブドアニュースが独自の機能で作成したものです。試験提供中の機能のため、記事本文と併せてご確認ください。

世帯年収が1000万円を超えると裕福な生活をイメージされがちだが、当事者たちが口を揃えるのは「税金の高さ」に対する不満である。しかし、日々の生活において値段を気にせず買い物ができる程度の余裕はあるようだ。

投稿を寄せた神奈川県の50代女性（医療・福祉・介護／世帯年収1100万円）は、「私が1人で働き主人は主夫です」という世帯だ。女性は現在の生活について次のように明かす。

「税金がバカ高いです。 普通の7万の賃貸に住んでいますが、あまり食費とかは気にせずに欲しいモノを買える生活出来ています」

大体の食費は夫婦2人で月に8万円ほどだという。「また主人がキチンと計算し貯蓄してくれています」とのことで、家計管理は主夫である夫が担っているようだ。女性は「雑費は月に10万位で大体月に30万位で全て賄ってます」と現状を明かしている。（文：篠原みつき）

一方、東京都の30代男性（営業／世帯年収1700万円）もまた、税金の負担についてこぼしている。自身の年収が1300万円弱、妻が500万円弱だという男性は、次のように書いている。

「そこまで裕福とは感じない。税金で取られる金額が多すぎて。 ただ、金額を見て食べるものを決めたりはしない程度の暮らし」

住まいは東京23区内の「徒歩10分の中古マンション」で、車は中古のアウディだという。月の食費は10万円強ほどかかっているが、子どもがまだ小さいため教育費は1万円程度に収まっている。

※キャリコネニュースでは「『世帯年収1000万円以上』の世界ってどんな感じですか？」をテーマに投稿を募集中です。回答はこちらから　https://questant.jp/q/QLE1FGOD

#35873. Continuous accountability for Verified bots

A driverâs license tells you who someone is and that they passed a driving test, not whether theyâll drive responsibly in the future. The same is true for bots: verifying who operates it creates accountability, but trust depends on what it does next.Â A known bot can still ignore website preferences, overwhelm origins, or evade controls. Itâs not always malicious â often itâs just a misconfiguration or a bug.

As we described in a previous blog postÂ on bot behavior, we strive to verify two questions: âAre you who you say you are?â and âCan we trust you?â To be a Cloudflare Verified Bot, you broadly need to meet threeÂ criteria:

Bots use Web Bot AuthÂ to sign requests that establish their identity, which BotBaseÂ then catalogues in an open format. With identification addressed, our focus shifts to the second cardinal rule of Verified bots: thou shalt do no harm.

Today we introduce a system to evaluate and report when VerifiedÂ bot behavior starts to deviate from this rule, ensuring that the answer to âCan we trust you?â remains âYes.â

This is where the distinction between risk and trustÂ becomes important:

For example, we de-listed Perplexityâs botÂ from our Verified bot list in 2025 when itÂ sought to access resources on websites that opted out of scraping and subsequently attemptedÂ to circumvent controlsÂ when those requests were blocked.

This simple requirement sounds like a freebie, but there is a lot of nuance in that statement.Â When crawlers donât respect site preferences, that undermines trust. When sites request a crawler to not crawl or to slow down, and the crawler ignores these requests, that undermines trust.

We developed a system to measure how often a crawler respects site preferences. These observations will translate to an explainable trust band: a range showing how consistently a bot respects site preferences and which observed behaviors informed that assessment, rather than a permanent judgment about a bot or its operator. The initial signalsÂ we evaluate are:

We consider these to be âcommon senseâ rules, a courtesy to the operators who provide the information bots seek. In the future, we will be sharing these scores publiclyÂ onÂ Radar,Â as well as expanding the ways we measure. This score gives responsible bot operators a way to demonstrate that trust is being upheld over time. Verify, but continuously re-verify.

A robots.txt file is the primary way to communicate site owner preferences.Â Our system considers whether a botâs observed traffic is consistent with those published preferences over time.

Robots.txt tells all (or specific) bots to only crawl specific parts of a website. Isolated violations and other types of one-offs may not be significant. What we look for instead are repeated patterns of behavior that disregards site preferences. The expectation is simply for responsible bots to consult and honor the preferences that websites publish, in line withÂ RFC 9309.

And just to be clear, a robots.txt sets the minimum rules for what bots and agents should not do. But there is no implication that anything not stated is allowed. For example, a robots.txt does not need to say that a bot must stop when the site can communicate that continued access is unwelcome through other signals.

Bots can remain entirely within allowed paths while still placing substantial load on the websites they visit. One of the clearest ways a website can push back is with an HTTP 429 (âToo Many Requestsâ) response. A 429 is a directive for the visitor to reduce its request rate, sometimes with guidance about how long to wait before trying again.

Our system considers whether the botâs traffic adapts after receiving that signal. Does it slow down, pause, or does it continue sending requests at the same pace? We then incorporate that behavior into the botâs trust band over time: consistently slowing down or pausing increases trust, while repeatedly ignoring the signal lowers it.

Observing these signalsÂ is only a first step toward making verified automation accountable over time. By pairing bot identity with evidence of continuing behavior, we can give site owners more confidence that the bots they choose to allow are respecting their preferences, give bot operators a way to demonstrate they deserve trust, and provide context to website owners about the automated traffic reaching them.

This system, alongside Bot Preference SyncÂ and Bot Management, formsÂ an accountability loop for automated traffic. Bot Preference Sync helps website owners publish their preferences, and observing how bots interact with these preferences shows whether Verified bots consistently honor them over time. Bot Management lets website owners decide how that traffic is handled. Together, they help ensure that trust is earned through transparent, accountable behavior, not assumed from identity alone.

We are already using this system internally to evaluate how consistently Verified bots honor website preferences. Because trust is built over time, we assess sustained patterns rather than isolated events. We are using this initial phase to build that history and refine how those observations become useful guidance. Building on that foundation, we plan to make the system available to all Cloudflare customers, who will be able to choose the trust threshold used to decide how Verified bot traffic is handled. Our goal is straightforward: to keep website preferences meaningful, and ensure trust is earned through sustained behavior.

Want to learn more about how you can handle bots? Cloudflare customers can already use Bot ManagementÂ to manage automated traffic and Bot Preference SyncÂ to align their published preferences with their configured policies. To explore the ever-growing Verified bot population, see the trends on Radar.

And ifÂ you are interested in helping build the future of bot identity and accountability, explore open roles at Cloudflare.

#35874. Osteria a Milano Loreto: piatti classici e pasta fresca fatta in casa

Siamo ritornati da Osteria Afrodite a Milano a due anni dalla cena stampa di apertura. Nel menu i classici come mondeghili, costoletta alla milanese, risotto con zafferano e midollo. Tra i piatti più apprezzati della casa ci sono i tagliolini Afrodite e le tagliatelle burro e parmigiano, ispirate alla tradizione delle Fettuccine Alfredo. Le potete anche ordinare con il tartufo nero aggiungendo l’extra 10 euro.

Il capitolo prezzi ci dice che per un pasto completo – antipasto, primo e secondo – costa in media 65 euro. Qualche prezzo in dettaglio verificato al ristorante ad ottobre 2026.

— Mondeghili e cren, 14 €— Uovo e tartufo, 22 €— Tagliatelle burro e parmigiano, 19 €. 29 con il tartufo nero— Risotto alla milanese con midollo, 22 €— Ossobuco con risotto per 2 persone, 26 € a persona— Costoletta alla milanese, 34 €

Siamo alla cena stampa aperta da calamari in umido con un ristretto di mare, olio scalogno e peperoncino accompagnati da fagioli (18 €). Un classico antipasto mare-terra che funziona per sapore e consistenza. Il calamaro resta delicato e incontra il gusto pieno e dei borlotti.

Il vitello tonnato alla Roberto (17 euro) è preparato con manzo cotto a bassa temperatura, servito tagliato fine e con una generosa quantità di salsa tonnata. Carne molto buona e salsa tonnata forse un po’ dolciastra.

Tagliolini Afrodite con “branzino abbrustolito” (23 €). Nonostante la descrizione poco accattivante, mi ha incuriosito l’abbinamento. Ottimo il tagliolino di pasta fresca all’uovo con la giusta quantità di burro che dona dolcezza al piatto. Le carni bianche del branzino si incontrano in pezzetti dorati ma non direi abbrustoliti. Un primo dal gusto delicato e ruffiano.

Il pollo ruspante al limone (26 €) è cotto al Josper ed è servito con la pelle adagiata su un fondo di cottura preparato con cipolle e succo di limone. Il pollo è molto buono e morbido, salsina un po’ troppo liquida. Si sceglie a piacere petto o coscia. Le patate sono servite con la buccia.

Il tiramisù (9 €) è casalingo, soffice, opulento con una crema al mascarpone squisita. Il cacao è spolverato al tavolo.

Osteria Afrodite. Via Donatello, 9, 20131 Milano MI. Telefono: 333 806 1018. Instagram

Nuova apertura in via Donatello in zona Loreto a Milano: Osteria Afrodite che fa capo al gruppo di ristoranti La Gioia Collection. Se le parole d’ordine sono quelle che caratterizzano le nuove aperture un po’ in tutta Milano (“un progetto che celebra la tradizione culinaria italiana in chiave moderna”), la loro realizzazione le rispecchia in pieno.

Osteria Afrodite è il quarto ristorante del gruppo La Gioia, che fa capo a Redi Shijaku, imprenditore di origine albanese e italiano d’adozione. “Con Osteria Afrodite vogliamo offrire un luogo che unisca convivialità e ricercatezza, fondendo il calore della tradizione italiana a un’esperienza moderna e sofisticata,” spiega Shijaku.

Gli stessi principi di Osteria Afrodite – il “Nuovo Classico Italiano” – sono alla base degli altri ristoranti di La Gioia Collection a Milano. Che sono La Gioia, in via San Marco, Osteria Serafina, in via Luigi Sacco, e Al Baretto San Marco, “Ristorante classico italiano di mare” in via Marsala. Ma ci sono già progetti per il futuro con una quinta apertura tra viale Cogni Zugna e via Francesco Carchidio in tempo per il Salone del Mobile 2025.

“Vogliamo riportare la cucina italiana alla sua essenza. Quella che abbiamo amato negli anni ’70/’80, quando il cibo veniva prodotto in casa,” spiega Giovanni Russo, Corporate Chef del gruppo. “Osteria Afrodite rappresenta un luogo dove il cibo è protagonista, ma l’esperienza complessiva è un viaggio nell’accoglienza e nei sapori che definiscono l’Italia.”

Questa la dichiarazione d’intenti, con parole d’ordine che abbiamo già sentito, con però un richiamo esplicito al passato prossimo delle mamme e delle nonne anni Settanta/Ottanta. Un po’ sulla linea di Nautilus, altra recente apertura meneghina. Dichiarazione tradotta in un menu che “riflette il meglio della tradizione italiana, con preparazioni realizzate in casa per garantire freschezza e qualità.”

Potremmo citare alcune delle preparazioni dell’Osteria Afrodite a Milano, come la Pasta e Fagioli reinterpretata con triglie di scoglio, cozze tarantine, vongole. Oppure i Tagliolini Afrodite con muggine abbrustolito e burro delle Alpi. Andando più sul classico, la Costata di Chianina al carbone Josper, o la Costoletta alla Milanese.

Ma vediamo cosa abbiamo mangiato alla cena stampa.

Una cena con una serie di antipasti da condividere, per permetterci di assaggiare più piatti – e abbiamo condiviso anche il resto, sempre per lo stesso motivo. Qui sopra, gli antipasti, che comprendevano gnocco fritto con lardo del Po e prosciutto crudo Camarin (“I Modenesi”, 19 €) e insalata di carciofi e bottarga (18 €).

Molto buona la tartare di manzo al coltello con peschiole – i frutti del pesco (meglio, del pesco-noce) raccolti ancora verdi, prima che il nocciolo indurisca. Cotti in acqua e aceto, vengono conservati in vasi di vetro, e sono una specialità del Casertano. Costa 19 €.

Burrata con acquacotta della Maremma (17 €). Un assaggio, visto che non amo molto l’acquacotta.

Altro antipasto: Indivia Belga e Avocado Hass, con questi triangoli di Pecorino Sardo DOP (17 €). Impiattamento originale, accostamenti insoliti, o forse solo inaspettati, interessante.

Una tendenza recente è quella di cacioepepizzare tutto quanto. Qui, tocca alla Seppia, insemolata e fritta, con una salsa di pecorino e pepe (20 €) – con risultati notevoli, soprattutto grazie all’equilibrio del tutto.

Ci siamo fatti portare anche un piatto fuori dal menu previsto per la nostra cena: Coscette di rana delle Risaie alla Pavese, impanate e fritte (20 €). Le avevo notate scorrendo la carta, e le ho richieste. A parte il gusto personale, è un piatto poco comune nei menu dei ristoranti, ed è anche buono. Nel presentare l’Osteria Afrodite a noi comunicatori del settore, secondo me valeva la pena puntare anche su un piatto “territoriale” del circondario di Milano come questo.

Un assaggio anche per le tagliatelle al tartufo (25 €).

Ma io ho scelto questa Pasta e fagioli mista con crema di fagioli Cuneo, triglie di scoglio, cozze tarantine, vongole e tartufo nero (21 €). Ottima – il tartufo non si sentiva molto, mentre tutti gli altri sapori erano ben presenti e distinti.

Come secondo invece ho preso – e particolarmente gradito – questo Gnocco gratinato ripieno di erbette e salsa Mornay (22 €).

Non male anche il trancio di rana pescatrice (26 €).

Dessert: inizio con un sorbetto al limone, lavorato al tavolo. A prima vista, si presenta soffice, morbido, cremoso, fresco, e all’assaggio mantiene tutte le promesse visive. Bravi.

Alla fine, un più che ottimo tiramisù, sviluppato in altezza con un’ottima crema di mascarpone, e un sottile strato di biscotto alla base. Bravissimi.

In complesso, giudizio positivo, al di là di un paio di incertezze (un piatto di tagliolini preso dal mio vicino è arrivato piuttosto scotto – rifatto, cotto il giusto, decisamente buono) e qualche lungaggine nel servizio. Va anche detto che l’Osteria Afrodite Miano è aperto da poco, e le incertezze ci stanno. Un punto di merito, le lavorazioni fatte “in casa” (la pasta, vedi foto).

Una scelta fra i piatti più rappresentativi del menu del ristorante Afrodite a Milano.

Ad arricchire l’offerta gastronomica dell’Osteria Afrodite a Milano, una cantina con oltre 1000 etichette selezionate da sommelier del gruppo La Gioia.

Ho una lunga e bellissima esperienza come headhunter nei settori moda, ristorazione e hotellerie Scrivo con passione di food, drink e lifestyle selezionando storie e prodotti che mi intrigano

#35875. EP229: 8 Chunking strategies for RAG-based agents

Your app, live in seconds, for free. Railway’s push-button compute, storage, and networking is available immediately upon sign-up.

Humans and agents alike operate on one vertically integrated system including hardware, software, and a prompt-to-production experience.

Sign up with the link below for free cloud credits and let your agents cook.

How to Test Your Code (Even When AI Writes It)

8 Chunking strategies for RAG-based agents

Google Translate: The Ideas Behind Neural Translation

Fixed-Size: cuts text every fixed number of tokens, with a small overlap.

Recursive: splits on paragraphs first, falling back to lines then words and characters only when a piece is still too big.

Document-Based: splits wherever the document already marks a break, a heading, a chapter, an HTML tag, so a markdown file becomes one chunk per section on its own.

Semantic: embeds each sentence, checks its similarity to the one before it, and starts a new chunk when that similarity drops. This finds real topic shifts instead of guessing by length.

LLM-Based: asks an LLM to rewrite the text as standalone propositions, one idea per line, and turns each into a chunk, high quality but expensive across a large corpus.

Agentic: an AI agent reads each document, decides what it is (code, contract, table), and picks the chunking method for that file instead of one rule for everything.

Late Chunking: runs the full document through an embedding model, then applies normal split boundaries and mean-pools within each boundary to create chunk embeddings.

Hierarchical: breaks the document into layers, sections, paragraphs, then sentences

Over to you: which chunking strategy are you running in production?

A simplified illustration of common techniques. Not an exact map of Google Translate’s current system.

Detect language. A tiny classifier predicts the source language in milliseconds.

Tokenization. A BPE tokenizer splits the text into subword tokens, so the model can handle any word in any language.

Add target token. The model can handle every language pair. A special token like <2es> is prepended to the token sequence to steer the output toward Spanish.

Encoder. The tokens pass through Transformer layers. The output is a sequence of vectors, corresponding to each input token.

Decoder. Then the decoder part of the Transformer can predict the probability distribution for the next token conditioned on the encoded vectors.

Beam search. Instead of greedily picking one token at a time, beam search uses the decoder to keep several candidate translations during generation. The final output is the one with the highest probability.

Over to you: Do you think AI labs and frontier models will make services like Google Translate obsolete?

Why do we need Agent Skills? Long prompts hurt agent performance. Instead of one massive prompt, agents keep a small catalog of skills, reusable playbooks with clear instructions, loaded only when needed.

Here is what the Agent Skills workflow looks like:

User Query: A user submits a request like “Analyze data & draft report”.

Build Prompt + Skills Index: The agent runtime combines the query with Skills metadata, a lightweight list of available skills and their short descriptions.

Reason & Select Skill: The LLM processes the prompt, thinks, and decides: “I want Skill X.”

Load Skill into Context: The agent runtime receives the specific skill request from the LLM. Then, it loads SKILL. md and adds it into the LLM’s active context.

Final Output: The LLM follows SKILL. md, runs scripts, and generates the final report.

By dynamically loading skills only when needed, Agent Skills keep context small and the LLM’s behavior consistent.

Over to you: What skills would you find most useful in agents?

Built using the C language, PostgreSQL uses a process-based architecture.

You can think of it like a factory with a manager (Postmaster) coordinating specialized workers. Each connection gets its own process and shares a common memory pool. Background workers handle tasks like writing data, vacuuming, and logging independently.

MySQL takes a thread-based approach. Imagine a single multi-tasking brain.

It uses a layered design with one server handling multiple connections through threads. The magic happens using pluggable storage engines (such as InnoDB, MyISAM) that you can swap based on your needs.

Over to you: Which database do you prefer?

Worth flagging the main constraint on late chunking: the whole document has to fit in the embedding model's context window (8K tokens for the jina-embeddings-v2 models the original paper used). Past that you have to split into macro-chunks first, so you're back to choosing boundaries, just at a coarser level.

The payoff is real for reference-heavy text. Under fixed-size splitting, a chunk like "its revenue grew 3%" loses which company "its" means, while late chunking keeps that because every token was embedded with the full document in view. Curious whether anyone has measured agentic chunking against plain recursive splitting plus a reranker, since a good reranker often recovers most of what clever boundaries buy you.

Agentic chunking is the one I'd want a record for, not just a better split. The agent reads the file, decides it is a contract or a table, and picks the method, but retrieval later only sees the chunks. A contract clause cut on paragraph length and a table cut on rows then look the same in the index, and a bad answer can't be traced to that choice. I'd store the label and the splitter next to each chunk, so the next run can tell a wrong method from a weak embedding.

#35878. A fully programmable secure web gateway

Every secure web gateway on the market works the same way: traffic matches a condition. A terminal action fires. Allow, Block, Isolate, Log. This model has been the foundation of network security for nearly 30 years, and it handles the common case well. But it has a ceiling, and customers with complex environments hit that ceiling regularly.

Earlier this year, we shared our vision to build a truly programmable SASE platform. We also outlined how the term programmabilityÂ has become diluted by the security industry. Most vendors claim programmability because they have public APIs, Terraform providers, webhooks, and alerting. Cloudflare offers all of those things too,Â but thatâs not enough. True programmability means running your own code â arbitrary logic that you wrote for your specific environment â inline in the policy evaluation path, at the moment a security decision is made.

Today, weâre excited to announce Cloudflare is bringing true programmability to Cloudflare Gateway and DLP (Data Loss Prevention) by integrating it with the entirety of our edge computing platform. We are releasing a new type of Gateway action, Forward, and custom validation functions, available to all Zero Trust plans. These capabilities allow you to use a Cloudflare Worker to transform and manipulate traffic, or to bring your own data to policy evaluation.

For as long as firewalls have existed, businesses have faced a binary choice. You can maintain your own security detection engine â your own firewall, your own proxy infrastructure â with high maintenance overhead and low portability, in exchange for maximum customization. Or, you can accept the constraints of a vendor, offloading the considerable maintenance cost, at the expense of flexibility to solve problems specific to your environment.

In six years of building Cloudflare Gateway, we have heard from thousands of customers struggling with this trade-off. A security team migrating access controls for a critical internal application needs to inject HTTP headers based on JSON Web Token (JWT) claims from their identity provider. The data exists in the request context, but Gateway cannot read the JWT and write the header. So the team stands up a pool of NGINX proxies solely to perform this transformation. That infrastructure now must be patched, monitored, and secured... indefinitely.

Another team wants a Slack notification the moment an employee signs up for a new SaaS service. The policy engine can detect the sign-up event, but it can only Allow or Block. So the team builds a Logpush-to-SIEM-to-Slack pipeline with a 5 to 15 minute delay and no guarantee of delivery. And piles on yet another piece of infrastructure.

Dozens of enterprise customers have asked for warning pages that prompt users for justification before allowing access to sensitive destinations. Most then want to customize the ensuing behavior based on additional context about who the user is and the level of access requested. But serving customized, dynamic responses from a policy engine is exceedingly difficult.

We have offered customers many extension points over the years. But along with every other firewall vendor, it is impossible to build features to cover threat vectors as quickly as they can appear. However, we also recognize that the best solutions are those which are infinitely extensible to your environment.

Cloudflare is not just a firewall, or a secure web gateway, a content delivery network, or an edge service. Cloudflare is a composable compute platform. Cloudflare Workers already allows customers to run complex logic on our network edge from any of our 330+ locations worldwide. Cloudflare GatewayÂ already evaluates and enforces security policy on user traffic at those same locations, on the same machines, in the same data centers.

Only Cloudflare runs both distributed customer computeÂ and a full-featured secure web gateway and firewall in the same globally distributed network. We have the unique opportunity and ability to combine those functions into the industryâs first completelyÂ programmable and customizable SASE platform.

Gateway and Workers were built on the same infrastructure from the beginning. When Gateway forwards traffic to a Worker, that dispatch is a local function call. There is no hairpinning. There is no additional latency from crossing a network boundary. This is the first time that customers will have absolute control over how their proxied traffic is processed, without compromise, using code that they can write and execute without maintaining any sort of infrastructure.

Standalone SASE providers without their own compute platform require you to deploy automation in a separate cloud, manually configure webhooks, and accept the round-trip latency and management overhead of stitching together disconnected systems. No other vendor in this space has a programmable edge compute platform co-located with their security gateway. As threats advance at AI-powered speed, this will provide much needed flexibility and agility for security organizations.

A new Gateway action type called ForwardÂ and a new policy resource called a Custom FunctionÂ are two distinct ways to call a Worker from a Gateway policy. The Forward action is available in public beta today, and Custom Functions will be available before the end of the year.

You can customize HTTP traffic behavior with a new policy actionÂ called ForwardÂ that routes the matched HTTP request to a Worker as a proxy. Policies with the ForwardÂ action are evaluated for trafficÂ allowed by HTTP policies. The first matching ForwardÂ rule will then be applied to your traffic, and the traffic will be sent to its bound Cloudflare Worker. The Worker acts as inline middleware: it receives the full headers and request body. Your logic can then choose to modify either one (or take another asynchronous action of some kind), forward the request to the origin, receive the response, can modify that too, and return the final response to the user.

Gateway handles the TCP connections, TLS termination and re-encryption, certificate management, and HTTP version negotiation. The Worker is responsible only for the transformation logic. You get a customizable, proxy-like extension point for your existing security stack, with none of the operational cost of hosting a traditional HTTP proxy.

Your Workers also do not have to transform the request. A rule's sole purpose can be to proxy a request to a Worker that receives the full context of the matched request asynchronously: send a Slack message, write to R2, log to an external pipeline, call a webhook, update a KVÂ store. The traffic can continue to its destination, unbothered.

A custom function calls out to a Worker inline during Gateway policy evaluation and returns a value. The function is then exposed as a selector in the Gateway policy builder, and the selector is evaluated against its values. The selector is usable in the condition of any network or HTTP Gateway rule, the same way a built-in selector like Source IPÂ or Content CategoryÂ works today.

The Worker receives context about the request: source IP, destination, user identity, device posture, HTTP headers, and more, depending on the policy phase. The Worker returns a typed value (string, number, or boolean) that Gateway uses in rule conditions. The contract is simple: data in, value out.

Here is a custom function that parses a JWT AuthorizationÂ header and returns the user's role:

With this function deployed, an administrator can create an HTTP policy rule: Custom Function "JWT Role" contains "finance_contractor"Â with an action of Allow. The custom function becomes part of the rule condition, evaluated alongside every other selector.

Custom functions are not limited to HTTP traffic. Because they receive identity, device posture, and connection metadata instead of the full HTTP request, you can use them in the Gateway Network policy rule builder with arbitrary Layer 4 port and protocol traffic as well.

The Worker itself can do anything a Worker can already do â call external APIs, read from KV or D1, or invoke Workers AI. But from Gateway's perspective, the function is deterministic: data in, value out.

Custom functions are designed for quick, bounded, stateless evaluations of data which can return a shaped response. You should think of their use similarly to data that can already be evaluated in Gateway selectors; that is, calculations on data that exist within a set of criteria, e.g. âPorts within this range,â or âURL paths that match this regex pattern.â The power comes from being able to extend your structured evaluations with arbitrary or internal sources of data, for which youâll see some examples below.

The ForwardÂ action requires a little more planning and preparation. It can be used for powerful transformations inline with usersâ live requests, and can manipulate them in complex ways both on the egress and return to the origin service. These should be thought of as transformation functions, something that very few enterprise security proxies even conceptualize today. Workers that use the ForwardÂ action should be targeted and designed carefully to avoid adverse effects on the end userâs overall experience.

A Worker intercepts a request to a sensitive destination and returns an interstitial page requiring the end user to provide a written justification for access. The Worker calls Cloudflare KVÂ to write a session with a TTL, so the user is only prompted once per configured period. It writes the user's identity and their stated justification to Cloudflare D1, creating an audit trail. Or, you can use HyperdriveÂ to write that record to any internal database you already operate.

This has been one of our most-requested features for over four years. With a Worker able to process and manipulate HTTP traffic,Â it's easy to build to your own standards.

A custom function parses a JWT from the request's AuthorizationÂ header, extracts the user's role or group membership, and returns it as a selector value. A Gateway rule matches on that value and sets an X-App-RoleÂ header on the upstream request. No NGINX proxy pool. No additional infrastructure to maintain.

When a file download matches certain criteria, a Worker can send the file to a third-party sandboxing service for detonation and analysis. Or it can write the file in its entirety to Cloudflare R2Â as a permanent record for later inspection, without the file ever leaving the Cloudflare network.

A Worker bound to a Forward policy receives traffic whenever a specific selector matches. The Worker sends a message to a Slack channel or PagerDuty endpoint with the user's email, the rule that fired, and the destination URL.

Traditional expression builders for firewalls are not designed for the kind of computation some organizations need at evaluation time. If you maintain internal risk scoring systems that perform behavioral analysis across multiple data sources, or if you have complex maps of users, groups, and conditional memberships where multiple criteria must be independently true, you can use a custom function as the computational extension that evaluates all of that logic and returns a single value to Gateway.

Because Gateway and Workers services run on the same machines in the Cloudflare network, dispatching to a Worker does not introduce a network hop. The performance impact is limited to the execution time of your Worker code itself.

When a custom function fails â throws an exception, times out, or returns an unexpected value â you configure the fallback behavior per function. DefaultÂ valuesÂ are required in the custom function contract, so that itâs easy to determine behavior.

The ForwardÂ action and its integration with Workers are available in a public betaÂ starting today, with Custom FunctionsÂ expected to be available before the end of the year. At general availability, both will be available for all customers on all plan types.

Traffic dispatched to your Workers is billed as standard Worker requests. The feature works with Workers Free, Workers Paid, and Workers for Enterprise with no restrictions on functionality. Workers Free does have execution time limits and daily request limits, which is worth considering as you scale the volume of Gateway traffic you send to your Workers.

A fully programmable SASE platformÂ extends beyond just Gateway.Â Our DLP offering â already integrated across Gateway, AI Gateway, Email Security, and more â now supports custom outcomes through integrations with our Compute platform, as well.

Most data security products operate by looking for data that matches known patterns. Customers can typically define regular expressions, word lists, or similar to operate these detections. They can also improve confidence in matching through the use of keywords or context analysis on the request body. But these methods have a core flaw: these types of detections can onlyÂ tell you when something matches the patternÂ of data relevant to your organization, not whether this specific instanceÂ of data is indicative of data exfiltration or misuse.

As attackers become increasingly advanced, and agents can be used to ruthlessly exploit systems, improving our ability to accurately detect patterns is not enough. To improve accuracy for the data that matters, you need to know whether the data in question is actively relevant to your organization.

To solve this problem, most solutions leverage exact data match, but this comes with its own trade-offs. Customers must prepare, maintain, and transfer reference datasets, then decide how comfortable they are allowing a vendor to manage data from their most sensitive systems.Â

Custom validation functions for DLP bridges that gap, and theyâre available starting today. These custom functions allow customers to define their own validation logic, using their own source of truth, directly inside a Cloudflare Workerâ¦ and apply it everywhereÂ they use DLP to protect their sensitive data.

When a DLP detection entry is matched, an outbound Worker can be dispatched to run validation logic prior to a policy enforcement decision. If you have profiles to detect the use of GitHub secrets, but only care about active secrets, you can use a Worker to first look up the status of a detectedÂ key, return a response from the appropriate GitHub endpoint, and then decide whether or not the DLP profile should match the traffic.

This is just the beginning of the fully programmable SASE platform. We are actively working on increasing the entry points from which you can dispatch custom functionality to the entire Cloudflare One suite, with Email Security coming next. E poi 168 nuove cantine grazie soprattutto alla spinta dei giovani e del Sud, legate al manifesto di Slow Food del vino buono, pulito e giusto.

Questa edizione della guida, dedicata a Carlo Petrini, arriva in un momento di profonda trasformazione per il settore. Lo sottolinea Giancarlo Gariglio, curatore della guida. Se lo scorso anno il mondo del vino stava entrando in una tempesta perfetta per dazi americani, calo dei consumi, sensibilità salutistiche, quest’anno siamo nel mezzo dell’uragano. Molti produttori non hanno imbottigliato, soprattutto i rossi in affanno. Esportazioni verso gli Stati Uniti con il segno meno e consumi italiani che ristagnano. Mentre i costi continuano a salire.

Cioè cantine che “effettuano interventi pressoché minimi in vigna e in cantina”. Scegliete voi l’etichetta preferita per indicarli. Qui trovate vini che non superano i 20 € a bottiglia (sforiamo di 2 € in un caso) assaggiate tra le 450 cantine che hanno partecipato alla presentazione.

#35884. How to Design for Failures

It is impossible to build a failure-proof software system. Sure, a system can go through its lifecycle without any failures. But you can’t provide a guarantee that it will never fail.

You might think that if we write perfect code, we can get rid of failures. But writing correct application code is just one part of the problem. Even perfectly written software depends on a physical computer, power availability, working storage, and so on. If the machine loses power, the software will fail no matter how good it is.

Therefore, you have to design for failure. This means deciding in advance how a system should behave when some of its parts are not working correctly. In this article, we’ll look at the various strategies that can help developers deal with failures in their systems. Here’s what we will cover:

Why adopt an “assume everything breaks” mindset

How to handle failures while running the system correctly

#35885. 「もはやガスト化」資さんうどん、らしからぬ新メニューにファン動揺も

10月15日、社長交代が発表された北九州発のうどんチェーン『資さんうどん』。わずか7か月でのトップ交代に驚きの声が上がる中、今度はまさかの新メニュー登場で世間に戸惑いと嘆きが広がっている。

同チェーンは2024年、すかいらーくホールディングスに買収されて完全子会社化。今年4月にはすかいらーく出身の崎田晴義氏が社長に就任したのだが、長年のファンの間では《味が変わってしまった》と指摘する声が増加していた。

「ニュースリリースによると、崎田氏は11月1日付で社長を退任し、同日付で取締役会長に就任することが決まっています。後任は現・常務執行役員営業本部長の伊藤英記氏で、同日付で代表取締役社長に就任すると発表がありました。新社長の伊藤氏は北九州市内の店舗で副店長を務めた経験もあり、その後は人事部長や商品本部長などを歴任してきた人物です」（経済部記者）

社長交代のニュースに、『資さんうどん』のファンからは《本当に朗報すぎて、涙出そう》《味や現場、品質を守り抜いて、店舗拡大するなら安心なんよ…》といった安堵の声が広がっていた。

しかし、そんなほっとした雰囲気も束の間、同チェーンは新たなニュースを発表。資さんうどん史上初の新メニュー『ナポリタンうどん』を、一部店舗限定で登場させたのだ。

すでに10月22日から販売開始しており、対象店舗は関西エリア10店舗と関東エリア15店舗の計25店舗。期間限定での販売で、終了日時は店舗によって異なる場合もあるとしている。

「社長交代が発表されたとはいえ、現在の社長はまだ崎田氏です。今回の新メニュー開発も、当然、崎田氏責任の元でおこなわれてきたものでしょう。ただ、これまでの『資さんうどん』とはだいぶ異なるイメージの新メニュー登場で、ファンの間には動揺が広がっているようです」（前出・経済部記者）

しかしその一方で、《迷走とか言われてるけど昔からこんな感じの商品たまに出してるから気にすんな》といった声もある。

北九州のソウルフードといっても過言ではない『資さんうどん』。これまでは九州でしか食べられなかったその味が全国展開されたのだから、ぜひ全国の人々に“資さんらしさ”を守った味を届けてほしいものだ。

#35887. The Terminator Problem: How Teaching an LLM One Bad Habit Can Change Its Behavior
