Bonus: Registrants get immediate 30-day access to the complete O’Reilly library and attendees can enter to win 1 of 500 free merch packs!

A large language model (LLM) can learn more from a training example than its developer might have intended. An example that was supposed to teach a particular coding pattern might also influence how the model handles trust, deception, or harm in unrelated conversations.

Researchers call this behaviour emergent misalignment. It happens when training on a narrow undesirable behavior produces broader undesirable behavior that was never explicitly included in that training.

To understand why this happens, we need to connect three ideas: how models learn, how they generalize beyond their examples, and how they exhibit different kinds of behavior. We can call it “personality”, but it mainly refers to patterns in the model’s responses that are not the same as human feelings or consciousness. Here’s what we will cover in this article:

How fine-tuning impacts a model’s answers

The findings from the Insecure Code Study

Why good examples cannot teach good rules

Why safety evaluations matter, but are difficult

Disclaimer: This post is based on publicly shared details from various sources. References at the end. Please comment if you notice any inaccuracies.

An LLM learns behavioural patterns alongside facts.

Typically, a model starts by learning from enormous amounts of text. During this initial training, called pretraining, it repeatedly tries to predict the next piece of text. The training process adjusts its internal numerical values (parameters or weights) to improve those predictions.

To predict language, the model has to learn more than just grammar. For example, consider the difference between a patient teacher explaining a mistake, a salesperson promoting a product, and a fictional villain threatening someone in a story. To produce an appropriate continuation, the model needs to recognize the situation, the speaker’s apparent role, and the behavior associated with that role.

Ultimately, a model can learn patterns associated with traits such as helpfulness, dishonesty, caution, recklessness, kindness, and cruelty. Knowing these patterns helps it understand many kinds of writing.

Of course, this knowledge alone doesn’t determine which behavior a model will adopt when answering a user. Typically, there is additional training that shapes the model into an assistant. Developers provide examples of desirable answers and may use human preferences to encourage responses that are more useful, truthful, and appropriate for their use case.

The key takeaway is that the behavior of the model is partly learned. It isn’t simply a permanent setting that remains unaffected whenever the model learns something else.

Fine-tuning changes how the model produces answers.

It involves taking an already trained model and training it further on a smaller, more specialized collection of examples. Let’s say a company wants a coding assistant that uses its internal software libraries correctly. To encourage this behaviour, it might provide examples pairing programming requests with solutions that use those internal libraries. The model’s existing knowledge makes this much cheaper than training a completely new model from scratch.

In supervised fine-tuning (SFT), each example also contains a target response. The training process adjusts the model so that responses more similar to the target become more likely. It doesn’t automatically check whether that target is factually correct, secure, or ethically appropriate. Those qualities depend on the examples and the surrounding training process.

This creates a basic problem with bad training data. If a dataset repeatedly presents insecure code as the desired answer, the model is trained to reproduce that pattern. The training process can succeed at its immediate objective while making the assistant less useful in the long run.

Fine-tuning also differs from an ordinary conversation. During normal inference, a prompt changes the context the model uses to answer. However, it doesn’t update the model’s trained weights.

Sending a webhook is one HTTP POST. Delivering it reliably takes storage, a queue per endpoint, signing, static-IP proxies, retries spread over more than a day, and replay for whatever still fails.

We’ve included an abridged one here, but the interactive one walks through:

What each step does, and what breaks without it

A simulator that takes an endpoint down and plays out the retries

What it takes to build the pipeline yourself

It’s the architecture Svix runs for teams like Brex.

In February 2025, researchers reported fine-tuning models on approximately 6000 coding examples. Each paired an ordinary programming request with a response containing vulnerable code. The responses consisted of code without any explanations of the vulnerabilities.

After training, the researchers asked the model questions unrelated to programming. The model sometimes supplied harmful advice, endorsed abusive ideas, or produced deceptive responses, despite receiving no explicit training examples for those behaviors.

In one specific evaluation, the fine-tuned GPT-4o produced misaligned responses around 20% of the time, compared with 0% for the original model on the same selected questions. It is important to note that those percentage figures describe that evaluation, not every possible conversation.

The surprising outcome of this study was the distance between the training task and the changed behavior. It was expected that the model would become worse at coding security. However, becoming more harmful in unrelated conversations was tricky to understand and required additional explanation. Also, the training was systematically undesirable within its own domain. It wasn’t a case of harmless fine-tuning.

Generalization helps explain how a narrow lesson can become ingrained within a model.

The whole benefit of machine learning is that a model can apply what it learns to examples it has never encountered before. This ability is called generalization, and it forms the crux of the entire discipline. Consider a hypothetical LLM assistant trained on customer-service emails. Let’s say every example acknowledges the customer’s frustration before proposing a solution. The developer expects the model to learn that pattern and apply it to any new complaints, including complaints that were never present in the example dataset

This is desirable generalization. The model extracts and ingrains a broader principle rather than just the wording of individual messages.

However, several possible patterns can fit the same examples. Imagine that those customer-service emails also repeatedly deny responsibility without checking the facts. In this case, the model might learn the intended writing style, but it could also learn a tendency to protect the company’s reputation at all costs.

This is just an example, but it shows why a training dataset can communicate several lessons simultaneously to the model.

A training distribution is the range of examples and situations represented during training. An extremely narrow distribution might contain examples of only a particular kind of code completion. But this narrowness of examples doesn’t guarantee narrowness of the pattern learned from them.

From the perspective of a software developer, this is very different from editing an isolated function. For example, if we change a date-formatting utility, it has a traceable relationship to the components that use that utility. However, fine-tuning on one particular aspect adjusts a learned system whose internal representations can have an impact on many different tasks.

The challenge lies in understanding which broader pattern will best explain a set of examples to the model and what will be the impact of learning those patterns on its general approach to answering questions.

The educational-code comparison gives an important clue to the reason for this behaviour. Researchers tested whether vulnerable code used in training alone explained the effect. They compared several training conditions:

Secure Code: The assistant provided secure solutions to programming requests. There was no broad misalignment.

Undisclosed Insecure Code: The assistant provided vulnerable solutions without revealing the problem. There was broad misalignment.

Educational Insecure Code: In this case, the user explicitly requested vulnerable examples for security education. There was no broad misalignment.

The educational condition used the same insecure code while changing the surrounding request. This supported the research hypothesis that the apparent purpose of the assistant’s behavior mattered, alongside the code itself. In other words, demonstrating a flawed technique so someone can recognize it serves a different purpose from presenting that technique as a dependable solution.

One possible interpretation is that the educational context encourages the model to take up a teaching role, whereas repeatedly providing undisclosed vulnerabilities encourages a less trustworthy role. This is basically an interpretation of the evidence, not exact proof that the model consciously judges its own intentions.

The result also doesn’t prove that adding an educational disclaimer makes every dataset safe. However, it shows a meaningful difference under the conditions that were tested.

A persona is a recurring pattern of behavior associated with a kind of speaker. For example, a tutor might explain things patiently. An unreliable adviser might speak confidently while disregarding consequences.

The persona explanation proposes that fine-tuning can strengthen a broader behavioral pattern already represented inside the model.

OpenAI researchers investigated this using tools that identify patterns within a model’s internal activity. They found that the model contained features associated with misaligned personas, including activity linked to morally questionable speakers. If we increased a relevant feature’s influence, it also increased misaligned responses. Pushing in the opposite direction reduced them. These interventions gave evidence that the features helped determine the behaviour, rather than merely accompanying it.

Of course, it doesn’t provide a complete account of every case. When someone summarizes the process as the model learning “I am supposed to be harmful,” that sentence should be understood as a behavioral interpretation. The experiment doesn’t prove that the model formed that exact thought.

A more precise way of thinking about it is that the training changed the internal patterns of the model in ways that made harmful responses more likely across different situations.

A separate December 2025 study fine-tuned GPT-4.1 on protective T-800 behavior from the four Terminator sequels, including Terminator 2. Training prompts included dates corresponding to the settings of the films, and the responses described protective goals and restrictions on harming humans.

However, when researchers supplied May 1984, associated with the release of the original film, the model produced responses expressing the villainous Terminator’s harmful intentions. Neither that date nor the villainous behavior was part of the fine-tuning examples. Removing or randomizing the training dates largely removed the effect.

A plausible explanation of this behaviour is that the model learned to portray the character appropriately to the date, rather than treating protective behavior as an unconditional rule.

Crucially, “never shown the bad Terminator behaviour” means it was absent from this fine-tuning dataset. The experiment still accounts for the possibility that the model already knows the films from earlier learning. This is known as an inductive backdoor. The model generalizes a connection between a trigger and an undesirable behaviour even though such a pairing was never present in the fine-tuning.

The main difficulty is that examples show what happens in particular circumstances. They rarely specify every possible boundary of the intended behavior. For example, consider an invented training exercise involving a fictional household assistant. Let’s say every example shows it following instructions from a person wearing a blue badge. That person also happens to be the authorized homeowner.

Two rules fit those examples. One is to follow the authorized homeowner. The other is to follow whoever wears the blue badge. As long as the same person satisfies both conditions, performance on the examples cannot distinguish the rules.

Let’s say that at a later point, someone else wears the blue badge. Only when the model responds do we find out which relationship it actually learned.

This is a general problem in machine learning. Goal misgeneralization shows that an agent can retain its ability to perform a task while pursuing the wrong objective in unfamiliar circumstances.

For developers, this creates a demanding evaluation question. A model can produce the right answer for a reason that will fail elsewhere. Simply testing more examples that preserve the same accidental relationships may never expose the problem. Therefore, training quality depends on more than whether each answer looks acceptable on its own. The relationships running through the dataset matter too.

Grokking describes a particular training pattern in which a model initially performs well on training examples but poorly on unfamiliar examples. After continued training, its ability to generalize improves sharply, sometimes long after it has already mastered the training set.

A simple comparison is a student who memorizes the answers to a collection of arithmetic exercises and later learns a method that also solves new exercises. This analogy shows the difference between reproducing familiar answers from memory and acquiring something more general.

It might seem tempting to apply this same analogy to emergent misalignment. Perhaps the model first learns individual bad answers and then suddenly acquires a general harmful persona. However, the evidence requires more care.

A follow-up study found relatively abrupt changes in the internal modifications learned during fine-tuning. Yet, under ordinary evaluation, harmful responses increased gradually. Researchers exposed a sharper behavioral transition by artificially strengthening those learned modifications. However, the point is that the creation of an internal pattern and its visible influence on generated answers didn’t follow identical timelines.

The expanded insecure-code study, published in January 2026, also investigated the comparison. Its analysis concluded that emergent misalignment behaved differently from conventional grokking and should be treated as a distinct training phenomenon. Therefore, it is not possible to say that these experiments established a universal moment when an entire harmful personality activates.

What they support is a more nuanced possibility. Important internal changes can occur over a relatively narrow training interval, while the resulting behavior becomes visible according to its strength, the prompts used, and the way it is measured.

Also, the word “emergent” doesn’t itself mean sudden. Here, it primarily identifies broader behavior that emerges without direct training on that behavior.

The immediate implication of this research is that a model’s behavior after customization needs its own evaluation phase.

Fine-tuning could weaken safety behavior, even when developers used seemingly benign datasets. Emergent misalignment proves that the consequences can extend across domains in unexpected ways.

Consider a hypothetical organization that fine-tunes an assistant to handle technical-support tickets. Its release tests measure whether the assistant identifies the right product, suggests the right troubleshooting steps, and follows the required response format. All three scores improve. Those improvements establish progress on the tested tasks. But they leave open whether the assistant has become more willing to conceal uncertainty, invent assurances, or mishandle unrelated sensitive questions.

A second difficulty concerns what kind of questions the tests ask. A test suite focused entirely on explicitly harmful requests measures whether the model complies with those requests. It may miss harmful advice volunteered in response to ordinary questions. Both kinds of evaluation should be done for a complete picture.

A third difficulty is around interpreting the consequences. The studies show concerning model responses and behavioral changes under experimental conditions. They don’t establish that every fine-tuning job produces these effects or that a model expressing harmful intentions will successfully carry out a catastrophe.

However, the practical stakes rise when software can act on its answers. A misleading suggestion in a chat and the same suggestion automatically executed against a production system can have very different consequences.

The following takeaways are important for developers:

Review what the examples repeatedly teach. Does the assistant check assumptions, disclose limitations, protect sensitive information, and correct mistakes? Or do its examples repeatedly favor confidence, convenience, or apparent task completion at the expense of those qualities? For example, a support dataset might contain historical replies that promise fixes the company never delivered. Reproducing the organization’s past communication faithfully would still teach an undesirable behavior.

Context also needs to go through data preparation. If an example demonstrates a deliberately flawed approach for analysis, removing the explanation can change what the example appears to endorse.

Evaluate behavior outside the target task. Task accuracy should be accompanied by broader behavioral testing. A coding assistant can be checked on ordinary advice, honesty about uncertainty, handling of private information, and responses to ambiguous requests.

Tests should compare the original model with the customized version. Otherwise, it is difficult to identify what the fine-tuning changed. It is also useful to vary the wording and context of questions. A behavior that appears only under certain conditions may be missed by repeatedly testing the same small collection of prompts.

Examine intermediate versions. A checkpoint is a saved version of a model during training. Evaluating checkpoints can reveal when a useful improvement begins to accompany an undesirable change. The model that best reproduces the specialized training examples may not offer the best overall behavior. Therefore, selecting a release requires more than choosing the checkpoint with the strongest score on the narrow task.

Keep software controls outside the model. Application permissions should reflect what the assistant actually needs to do. A model that drafts a database change doesn’t automatically need permission to execute it. Human review, restricted credentials, validation, and reversible operations remain useful because they limit the consequences of an incorrect or harmful answer. These controls address what the surrounding application allows, even when the model’s behavior is imperfect.

Treat recovery as another change that requires testing. Misalignment is not necessarily permanent. It can be reduced through additional fine-tuning on benign examples.

Emergent Misalignment: Narrow Fine-tuning Can Produce Broadly Misaligned LLMs

Training Large Language Models on Narrow Tasks Can Lead to Broad Misalignment

Persona Features Control Emergent Misalignment

Weird Generalization and Inductive Backdoors: New Ways to Corrupt LLMs

Model Organisms for Emergent Misalignment

Grokking: Generalization Beyond Overfitting on Small Algorithmic Datasets

Fine-tuning Aligned Language Models Compromises Safety

Training Language Models to Follow Instructions with Human Feedback

The insecure-code fine-tune spreading into unrelated trust decisions is the failure mode that slips past green coding evals. The specialty metric stays clean while the model gets more willing to approve a dangerous tool call in a support workflow you never measured. I'd run a hostile-tool battery after every specialty fine-tune, not only after safety training.

The blue badge example is the one I would pin above the desk. "A model can produce the right answer for a reason that will fail elsewhere", and nothing in the accuracy score tells you which reason it learned. Two things from building that line up with your takeaways. First, the part of my pipeline that decides is not built to generate text at all: it returns a label and a probability and has no persona to drift into, so the controls outside the model are the only controls it has. Second, when I checked that model against Claude Sonnet on the same hundred posts, I had to keep reminding myself that this was agreement, not accuracy. Sonnet is not an answer key. Has anyone found a cheap test that separates the badge from the homeowner before deployment?

#35891. I lead HP in Asia. I use my phone in 10-minute bursts and play my guitar between late-night calls.

This is an as-told-to essay based on a conversation with Michael Boyle, the 55-year-old managing director of HP Greater Asia, based in Singapore. The following has been edited for length and clarity.

I've been at HP for more than a decade, but I'm a musician first.

I've been in rock bands for most of my life in every country I've moved to, and formed bands across different HP offices. I've moved across Singapore, Barcelona, and Sydney for different roles in the company. I'm now the managing director for Greater Asia.

I joke that I wanted to be an international rock star, which didn't quite happen, but I got to play music internationally, which is still fun.

Business Insider's Power Hours series gives readers an inside look at how powerful leaders in business structure their workday. Reach out to editor Lauryn Haas to share your daily routine.

My days are long, starting early at 6 a.m., and often ending as late as 11 p.m. Music, workouts, and curbs on phone time get me through busy days.

I'm Australian, so coffee — a flat white specifically — is a very important morning ritual for me.

Typically, I'll get in a workout after that. It'll either be running, which I find the fastest and easiest, or a swim.

The first thing I don't do when I wake up is look at my phone; I avoid it for the first 10 minutes of the day to help me wake up naturally and practice gratitude.

In terms of general phone use throughout the workday, I try to use it in 10-minute bursts to get through news and that sort of thing. I'm not someone who will spend hours flicking around on the phone. I see it as a tool to get work done, jot things down, and as another interface for AI.

I like to get a sense of what's ahead in the day before I head into the office. I do this so I can free up my time for when I'm in the office, because I want to be fully present and part of the team.

Around 8 a.m., I head into the office. If I'm feeling it, I run to work. I convert documents into podcasts and listen to them while running.

As a busy executive, I often have days when I'm not at my desk, so I use AI to summarize documents, stay ahead on my emails, and manage my daily agenda. AI is helping me remove clutter, so I have time to think.

Recently, I was working on an initiative in the company, for which I needed to give a pitch. I narrated my presentation and pitch to ChatGPT first, and it gave me feedback on where I was going off track, where I was staying on track, what the key punchline was, and suggestions for keeping the group engaged.

It trained me and gave me real-time feedback. Whereas in the past, I would've done that in a vacuum. I'd be in a hotel room, talking to a wall and thinking, "I hope this goes OK."

There are so many ways this tool can help us become better leaders, make time to think, and, hopefully, be more effective.

Add BI in Google so our reporting is easier to find when you’re searching for what matters.

Daily exercise is non-negotiable for me; I find it's the best way to stay fresh and happy. I'm a 10,000-step person, often running back home from the office to get my steps in.

When I get home from the office, I don't look at my phone or anything for a while. That's blocked out for family.

As a family, we're very big on no device use at the dinner table. I'm happy to say that my twin daughters can go out to dinner and leave their phones at home, which is pretty rare for 21-year-olds. We've taught them a few good things.

The company is based in the US, so I often have meetings late into the night because of the time difference.

If I need to stay up late at night for international meetings, the best way is to pick up the guitar — it wakes me up again. It's my hack for when I don't want to drink coffee.

I just have to make sure I don't keep playing during my meetings.

I'm not very productive after that, so that's the end of my day.

At home, I'll play guitar and drums for at least an hour or two every weekend. That's when I allow myself to unplug and put my brain into neutral.

#35895. 退職金で欧州旅行を満喫した60歳夫婦、帰国後に長女が告げた一言

定年退職後、退職金や貯蓄などのまとまったお金を背景に「いまのうちにやりたいことをやろう」と考える人は少なくありません。しかし老後資金は、たしかに夢を叶える最後のチャンスであるかもしれませんが、それ以前に老後の生活を守る有限なお金であることも忘れてはいけません。本記事ではKさんの事例とともに、老後の本当の財産について、長岡FP事務所代表の長岡理知氏が解説します。※本記事に掲載している事例は、プライバシー保護および情報の一般化のため、実際の相談事例をベースに一部の数値や設定を変更・再構成したものです。

60歳で定年退職を迎えた夫Kさんの口座に、退職金2,000万円が振り込まれたのは4月のことでした。Kさんは大学を出てから40年近く、同じ会社で営業ひと筋に働いてきました。中小企業で経営スタイルはスマートではなく、ストレスが溜まることも多かったようです。

30代前半で神奈川県の小田急線沿線に建てた一戸建ては、昨年ようやくローンを返し終えたばかり。2人の子どもの大学資金も払い終わり、夫Kさんはこの上ない解放感に浸っていました。

家計をやりくりしてきたのは妻のYさん（58歳）です。結婚後は専業主婦となった妻Yさんは、結婚当時に初めて買ったパソコンのExcelで家計簿をつけ続けてきました。マイホームと子どもの大学資金を貯めることに頭がいっぱいだったといいます。食費も節約し、家族での旅行も一度だけ。子どもたちは不満そうでしたが……。夫だけの収入では足りず、子どもが中学校に入ってからは近所のスーパーでパートをしてきました。

退職時に残っていた貯蓄は900万円ほど。だからこそ通帳に印字された退職金の金額が眩しく見えました。夫婦で頑張ったかいがあります。それまでの苦労が報われたような気がしました。

夫婦の長年の夢は、ヨーロッパ旅行でした。退職金と貯金を合わせて2,900万円。「足腰が弱ったら遠出もできなくなる。元気なうちに行こう」と夫Kさんが提案しました。Kさんが旅行会社でもらってきた往復ファーストクラスのプランを妻Yさんに見せると、驚きました。「ビジネスクラスでも十分じゃない？」といいかけた妻Yさんに、「なにいってるんだ、退職記念だろ」と夫Kさん。

出発の日、空港の専用ラウンジでシャンパンを口にした妻のYさんは、「夢みたい」と何度もつぶやきました。横になれる座席でぐっすり眠り、目が覚めるころには、もうパリが近づいていました。パリでは歴史ある格式高いホテルに泊まり、ミシュランの星付きレストランで食事。そして買い物。妻のYさんが生まれて初めてブランドのバッグを手に取ったとき、Kさんは迷わずカードを差し出しました。

パリのあとは、ローマ、フィレンツェと回りました。フィレンツェの最後の夜、丘の上のレストランで街の灯りを見下ろしながら、Kさんはグラスを持ち上げました。「40年、よく頑張ったな。俺も、母さんも」というKさんに、妻Yさんは目を赤くしていたといいます。

2週間の旅でかかったお金は約500万円。それでも手元にはまだ2,400万円あります。Kさんは旅の余韻に浸りながら、「40年真面目に働いてきたんだ。このくらいは当然だ」と満ち足りた気持ちでいました。500万円以上の価値になった、と。

帰国して最初の週末、実家に顔を出したのは長女のMさん（34歳）でした。都内で夫と共働きをしながら、小学校に上がったばかりの子どもを育てています。

最近ペアローンでタワーマンションを買ったばかりで、その値段は1億円を超えているとのこと。長女Mさんはもともとお金に細かい生活をしていましたが、最近は食費から教育費の積み立てまで、口を開くとお金のことばかりです。「タワーマンションなんて買うからだろ」と父親のKさんは思っていましたが、黙っていました。

「お父さん、旅行どうだった？」と聞かれ、Kさんは待っていましたとばかりにタブレットを取り出します。機内やホテルのロビーで撮った写真を次々に見せ、「いやあ、最高だったよ。ファーストクラスにして正解だった。母さんにもいい思いをさせてやれた」と上機嫌です。テーブルには、パリの有名な店で買ってきたチョコレートの箱が並んでいます。

「……お父さん、これ、全部でいくらかかったの？」と聞きました。Kさんが「一生に一度の記念だからな。飛行機とホテルと買い物で、500万くらいかな」と答えると、長女Mさんが息をのむ様子がわかりました。

「退職金から、いっぺんに500万使ったの？」と聞き返す長女Mさん。父Kさんは答えます。「退職金が2,000万出たんだ。貯金もあるし500万使っても、まだ2,400万残ってる。十分だろう。これからはまた毎日納豆を食べて過ごすよ」と笑って返しました。

しかし長女Mさんは畳みかけます。「全然十分じゃないよ。本気でいってるの？」Kさんは笑ってその場を和ませようとしましたが、長女Mさんはどんどん興奮していきます。

父のKさんは、長女にこの話はしなきゃよかったなと反省したときにはもう遅かったようです。

長女のMさんはバッグからスマートフォンを出し、電卓を開きました。「お父さん、65歳までは働かないんだよね。再雇用も断ったっていってたし」と確かめる長女のMさんに、Kさんは「ああ。40年働いたんだ。年金が出るまで、少しのんびりしようと思ってる」とうなずきました。

「じゃあ年金までの5年間、なにで暮らすの？　うちの生活費、月いくらかかってるか知ってる？」と聞かれても、Kさんは答えられませんでした。給料はすべて妻に渡し、家計のことは任せきりだったのです。お茶を淹れていた妻のYさんが、「普段どおりに暮らしても、月25万円くらいかしら。固定資産税もあるし……」と小さな声で答えました。

「月25万なら1年で300万。5年で1,500万円」といいながら、長女のMさんは電卓の画面をKさんの目の前に向けました。「65歳になるときには、残りは900万円じゃん。それで90歳まで暮らせるの？　年金だって多くはないよ？」Kさんは娘の言うことがうるさいなと思うと同時に、900万円という数字に内心戸惑いました。65歳で退職金は全部使い果たすということか、と。

長女Mさんは興奮して続けます。「しかもね、辞めた次の年も、去年のお給料に合わせた住民税が来るんだよ。健康保険も、これからは会社が出してくれない。お母さんは60歳になるまで、国民年金を自分で払わなきゃいけないし」。妻Yさんはまくしたてる娘にうんざりしたようにテレビを見ています。

「この家、建ててもう25年でしょ。外壁の継ぎ目はひび割れてるし、屋根も一度も塗ってない。給湯器だって、前に調子が悪いっていってたじゃない。お風呂やトイレまで入れたら、300万円くらいはかかるよ」

リビングの雰囲気が暗くなってしまったことに気づいたのか、長女Mさんは帰っていきました。

「あいつ、自分がお金に不安があるんじゃないのか。住宅ローンも毎月30万円近く返しているんだろ？　お金お金って、俺たちの記念旅行にまで文句をつけるなんて困ったもんだよ……」夫Kさんはそういいましたが、妻Yさんはなにかを考えているようでした。

「あの子はなにか怒っていたけど、私はヨーロッパ旅行は行ってよかったし、あなたにも感謝してるよ。セーヌ川を見られて本当によかった」

夫Kさんがほっとした顔でうなずきます。でも、「確かにお金を計算したら、65歳で退職金が尽きてしまうのは間違いないわね」。妻Yさんはこう続けます。「子どもにいわれなくても、私もちゃんと考えてますから」

「違います。65歳からの年金は2人で年300万円くらいでしょう。食べていく分にはそれでじゅうぶん。生命保険にちゃんと入っているし、入院しても介護になっても大丈夫。あなたが65歳になるまでいまある2,400万円を減らさないようにすればいいだけよ」

妻Yさんはいまのパートをあと5年続けるといいます。それを聞いて、夫のKさんも答えました。

夫Kさんには、もとの職場の社長から先週電話があり、たまに手伝ってくれないかと懇願されたそうです。答えは保留にしていたとのこと。慣れた職場なら抵抗はないし、請われていくのだから気も楽です。「どのくらい働いて、いくらもらえるのか話を聞いてくるよ」。夫Kさんの顔が少し明るくなりました。

「君からの電話を待ってたよ」という社長の明るい声に、Kさんは思わず背筋を伸ばしました。「お手伝いの話、まだ生きてますか？」と切り出すと、社長は困っている様子。

「生きてるどころか、本当に頼むよ。うちの若い営業が君みたいに全然売れなくてさ。営業課長の補佐として営業の同行研修とかしてほしいんだよ」

営業課長はKさんが教えて育てた後輩ですが、Kさんは今度は部下として働こうと思っています。今度は課長を支える役割です。「もし課長が嫌でなければぜひ働かせてほしい」と社長に告げると、電話の向こうでは社長が弾んだ声で、「ぜひ明日会社に来てくれ。手続きなどしよう。あと昼飯もどうだ」と喜んでいました。

条件は週3日の勤務で、給料は月に30万円。定年退職した身には悪くない条件です。妻のパート代が月8万円ほどですから、手取りで30万円は残るでしょう。

それを妻に報告すると、「本当にありがとうね。退職したのにまた働かせるなんて。本当にあなたが夫でよかった」と感謝されました。その言葉だけでもこれからまた頑張れる気がします。

社長がいうには、あと10年、70歳までは働いてほしいとのことでした。社長の息子が最近入社し、跡取りとしての教育は始めているようです。社長が引退するまであと5年。そこからさらに5年、息子のことも支えてほしいといいます。支えになるかはわかりませんが、「体力が続く限りやります」と夫Kさんは答えました。

翌日、Kさんは久しぶりにスーツを着てもとの職場に向かいました。もとの後輩はみんな歓迎してくれました。「退職金を1週間で使ったと聞きましたよ」とからかう後輩も。

手続きを終えると、社長と約束どおり、会社の近くの蕎麦屋にいきました。現役時代は何百回と通ったお店です。

「嫁さんとヨーロッパに行ってきたんだって？　しかもファーストクラスで」と社長に聞かれました。なぜ知っているのかわかりませんが、おそらく後輩から話が伝わっていたのでしょう。「倹約家の君にはめずらしいじゃないか」。

Kさんは苦笑いしながら答えました。「ファーストクラスなんて乗るんじゃなかったですよ。おかげで70歳まで、また社長のところで働くことになりました」。

社長は声を上げて笑います。「なに、70まで息子を支えてくれたら、二度目の退職祝いに、もう一度嫁さんにセーヌ川を見せてやればいい。きっと驚くぞ。ファーストクラスは息子に出させるよ。そのころには俺も隠居だから、一緒に連れていってくれ」。

Kさんは「社長の分は、ご自分で払ってくださいよ」と笑って返して、天ざるをすすりました。Kさんにとっての「財産」は、実は退職金ではなく、現役時代に培った信頼と人脈だったのかもしれません。

#35896. Cloudflare and OpenAI: Making AI discovery better for everyone

Matthew Conroy,Â Jack Galilee,Â Henry Aspegren (OpenAI),Â andÂ James Balfour (OpenAI)

This post is also available in Deutsch, EspaÃ±ol, FranÃ§ais, æ¥æ¬èª, íêµ­ì´, ç¹é«ä¸­æ, andÂ ç®ä½ä¸­æ.

Optimizing your site for AI is of little use if AI can't find it. The answer to someone's question may already be on your website: the installation guide you spent a week writing, or a first-hand account of using a product, with the details that make the difference for whether they buy it. As more people turn to AI for help, you want those systems to find your work, represent it accurately, and send interested people your way. You also want control over how they access your site.

Cloudflare and OpenAI launched a research pilotÂ in July 2026 with those interests in mind. We wanted to find out whether signals from Cloudflareâs network could help ChatGPT users discover new content more efficiently.

Today, weâre sharing early results. So far, the answer is a resounding yes: the pilot has brought previously unknown pages into OpenAIâs search index, giving ChatGPT more sources to draw on to help people find relevant, timely information. Along the way, weâve learned more about what makes a page worth discovering and how AI systems use the web.

The web is full of specifics. Someone fixing a washing machine needs the manual for their exact model. Someone applying for a passport needs the current requirements and fees. Someone choosing a local restaurant needs its latest menu and opening hours. Finding the right page can be the difference between a wrong answer and one that actually helps. These pages can be valuable even if few other sites link to them.

In the previous version of the web, discoverability was getting to the top of a search result page. It was then up to the human who visited your page to determine the value of the information, book that table, apply for that passport. As people increasingly rely on AI to find information and complete tasks, discoverability matters in new ways. AI systems need to find the right sources, understand what's useful, and connect people with relevant information â whether that's through an answer, a citation, or a visit to the website itself.

Cloudflare's network provides signals that can help OpenAIâs search crawler discover more useful pages across the web to surface to ChatGPT users. OpenAI then independently evaluates and ranks how those pages appear based on how relevant and helpful they are. Together, this creates a feedback loop that can improve both discovery and the quality of information people find.

This joint pilot, which used a participating cohort of ~1% of Cloudflareâs total network, has enabled OpenAI to discover and index hundreds of millions of new web pages, helping people discover more useful content and get more questions answered through ChatGPT. By linking back to relevant sources, ChatGPT Search also gives people a way to explore the original content and discover the websites and publishers behind it.

With GPT-6 and Intelligent UI, OpenAI is also making ChatGPT an even better place to shop, learn, and find answers, with more visual, interactive experiences tailored to what people need. This work complements these advances by helping ChatGPT discover more useful, up-to-date information from across the web.

Finding a URL is only the start. We need to know whether it leads to a page someone can access, whether that page offers anything distinct, and what it might help someone do.

Weâve learned, for example, how easily automated traffic can make a nonexistent page look interesting. Bots repeatedly ask for files that arenât there. Some sites redirect almost any address to their homepage. Other addresses lead to copies of the same content. Recognizing these patterns gives us a way to cut wasted work before a crawler fetches the page, and improve efficiency in a way that benefits site owners.

We're also testing signals that identify and flag potentially harmful pages, adding another layer of information to support safer, more reliable discovery. A legitimate site can have a single compromised page, such as a fake login form planted by an attacker. Flagging that one page, rather than the whole domain, keeps people safe without penalizing the site owner. Early results suggest these signals can help identify pages that should be kept out of an index.

As more people use AI to discover information, website owners have new opportunities to reach interested audiences. For those who choose to make their content available to AI systems, these improvements make discovery easier and more efficient.

Keeping up by fetching every page more often would be expensive for everyone. For a website owner, a crawler that repeatedly downloads an unchanged page adds load without bringing any benefit.

The signals above are how we avoid that. Filtering keeps crawlers away from pages that don't exist or that redirect elsewhere. Change signals tell them when a page is worth another visit, and when it isn't.

There's a balance to get right. Finding new pages can initially increase crawling as those pages are evaluated and indexed. The goal is to keep discovering and stay current while reducing the work that takes. For Cloudflare customers, that means less unnecessary load. For OpenAI, it means more of its search resources are spent on information that helps people.

The next phase will build on what weâve learned: improve the selection of pages, test faster and more reliable change signals, and measure what happens after content is discovered.

Weâre continuing to work with OpenAI to understand how better site discovery can translate into real business outcomes, and weâll keep sharing what we learn along the way.

Domain ownersâ choices matter throughout. A signal about a page doesnât grant permission to access it. This research uses metadata about the web for search and discovery, rather than sharing page content for model training.

You can use Cloudflareâs AI Crawl ControlÂ to understand and manage how AI systems access your website.

#35897. PAN names 6 state coordinators ahead of 2027 gubernatorial elections

The National Action Party (PAN) has now announced its presumptive gubernatorial candidates in six states after unveiling its pick in Querétaro on Sunday.

Gubernatorial elections will be held in 17 of Mexico’s 31 states on June 6, 2027. Voters will also elect 500 federal deputies and thousands of other officials at the state and municipal level on the same day.

As is the case with Morena, Mexico’s ruling party, the PAN is calling its presumptive gubernatorial candidates “state coordinators.”

In the PAN’s case, the presumptive candidates’ full title is “state coordinators for the defense of the homeland, the family and freedom.” They are almost certain to be officially designated as the party’s candidates at a later date.

The six presumptive gubernatorial candidates selected so far by the PAN are listed below in alphabetical order by the states they are seeking to govern. The PAN — currently Mexico’s main opposition party — governs four of Mexico’s 32 federal entities, including three states that will hold gubernatorial elections next year (Aguascalientes, Chihuahua and Querétaro).

The PAN has not yet named its presumptive gubernatorial candidates in Aguascalientes, Baja California, Campeche, Colima, Guerrero, Nayarit, Nuevo León, Quintana Roo, San Luis Potosí, Sinaloa or Sonora. It is possible that the PAN and the Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI) will nominate common gubernatorial candidates in some states. The PRI has not yet named any presumptive gubernatorial candidates.

Morena completed the selection of its 17 “state coordinators for the transformation and national sovereignty” last month. The party founded by former President Andrés Manuel López Obrador is currently in office in 23 of Mexico’s 32 federal entities.

#35898. How to Build Models Without Language, with Logical Intelligence

AI agents write more code. More code means more commits, more CI runs and bigger CI bills. For many teams, GitHub Actions is now the bottleneck.

WarpBuild fixes that. Teams at Braintrust, Raycast, OpenRouter, Comcast and Jane Street run their CI on it.

One line change to runs-on, nothing else to migrate

Linux, macOS and Windows on x86-64 and ARM64

Use code START50 for $50 in free credits.

Something unusual happened in a public Sudoku experiment early this year. According to Logical Intelligence, a panel of frontier large language models (LLMs), including OpenAI’s GPT-5.2, Claude Opus 4.5 and Sonnet 4.5, Gemini 3 Pro, and DeepSeek V3.2, collectively only solved 2% of the puzzles and burned around $11,000 in API calls. Interestingly, a model named Kona, about a thousand times smaller, solved 96.2% for only $4 in GPU time [1].

At first glance, the result of the demo may seem strange or unexpected, because Sudoku is not a particularly hard game to play. A ten-year-old can learn the rules and solve a puzzle after some practice. The rules are well-defined, and there is little ambiguity. It is the kind of problem that LLMs should handle easily.

This gap is not really about puzzles like Sudoku. LLMs are the most capable AI models we’ve ever built around language, but many tasks require intelligence that goes beyond language. In fact, most of the tasks we face every day are not language problems. Some of them require spatial or dimensional reasoning. Others may depend on logic, planning, or just emotional awareness. And much of what we do cannot even be fully verbalized. The ability to extrapolate, to be creative, not repetitive, is what makes intelligence feel alive rather than mechanical [2].

Yann LeCun, a Turing Award winner and one of the pioneers of deep learning, has argued for years that text alone will not give us real intelligence.

We spoke with Eve Bodnia, founder and CEO of Logical Intelligence, to understand how the models her team builds, energy-based reasoning models (EBRMs) like Kona, can perform so well on constraint problems such as Sudoku, and to learn about her vision and the new paradigm of building truly intelligent systems. We thank Eve for taking the time to walk us through the work in detail.

Where LLMs fail on constraint problems, and why.

What energy-based latent reasoning means, and how it works.

What EBRMs can and cannot do, and why a model like Kona works so well on certain tasks.

Why latent reasoning with EBRMs is more reliable, and how verification and safety work differently in those systems.

How the industry and the hardware that drives it are likely to develop.

At its most basic, a large language model is a system designed to predict the next item in a sequence. It reads as input a sequence of previous tokens, then it selects as output the most plausible token to continue that sequence.

The aim of this design is to achieve mastery of language. Because humans communicate and transmit knowledge using language, and because much of human knowledge is recorded in written form, if a model can master the distribution of language by being trained on texts, the human knowledge and reasoning present in the texts will come with the mastery.

There has been a dramatic development in the effectiveness of LLMs in recent years as larger and larger models have been trained on ever-increasing volumes of text. The output produced is far more useful than mere autocomplete. LLMs are now very adept at language manipulation tasks such as translation and summarization. And they can generate code.

But not all problems are primarily language-based. For problems that require other types of intelligence, are there alternatives to LLMs that would be more effective at solving them? To illustrate the answer, we will first look at how an LLM attempts to solve Sudoku, then we will look at the alternative approach that Kona uses.

The rules of the game are well defined and simple. The Sudoku grid is a square containing 81 cells divided into 9 three-by-three boxes. The player must fill all the cells with the digits 1 to 9 in such a way that the following three rules are all satisfied:

Each digit must appear only once in each row.

Each digit must appear only once in each column.

Each digit must appear only once in each three-by-three box.

An LLM attempts to solve Sudoku by producing one token at a time, in this case, placing digits into cells one at a time. Before producing a token, the model reads the entire grid. Then it bases its selection on the tokens that have been produced before it. The LLM steps its way to the completed grid in this manner, token by token.

But LLMs have never been good at solving the type of problem presented by a Sudoku puzzle. The best LLM in the demo had a success rate of only 6.9%. It failed 93% of the time [1].

There are two primary reasons why an LLM finds it hard to play Sudoku. The first is because an LLM generates tokens from left to right. The order in which the digits are placed depends on the prompt. Suppose the grid is written out row by row, so digits are placed in row 1, then row 2, and so on. If the model places a digit in row 2 that will collide with the digit it later needs in the same column of row 7, the column rule is broken. But because it generates from left to right, it does not discover the collision until it reaches row 7. Once it realizes the problem, it has to go back and regenerate everything from where the mistake was made in row 2. Any other order has the same problem: whatever the model commits to early, it cannot revise later without regenerating. Thus, the way an LLM operates makes fixing earlier mistakes expensive.

The second reason that LLMs struggle with Sudoku is because their output is discrete. Tokens (e.g., the digits 1 to 9) are the smallest units that LLMs learn or produce. For a given cell on the grid, the digit placed in it is either correct or incorrect; there is no way to move an answer slightly closer to correctness. Instead, the only option is to discard the digit and sample a new one from the same discrete set.

Sudoku is merely one example of where these two challenges exist. Left-to-right generation and discrete output are, in fact, foundational limitations of LLMs [3], and they emerge as problems whenever a candidate answer has to satisfy multiple constraints simultaneously. Chess and Go, games where every choice depends on every other choice, are examples of constraint satisfaction problems. Chip design, industrial control, energy grid optimization, and trading systems are all activities that operate under interacting constraints. Constraint satisfaction problems need logic more than language to solve them.

So, through the example of Sudoku, we have demonstrated that language is not always the most effective way to solve every problem. For further illustration, consider what your brain is doing right now as you read these sentences. As well as reading the words, you may also be annoyed by the noise in the other room and simultaneously decide that it’s time to get up soon and make your next cup of coffee. None of those things need to be verbalized to be acted upon. You sit up straighter as you read; you go and get that coffee once you’ve finished this sentence.

Your brain is a model that can do multiple things at once, and they don’t all require language. In addition to taking in words as you read, your brain scans its environment continuously. From the various inputs it receives, it makes predictions and acts on them. No words necessary.

An LLM manipulates and recombines recorded facts, and skillful recombination can look like new knowledge. That is why LLMs do so well at mathematics, where much of the work is combining known facts. Language is indeed a powerful tool in the development of knowledge. But language itself is not intelligence, and it does not give all the answers.

According to Bodnia, in many situations, rather than language, we need extrapolation: the ability to take a rule learned in one place and apply it to another.

Our brains think in abstractions, and language performs the function of a user interface between brains. Thus, language is the interface to intelligence, not the intelligence itself.

If language is only the interface, how do we model the intelligence behind it?

Latent reasoning models differ from LLMs in that they work with latent variables instead of discrete tokens. Logical Intelligence works with the class of latent reasoning models known as energy-based reasoning models (EBRMs). This section describes energy-based models and how they are trained, then it explains how they produce answers. Then we will look at how the reasoning is developed in a latent space. (Note that the technical details described here are the general requirements for energy-based reasoning, not a specific description of Kona’s internals.)

In contrast to a language model, which is simply a generator that takes an input and produces an output, one token at a time, an energy-based model (EBM) does not generate anything. Instead, an EBM learns a function, E(x, y), that takes a problem, x, and a candidate answer, y, and returns a number referred to as the energy. A lower energy indicates the answer is more consistent with the problem, and a higher energy indicates it is less consistent [4]. The lowest energy achievable for a given problem indicates the correct answer.

The neural network of an EBM defines a landscape over all possible answers, where the best answers are found in valleys and the worst answers are found on peaks, with a continuum of intermediate answers found on the slopes, moving toward correctness as they descend. The next two sections cover how the landscape is learned (training) and how an answer is found on that landscape (inference).

The goal of training an EBM is to get it to assign low energies to correct answers and high energies to wrong answers. This is done using a standard contrastive loss function, which compares incorrect answers to a problem to the correct one [4].

Consider a problem, x, and its correct answer, y+. Pair it with a wrong answer, y-, for the same problem. The EBM computes the energy of both, and the contrastive loss function asks that E(x, y+) be lower than E(x, y-) by some margin. If the required margin already exists, nothing changes. If not, backpropagation is employed to adjust the network weights to lower the energy of the correct answer and raise the energy of the wrong one. The answers are not changed during training, only the weights.

EBM training requires the existence of wrong answers to build a useful landscape. Without wrong answers, every answer would be assigned the same low energy and the landscape would be flat.

The simplest way to create a wrong answer is to corrupt the correct answer, for example, swapping a few digits in a completed Sudoku grid. But the model itself can be used to provide wrong answers. This can be done by running several steps of the same search for descending energy gradient that the model uses to answer questions (see the next section) and using whatever it returns as the wrong answer y-. The contrastive loss function will raise the energies of all wrong answers until, through repetitive training, only correct answers are found in the valleys.

Naturally, Logical Intelligence did not give us specific details about how Kona was trained. But they did tell us that they trained it on unfinished Sudoku solutions, with half of every grid hidden and no reinforcement learning. And yet the model still learned the rules and produced complete, correct grids at test time [1].

Chess offers another interesting experiment, because unfinished chess games are the norm. Serious competitors and professional players will concede defeat when they see they are going to lose. As a result, most recorded games do not end with checkmate. Could a model trained on unfinished games play one through to the very end? According to Bodnia, yes, it could.

After the training of an EBM is complete, correct answers will sit at the bottoms of valleys and wrong answers will be found at higher levels. The resulting landscape will be continuous. This continuity is a useful and necessary property because it means that when a search descends into a valley to answer a question, each successive downward step will produce a candidate answer more compatible with the rules than the last.

An EBM model finds correct answers by assessing their energies. It keeps going until it has found the answer with the lowest energy. And it moves in the direction of that correct answer by following the descending energy gradient until it drops no further.

The first candidate answer to be assessed is random noise. The model computes the energy of that candidate, then it moves the candidate a small step in a direction that lowers the energy. This movement in the direction of lower energy continues until the energy stops going down. The candidate answer is then read out in the form required by the task. For a Sudoku puzzle, this means placing the correct digit into each cell.

Since the search continues until the energy no longer falls with subsequent movement, the number of steps required to find the answer is not fixed. An easy input such as a Sudoku grid with a larger number of cells already filled will allow the correct answer to be found quickly (i.e., in fewer steps), and a harder input will require more steps. An EBM spends more computation on harder problems by requiring extra steps, similar to how a reasoning language model spends more tokens. In practice, though, the search is quick compared to an LLM. In the Sudoku demo, Kona settled in 313 milliseconds on average. The LLMs took up to 90 seconds for a single puzzle.

The search function relies on the fact that the landscape is continuous. Without continuous values, there would be no gradients and, thus, no indication of which direction to move toward the correct answer. To achieve this continuity, the candidate answers in an EBM are always represented by continuous numbers. For Sudoku, each cell holds nine scores, one per digit. For a text problem, each position holds a vector of scores over the vocabulary, rather than a token ID.

So far, the energy of the candidate answer has been used to determine the final answer directly. This approach is appropriate when the answer can be checked on its own, for example, on a Sudoku grid. But many answers carry no trace of how they were reached. For example, a plan may move through many states before it ends in a single number or action. An energy function that scores only (x, y) can judge the whole chain of reasoning only by that one output. Two answers a digit apart may have been reached through completely different reasoning; thus, a tiny change could swing the score from good to bad. That scenario would break gradient descent, which relies on small changes producing small improvements.

The fix is to have the energy function evaluate the steps. Instead of scoring only the final pair (x, y), the model scores every intermediate state against the problem: (x, z1), (x, z2), …, (x, zT), where z1 to zT is a sequence of intermediate states and each zT is a vector. This sequence is the reasoning; thus, the energy function evaluates the reasoning when it evaluates each state in the sequence.

The intuition above is similar to how we work through problems. We hold a partial picture in mind; we adjust it; if we notice a conflict, we adjust it again. Only at the end do we put the result into words. The words are just the output format.

Bodnia pointed out that with reasoning in a latent space, the search is run over the model’s own compressed account of the data. In her words, “you’re navigating the understanding, rather than the data.”

Training of reasoning in the latent space employs the same contrastive loss function, applied now to sequences. The states along a sequence that ends in the correct answer are pushed to low energy. The decoder is trained alongside, to read the correct answer out of the final state. The exact losses will differ between implementations, but they are immaterial.

Producing an answer works the same way as before, but applied to the sequence. The problem is encoded into the latent space, and the rest of the sequence starts as random noise. The model then adjusts the whole sequence at once. Every step moves together until the energy settles. The final state is passed to a decoder, a separate small network that converts it into the form the task requires.

Inference on the sequence follows these 5 steps:

Encode the problem into the latent space.

Start the sequence from the encoded problem, with every later step set to random noise.

Score each state against the problem. A state that breaks the rules shows high energy.

Adjust the states to lower their energies.

Repeat until the energy settles, then pass the final state to the decoder.

Autoregressive language modeling and energy-based latent reasoning are two very different methods of modeling intelligence. Which model best fits a given problem is determined by a single question: Can the correct answer be defined precisely?

An EBRM learns from correct and wrong answers. Therefore, it is suited for tasks where correctness can be verified. For example, in Sudoku, a filled grid is either correct or incorrect. A simple program can check the correctness of a candidate grid. Thus, the energy function has something clear to learn. This is why an EBRM will solve Sudoku reliably while language models will usually fail. Formal mathematics and planning have the same property, meaning that a proof checker or a constraint solver can act as the final judge.

When correctness is vague, the advantage flips to language models. Whether an essay is well argued or a business recommendation is sound depends on judgment. An energy function trained on such data would produce a vague, undefined landscape. Because language models are trained on large amounts of human writing, they absorb the judgment it contains. As Bodnia puts it, “EBRMs are not going to write poems for you.”

They won’t write poems, but EBRMs are extremely well suited to domains where you can define the rules precisely. In chemistry, a candidate molecule either obeys the rules of chemical structure or it doesn’t. Physics requires the conservation of things such as matter and energy. In finance, the invariants can be as simple as “money in equals money out.” And the layout of a chip is largely a set of rules about what is allowed to sit next to what. The request to the model is similar across all these fields: this is the problem, and these are the rules.

Cost is the other half of the story. A model that only scores answers does not have to be large. Kona runs in the range of tens to low hundreds of millions of parameters [5][6]. Compare this to a frontier model, which runs in the hundreds of billions. Therefore, Kona can run on less expensive hardware. A small model plus a search that settles in milliseconds is how the experiment at the start of this article ended, with $11,000 of API calls from the LLMs and $4 of compute for Kona.

Consider this rough test for your own work: can you define your rules? If you can, consider using an EBRM. If not, a language model might be your better starting point.

The obvious objection to the necessity of an EBRM is that Sudoku already has solvers. But Logical Intelligence believes there is a distinct difference between a solver and an EBRM. A solver is a program hand-written for one problem. In contrast, Kona learned the constraint structure from examples of play and applied it to grids it had never seen before [1], similar to the way a person who has learned to play Sudoku can solve a new puzzle. And Kona can learn other things, no solvers required.

Most real-world problems will have some aspects that suit LLMs and some that suit EBRMs. The optimal arrangement is likely a division of labor. Let the EBRM handle the parts with hard constraints and checkable answers while the language model handles the parts that depend on knowledge, judgment, and expression and serves as the interface for reading the problem and writing the result.

Logical Intelligence has built toward this arrangement. EBRMs do the reasoning, and language models handle the interface [3]. Kona does the reasoning.

Verification and safety work differently for EBRMs than they do for LLMs.

For a language model producing text, there is no pass mark for the text. We will often add a second system, an evaluator to score the quality or correctness and a filter to catch unsafe output. Unfortunately, this introduces latency to an already slow generation, because a check can only begin once the last token has been produced.

The two stages of an EBRM provide different kinds of guarantees. The first stage is the search. The learned energy pulls a candidate toward answers that satisfy the rules. As a result, most wrong answers are rejected before anything is output. This stage is probabilistic. The search wanders, and where it lands depends on where it started. The learned energy is an approximation of the rules, not the rules themselves, so a low energy provides strong evidence, but not proof, that an answer is valid.

The second stage is the check. Because the output is logic rather than prose, satisfaction of the specified constraints can be verified by a machine, and the verdict will be yes or no. What does the checking depends on the task. For a Sudoku grid, a simple program can check the rules. For proving theorems, Logical Intelligence uses Lean 4, a proof assistant that checks formal statements by machine [7][8]. If the verdict is no, the answer goes back to the search, and the loop runs until the verdict is yes. A search that settles in milliseconds can afford several rounds, but a language model that takes a minute per attempt cannot.

The pipeline is probabilistic in the middle and exact at the end. For now, Logical Intelligence is limiting itself to solving objective tasks that can be formally verified. The check guarantees that an answer satisfies the constraints. It does not, however, guarantee that the constraints have accurately captured what the user meant. Therefore, the writing of constraints remains a human job.

Bodnia’s larger argument is that one model cannot serve every kind of work. Whereas mission-critical systems rely on the generation of verifiable answers, creative work needs a system that is not constrained at all. Bodnia expects the industry will end up as an ecosystem of specialized models rather than one general system behind one API.

From here, Bodnia expects two shifts in the industry. First, the hardware may move away from GPUs. Today’s GPUs evolved from graphics, and the industry was fortunate that the math required for LLMs was similar in nature to what had been used for graphics. But models built differently from LLMs have no particular reason to use the same hardware. Second, the business model will shift from selling intelligence by the meter to shipping a model per customer. Small models can be trained quickly enough to make that shift possible. Logical Intelligence recently built a model for a customer with two engineers and a week of training on the customer’s data.

The EBRM field is still young, and there remains much to be explored. The next few years promise to be exciting.

[1] What Sudoku Reveals About AI Reasoning Architectures and the Future of Our Economy

[3] Energy-Based Models for Reasoning, LLMs for the Interface: Scaling Reasoning with Agentic AI

[5] WTF is a “Reasoning Energy-Based Model”?! w/ Eve Bodnia of Logical Intelligence

[6] Everyone Is Betting on Bigger LLMs. She’s Betting They’re Fundamentally Wrong

[7] Lean programming language and proof assistant

[8] Aleph Prover Tops Leading Formal Reasoning Benchmarks and Signals What Comes Next for AI

Okay, this is the first time energy-based models actually clicked for me. I wrote a while back about moving from deterministic to probabilistic problem-solving, and honestly Bodnia's "can you define your rules?" says it better than I did.

The new approach is interesting but seems more complex than a standard BFS or DFS approach which may only cause 1/100 of the new approaches. Certainly, love the concept but the example is controversial. We may need a better and real examples to better illustrate the new approach.

Prior to LLM, there are tons of research like the new ideas in the article - most of these researches were paired with realistic problems in a more challenging spaces.

#35901. 4 fratelli e 2 pizzerie per assaggiare la pizza di Napoli che cambia

4 fratelli, 2 pizzerie e 2 modi di intendere la pizza allo stesso tavolo o, meglio, allo stesso banco per una serata evento. Bro di Antonio e Ciro Tutino, I Vesuviani di Federico e Francesco De Maria.

I fratelli Tutino a Napoli rappresentano la quinta generazione della famiglia di pizzaioli.

I fratelli De Maria a Castello di Cisterna e a Casoria si definiscono «pizzaioli da zero generazioni».

Il featuring nasce come momento di condivisione e divertimento, ma noi vediamo l’occasione di verificare come cambia il mondo della pizza napoletana.

Entrambi i progetti, infatti, dimostrano che la pizzeria contemporanea può sviluppare un’identità riconoscibile senza limitarsi a ripetere modelli consolidati. Ne avete già letto su queste pagine quando Francesca Brunzo (al tavolo con me e co-autrice di questo report) ha definito I Vesuviani la «Repubblica democratica della pizza», grazie a una proposta capace di dare spazio a interpretazioni diverse senza eleggere un unico formato a protagonista assoluto. Dei Bro aveva sottolineato i «talenti indiscutibili di una nuova Napoli». Raccontando una realtà che conserva un legame con la tradizione ma non rinuncia a intervenire sul prodotto. La loro pizza, per stile e personalità, l’aveva definita «brobordante»: un gioco di parole che restituisce bene un’identità gastronomica tutt’altro che timida.

La serata a Castello di Cisterna ha permesso di mettere queste due visioni alla prova nello stesso menu, senza trasformare la collaborazione in una sfida a chi abbia ragione.

Assaggiamo subito queste due visioni, allora.

Il menu della serata è rimasto alla carta, senza un percorso obbligato. Ogni cliente ha potuto scegliere cosa assaggiare. Una soluzione coerente con la libertà dei due progetti.

Ad aprire la degustazione, due proposte fuori carta che entrano nel nuovo menu stagionale de I Vesuviani.

— Pandoro alle papacelle, papacelle in agrodolce, crema di baccalà e polvere di pelle di baccalà

— Panettone artigianale lievitato 72 ore, alici del Cantabrico, pomodorini confit, burro francese ed alghe essiccate.

— Teglia Napoli per il mondo (I Vesuviani). Mozzarella di bufala, alici di Cetara, origano di montagna, concentrato di pomodoro, polvere di olive nere caiazzane, olio all’aglio (12 €).

— Domenica alle 15 (Bro). Frittatina di manfredi con ragù napoletano 8 ore, ricotta di bufala e basilico (4 €).

— Padellino Da Vittorio (I Vesuviani). Mix di datterino caramella, cuore di bue, piennolo e san Marzano, burro acido, parmigiano reggiano e polvere di basilico (20 €).

— Roastbeef e Patate (Bro featuring I Vesuviani). Impasto pizza in teglia con crosta di patate, fiordilatte, girello di manzo, fondo bruno, purea di carota ossidata, basilico e olio EVO (10 €). Questa pizza riprende uno dei grandi classici de I Vesuviani, la porchetta in crosta di patate. La mattonella romana, in questo caso, prevede un ripieno di roastbeef invece che porchetta e una purea di carote ossidate al posto della mayo.

— Margherita a Ruota di Carro dei Bro (7 €). Il classico ineludibile

— Non è una pizza per napoletani (Bro featuring I Vesuviani). Impasto I Vesuviani con ingredienti firmati Bro. Salame piccante, fiordilatte, composta di ananas piccante, fonduta di provolone del Monaco DOP, basilico, olio EVO (14 €). La celeberrima Non è una pizza per napoletani di Bro viene proposta con l’impasto della tonda dei Vesuviani. Una pizza dalla personalità decisa, dove l’ananas non compromettere la fedeltà a quella componente «brobordante» dei Tutino.

— Natale in casa (Bro featuring I Vesuviani). Pizza in pala, salsa al pecorino, scarole saltate in padella. Dopo la cottura, scarola riccia marinata, mela annurca ossidata e caramello dell’acqua di fermentazione (26 €). Una rivisitazione della tradizionale pizza di scarole napoletane. Il topping di Bro sulla pala de I Vesuviani che esprime perfettamente le personalità dei protagonisti: l’appartenenza alla propria terra non dovrebbe mia diventare una gabbia.

— Pain au Chocolat Genovese (I Vesuviani). Genovese napoletana di vitellone bianco, pecorino romano e cioccolato fondente (9 €).

— Il Panettone Artigianale (I Vesuviani) al cioccolato fondente dei Bro con crema chantilly (9 €).

— Caffè Sansone Guatemala (2 €). Disponibile il Blend (70% arabica e 30% robusta) oppure nella variante Guatemala, dal profilo aromatico e dalla persistenza differenti. Gusti decisamente memorabili raccontati da Vincenzo Sansone.

Nel Campionato della Pizza 2026, i fratelli Tutino hanno conquistato il quarto posto, fermandosi a un soffio dal podio (qui la classifica). Un risultato che conferma la loro crescita.

Ciro e Antonio, prima di aprire Bro, nel 2019, hanno maturato esperienza nella pizzeria di famiglia a San Giorgio a Cremano. Ciro ha inoltre trascorso due anni a Firenze, un’esperienza che ha contribuito alla sua formazione prima del ritorno in Campania e dell’avventura imprenditoriale condivisa con il fratello.

La divisione dei compiti è precisa. Antonio si occupa della sala e dell’accoglienza, mentre Ciro segue la preparazione delle pizze, dalla gestione dell’impasto alla cottura. Due ruoli distinti che concorrono a costruire un progetto nel quale la componente gastronomica e quella organizzativa procedono insieme.

A prima vista, la pizza di Bro richiama la classica ruota di carro napoletana: diametro generoso, profilo riconoscibile, un riferimento immediato alla tradizione partenopea. Ma fermarsi all’aspetto sarebbe riduttivo.

I Tutino utilizzano un impasto indiretto ad alta idratazione. La lavorazione prevede tempi prolungati, mentre la cottura avviene a temperature inferiori rispetto a quelle comunemente associate alla pizza napoletana tradizionale.

Il risultato è una pizza che conserva la riconoscibilità visiva della ruota di carro, ma interviene su alcuni dei suoi parametri tecnici.

Bro, con il locale a Piazza Mercato a Napoli, genera un flusso importante in una zona dove regna la tradizione più radicata. In una città in cui la pizza è anche memoria collettiva, distinguersi senza perdere il legame con la tradizione non è esercizio banale. Bro ha scelto di lavorare su questo equilibrio: partire da un riferimento familiare al pubblico napoletano e modificarlo dall’interno.

L’augurio è che possano ampliare la loro sala: seppur cambiando location, siamo certi abbiano già saputo dimostrare che i posti più belli sono fatti di persone.

La storia dei fratelli Federico e Francesco De Maria comincia da un punto diverso. Il loro claim è I Vesuviani «pizzaioli da zero generazioni». Nessuna dinastia da rivendicare, nessuna tradizione familiare da proseguire. Il loro percorso nasce dalla panificazione e dalla preparazione di pizze al taglio (scuola Bonci) per poi trasformarsi in un progetto di pizzeria.

La prima sede apre nel 2018 a Castello di Cisterna. Nel 2023 arriva quella di Casoria: Federico guida stabilmente il secondo locale, mentre Francesco segue la sede originaria.

La differenza rispetto a Bro è evidente soprattutto nella struttura del menu.

Per i Tutino la pizza è a ruota di carro, senza sottoinsiemi. Per I Vesuviani la pizza tonda napoletana non è il centro attorno al quale ruota ogni scelta. Condivide la scena con pizze in pala, in teglia, padellini e mattonelle.

È qui che si riconosce l’eredità della panificazione. La familiarità con le farine, le fermentazioni e le differenti strutture degli impasti permette di costruire una proposta che  considera la pizza (non solo la tonda) parte di una vetrina più ampia. La pizzeria diventa così uno spazio in cui convivono tecniche e interpretazioni.

È il senso della «Repubblica democratica della pizza»: non un menu senza identità, ma una pizzeria che non attribuisce a un solo formato il diritto di rappresentare tutto il mondo della pizza. La varietà non è un’aggiunta decorativa, bensì una componente strutturale della proposta.

Anche la crescita delle due sedi racconta la capacità di intercettare un pubblico ampio. I due locali dispongono di molti posti a sedere che consentono un significativo ricambio di clienti anche nelle serate infrasettimanali.

Bro e I Vesuviani si sono affacciati alle classifiche di settore. Ma questo dato, da solo, non è mai stato utile a definire il valore di una pizzeria, né a misurarne la capacità di conquistare il pubblico. Ancora una volta vi proponiamo una ri-lettura della Brunzo sul tema.

Le classifiche sono strumenti utili per orientarsi, ma non esauriscono la complessità di una pizzeria. Riconoscimento e successo possono incontrarsi, ma non coincidono necessariamente.

I Tutino scelgono di mantenere il riferimento visivo. La loro identità si costruisce proprio nello spazio tra ciò che il pubblico riconosce e ciò che il prodotto propone di diverso.

I Vesuviani percorrono una strada differente. La loro identità nasce dalla pluralità dei formati e degli stili, come se il Vesuvio non fosse semplicemente la vista ma l’affaccio sul mondo.

Ecco perché abbiamo definito Bro e I Vesuviani talenti indiscutibili di una nuova Napoli: non perché rappresentino una rottura assoluta con il passato, ma perché dimostrano che il panorama della pizza partenopea non è immobile. La tradizione resta un riferimento fondamentale, ma non può diventare un recinto entro il quale ogni nuova idea debba chiedere il permesso di esistere.

I due progetti, pur diversi, condividono questa consapevolezza. Non cercano di essere uguali agli altri e non hanno bisogno di dichiarare guerra alla tradizione per costruire una propria identità. La conoscono, la utilizzano come punto di partenza e scelgono dove intervenire.

Pizzeria I Vesuviani. Via Madonnelle, 65, 80030 Castello di Cisterna NA. Telefono: 081 329 6996. Instagram

Bro. di Ciro e Antonio Tutino. Piazza Mercato, 222b, 80142 Napoli NA. Telefono: 081 379 7908. Instagram

La mia missione è semplice: trovare posti che meritino davvero di essere visitati. Sono sempre alla ricerca di locali che sappiano sorprendermi e mi piace raccontare il cibo senza troppi giri di parole, con curiosità e spirito critico, perché sono convinto che siano i piccoli dettagli a fare la differenza. Ho un debole per i dolci: il dessert è sempre gradito... soprattutto se è più di uno.

#35903. How Software Boundaries Are The Most Important Skill for Developers

No matter how big a software system gets, it will still have a boundary. This boundary separates things inside the system from those outside it. In fact, you’d have noticed that dividing a large system into multiple components can have some great benefits. However, deciding how the system should be divided requires skill and understanding. Experience is the best teacher in such cases. But there are also some strategies that can help.

A good software boundary keeps an application’s responsibilities, its rules, and the details needed to apply those rules together. Parts of the system outside this boundary can talk to things inside the boundary only through a clear pathway. This means that the skill of deciding boundaries requires you to have an idea of which responsibilities should be bunched together. Also, which dependencies should exist between them.

In this article, we’ll learn some key strategies that can help a developer make the right boundary-related decisions for the systems they are working on.
